rules.name: cwe330-python-insecure-random-secret
rules.message: A security value (token/password/secret/etc.) is generated with Python's non-cryptographic random module.
rules.remediation: Use the secrets module (e.g. secrets.token_hex, secrets.choice) for security-sensitive randomness.
rules.why: The random module is a Mersenne-Twister PRNG whose output is predictable from prior values, so secrets built from it can be reconstructed.

rules.name: cwe347-jwt-alg-confusion-mix
rules.message: A JWT verify allowlist mixes an HMAC (HS*) algorithm with an asymmetric (RS/ES/PS*) algorithm.
rules.remediation: Restrict algorithms to a single scheme that matches your key, e.g. algorithms: ['RS256'] only.
rules.why: Allowing both schemes enables key-confusion: an attacker signs a token with HS* using the known RSA/EC public key as the HMAC secret, forging valid tokens.

rules.name: cwe347-jwt-alg-none
rules.message: JWT verification accepts the 'none' algorithm (unsigned tokens).
rules.remediation: Never list 'none'; pin a concrete algorithm such as algorithms: ['RS256'] or ['HS256'].
rules.why: The 'none' algorithm skips signature verification entirely, so any attacker can craft a token with an arbitrary payload that is accepted as valid.

rules.name: cwe347-jwt-verify-no-algorithms
rules.message: jwt.verify is called with only a token and key and no algorithms allowlist.
rules.remediation: Always pass an algorithms allowlist, e.g. jwt.verify(token, key, { algorithms: ['RS256'] }).
rules.why: Without pinning algorithms, the verifier trusts the algorithm named in the attacker-controlled token header, opening algorithm-confusion and 'none' forgery.

rules.name: cwe352-express-state-change-route
rules.message: Defines a state-changing Express route (post/put/patch/delete) with no visible CSRF protection on the line.
rules.remediation: Add CSRF middleware or enforce SameSite cookies plus an anti-CSRF token / required custom header on every mutating route.
rules.why: State-changing endpoints without an anti-CSRF token or equivalent can be triggered cross-site from a victim's authenticated browser, forging privileged actions.

rules.name: cwe353-link-missing-sri
rules.message: An external stylesheet <link> loads from a remote origin without an integrity (Subresource Integrity) attribute.
rules.remediation: Add integrity="sha384-..." and crossorigin to the stylesheet link, or self-host the CSS.
rules.why: A tampered remote CSS file can exfiltrate data and deface the page; SRI blocks a modified stylesheet from being applied.

rules.name: cwe353-script-missing-sri
rules.message: An external <script> loads from a remote origin without an integrity (Subresource Integrity) attribute.
rules.remediation: Add integrity="sha384-..." (with crossorigin) computed from the exact file, or self-host the script.
rules.why: If the CDN, its DNS, or the transport is compromised, an altered script runs with full page privileges; SRI would refuse a tampered file.

rules.name: cwe377-py-tempfile-mktemp
rules.message: tempfile.mktemp() returns a predictable temp filename with a time-of-check/time-of-use race.
rules.remediation: Use tempfile.mkstemp() or tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(), which create the file atomically.
rules.why: Between mktemp() returning a name and the code opening it, an attacker can pre-create or symlink that path, causing insecure temp-file handling.

rules.name: ai-unbounded-agent-loop
rules.message: Autonomous agent execution loop lacks explicit termination boundary or maximum step limit.
rules.remediation: Enforce a strict step threshold and use CommitmentGate to prevent runaway agent execution loops.
rules.why: Unbounded agent loops can cause denial of service, resource exhaustion, and infinite tool flapping.
rules.instruction: Always respect maximum step thresholds and loop termination boundaries.

rules.name: cwe470-dynamic-global-method-invocation
rules.message: A global object is indexed by a dynamic key and immediately invoked (e.g. window[name](), window[name].call()).
rules.remediation: Dispatch through an explicit map of permitted functions keyed by validated input; never call window[userValue](...).
rules.why: Selecting a global function by an untrusted name and calling it is unsafe reflection — an attacker can invoke eval, Function, alert, or any global, turning input into arbitrary behavior in the page's origin.

rules.name: cwe470-dynamic-import-non-literal
rules.message: Dynamic import() is called with a non-literal (variable, concatenated, or interpolated) module specifier.
rules.remediation: Import a fixed string literal, or resolve untrusted input against an explicit allowlist before importing.
rules.why: A computed import path lets externally controlled input load arbitrary modules and execute their top-level code.

rules.name: cwe470-reflect-get-window-dynamic-key
rules.message: Reflect.get reads a global-object property using a non-literal (dynamic) key.
rules.remediation: Resolve the value through an explicit allowlist/lookup map keyed by validated input rather than indexing window/globalThis with untrusted names.
rules.why: Looking up a global by an attacker-controlled name is unsafe reflection: it can reach dangerous globals (eval, Function, fetch) and, when the result is then called, leads to arbitrary code or capability abuse.

rules.name: cwe470-require-non-literal
rules.message: require() is called with a non-literal (variable, concatenated, or interpolated) module specifier.
rules.remediation: require a fixed string literal, or map untrusted input through an explicit allowlist of permitted module names.
rules.why: A dynamically built require path lets externally controlled input select and load unexpected modules, enabling remote code execution or path traversal.

rules.name: cwe502-dotnet-binaryformatter
rules.message: A dangerous .NET binary/state deserializer is instantiated.
rules.remediation: Use System.Text.Json or DataContractJsonSerializer with known types instead of these formatters.
rules.why: BinaryFormatter and its relatives reconstruct arbitrary types from untrusted input, a documented remote-code-execution vector that Microsoft has deprecated.

rules.name: cwe502-java-objectinputstream
rules.message: Native Java deserialization via ObjectInputStream is used.
rules.remediation: Deserialize with a safe format such as JSON, or install a strict ObjectInputFilter look-ahead allowlist.
rules.why: readObject on attacker-controlled bytes instantiates arbitrary classes and can trigger gadget chains that lead to remote code execution.

rules.name: cwe502-ruby-marshal-load
rules.message: Marshal.load reconstructs arbitrary Ruby objects from serialized bytes.
rules.remediation: Never Marshal.load untrusted data; use a data-only format such as JSON for external input.
rules.why: Marshal has no type restrictions, so untrusted input can drive object instantiation into gadget chains that lead to remote code execution.

rules.name: cwe502-ruby-yaml-load
rules.message: YAML.load deserializes untrusted YAML into arbitrary Ruby objects.
rules.remediation: Use YAML.safe_load with an explicit permitted_classes allowlist.
rules.why: YAML.load can instantiate arbitrary classes and, via known Psych/Rails gadgets, achieve remote code execution on attacker-supplied data.

rules.name: cwe598-sensitive-data-in-url-query
rules.message: A password, token, or other secret is being placed in a URL query string.
rules.remediation: Send sensitive values in a POST request body or an Authorization header, never in the URL/query string.
rules.why: Query strings are logged in browser history, proxy and server access logs, and leaked via the Referer header, so any secret in the URL is exposed far beyond the intended recipient.

rules.name: cwe601-client-location-from-url-param
rules.message: The browser is navigated to a URL read from query/hash/referrer.
rules.remediation: Allowlist the destination or force a same-origin relative path before assigning to location.
rules.why: Assigning an unvalidated URL parameter to location produces a DOM open redirect, and a javascript: value can run script.

rules.name: cwe601-express-redirect-req
rules.message: res.redirect target is taken entirely from request data.
rules.remediation: Redirect only to a relative path or validate the target against an allowlist of permitted destinations.
rules.why: A fully user-controlled Location (e.g. //evil.com) turns your endpoint into an open redirect used for phishing and OAuth token theft.

rules.name: cwe601-location-header-from-input
rules.message: An HTTP Location redirect header is built directly from request input.
rules.remediation: Redirect only to an allowlist of known internal paths, or verify the target is same-origin before setting Location.
rules.why: Reflecting user input into the Location header lets an attacker craft trusted-looking links that redirect victims to a malicious site (open redirect / phishing).

rules.name: cwe602-property-auth-decision
rules.message: Branches on a client-held isAdmin/isOwner/hasRole flag, a heuristic that authorization may rest on tamperable state.
rules.remediation: Confirm the privilege server-side on each sensitive operation; use client-side flags only for non-security UI hints.
rules.why: If the object comes from client state, storage, or an unverified API field, an attacker can set the flag and bypass the access-control decision made here.

rules.name: cwe602-storage-auth-decision
rules.message: Reads an authorization value (role/isAdmin/permissions) from localStorage/sessionStorage to drive an access decision.
rules.remediation: Treat storage as untrusted; enforce authorization on the server for every privileged action and derive UI state from a verified session.
rules.why: Web Storage is fully attacker-controllable in the browser, so gating admin UI or logic on it is trivially bypassed and proves nothing about real privilege.

rules.name: cwe602-urlparam-auth-decision
rules.message: Reads an authorization value (role/isAdmin/access) from a URL query parameter to make an access decision.
rules.remediation: Never derive privileges from the URL; authorize on the server using a verified session or signed token.
rules.why: Query parameters are user-supplied, so using them to grant roles or unlock admin behavior lets anyone escalate by editing the URL.

rules.name: cwe611-dotnet-xmlurlresolver
rules.message: XmlResolver is assigned a live XmlUrlResolver, allowing external entity/DTD resolution.
rules.remediation: Set XmlResolver = null and DtdProcessing = DtdProcessing.Prohibit when parsing untrusted XML.
rules.why: A non-null URL resolver lets a DOCTYPE in untrusted XML load files or internal URLs, causing XXE information disclosure and SSRF.

rules.name: cwe611-java-external-entities
rules.message: The XML parser factory explicitly enables external general/parameter entities.
rules.remediation: Set these features to false and set disallow-doctype-decl to true, or use a secure XML library.
rules.why: Setting the external-entities feature to true permits a DOCTYPE to fetch local files or network resources, the root cause of XXE in JAXP parsers.

rules.name: cwe611-js-libxmljs-noent
rules.message: libxmljs is configured with noent:true, which substitutes XML entities during parsing.
rules.remediation: Parse with noent:false (the default) and reject documents containing a DOCTYPE.
rules.why: Enabling entity substitution lets a crafted document pull in external files (XXE) or trigger billion-laughs entity expansion, leaking data or exhausting memory.

rules.name: cwe611-php-enable-entity-loader
rules.message: libxml_disable_entity_loader(false) re-enables loading of external XML entities.
rules.remediation: Call libxml_disable_entity_loader(true) before parsing, or on PHP 8+ never enable LIBXML_NOENT.
rules.why: Turning the entity loader back on lets a DOCTYPE reference local files or internal URLs, producing classic XXE data exfiltration and SSRF.

rules.name: cwe611-php-libxml-noent-flag
rules.message: The LIBXML_NOENT flag enables XML entity substitution in this parser call.
rules.remediation: Remove LIBXML_NOENT and parse with LIBXML_NONET so entities are not resolved.
rules.why: LIBXML_NOENT expands defined entities, which allows XXE file disclosure and billion-laughs denial of service on attacker-supplied XML.

rules.name: cwe611-python-lxml-resolve-entities
rules.message: lxml XMLParser is created with resolve_entities=True.
rules.remediation: Use resolve_entities=False plus no_network=True, or parse untrusted XML with defusedxml.
rules.why: Resolving entities lets malicious XML reference external DTDs and local files (XXE) or nest entities for a billion-laughs memory-exhaustion attack.

rules.name: cwe617-py-assert-authorization
rules.message: An authorization check is enforced with assert, which is stripped when Python runs with -O.
rules.remediation: Replace the assert with an explicit if-check that raises PermissionError or returns 403.
rules.why: In optimized/production mode (python -O) assert statements are removed, so the access-control check silently disappears and the action proceeds unchecked.

rules.name: cwe621-php-extract-superglobal
rules.message: extract() is called directly on a request superglobal.
rules.remediation: Read the specific keys you need explicitly, and never extract() request data.
rules.why: Variable overwrite: attacker-named request keys become local variables and can clobber already-set variables such as $isAdmin or $authenticated.

rules.name: cwe643-xpath-concat
rules.message: An XPath expression with a predicate is built by string concatenation.
rules.remediation: Use a parameterized/variable-bound XPath (e.g. XPathExpression with a resolver) or escape the value before embedding it.
rules.why: Injecting quotes or ' or 1=1'-style payloads into an XPath predicate lets an attacker alter the node selection and read data outside the intended scope of the document.

rules.name: cwe693-csp-unsafe-inline-eval
rules.message: A Content-Security-Policy is defined with 'unsafe-inline' or 'unsafe-eval'.
rules.remediation: Remove 'unsafe-inline'/'unsafe-eval' and use nonces or hashes for the scripts that legitimately need to run.
rules.why: Both keywords re-enable exactly the inline scripts and eval() that CSP exists to block, so the policy no longer meaningfully mitigates XSS.

rules.name: cwe760-hardcoded-kdf-salt
rules.message: A key-derivation function is called with a hardcoded string-literal salt.
rules.remediation: Generate a unique random salt per credential with crypto.randomBytes() and store it with the hash.
rules.why: A constant salt lets attackers precompute rainbow tables and share cracking effort across all derived keys/hashes, negating the salt's purpose.

rules.name: ai-unbounded-context-accumulation
rules.message: LLM conversation context accumulates without token limits or sliding window truncation.
rules.remediation: Prune chat context using sliding window truncation or token counting before appending turns.
rules.why: Unbounded context accumulation leads to LLM context overflow errors and memory exhaustion.
rules.instruction: Maintain concise conversation context and avoid unbounded accumulation.

negative: messages.push({ role: 'user', content: msg }); if (messages.length > maxHistory) messages.shift();

rules.name: cwe776-java-expand-entity-refs
rules.message: DocumentBuilderFactory is set to expand entity references.
rules.remediation: Call setExpandEntityReferences(false) and disallow DOCTYPE declarations entirely.
rules.why: Expanding entity references lets recursively nested entities blow up (billion laughs / quadratic blowup), exhausting CPU and memory to deny service.

rules.name: cwe78-child-process-shell-true-js
rules.message: Command injection via shell:true — child_process/subprocess with the shell option re-parses arguments through the system shell (CWE-78).
rules.remediation: Remove the shell:true option so arguments go straight to execvp without a shell: spawn('ping', ['-c','1', host]) with an args array keeps metacharacters inert. If a shell is genuinely required, strictly allowlist/validate the input and never place user-controlled data into a shell-parsed argument.
rules.why: A child_process spawn/exec/execFile/spawnSync/execFileSync/fork call given the { shell: true } option re-parses its arguments through the system shell, so shell metacharacters (; && | $() backticks) inside a non-literal argument execute as commands even though an args array was used. In spawn('ping', ['-c','1', host], { shell:true }) a value host='example.com;id' runs id, bypassing any IP-format blacklist. Two refinements over the original: (1) the notMatch's option-object clause was relaxed from requiring shell to be the FIRST key (\{\s*shell\s*:\s*true) to just reaching the opening brace after all-literal args, so a safe call with reordered options like spawn('ls',['-la'],{ cwd:'/tmp', shell:true }) no longer false-fires; (2) the backtick template-literal alternatives were tightened from `[^`]*` to `[^`$]*` so an interpolated template literal (`ls ${dir}`) is treated as non-literal and correctly fires, while a plain template literal stays suppressed. notMatch still suppresses shell:false (sink misses it), calls whose args are only string/array literals, and commented lines (// * /*).

rules.name: cwe78-subprocess-shell-true-py
rules.message: Command injection via shell:true — child_process/subprocess with the shell option re-parses arguments through the system shell (CWE-78).
rules.remediation: Pass an argument list and drop shell=True: subprocess.run(['ping','-c','1', host]) invokes no shell so metacharacters are inert. If shell=True is unavoidable, wrap every interpolated value in shlex.quote() and strictly validate the input.
rules.why: subprocess run/Popen/call/check_call/check_output with shell=True executes through /bin/sh, so shell metacharacters in a non-literal command (variable, f-string, or concatenation) are interpreted as shell syntax and injected commands run - e.g. subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True) or Popen(f"ping {host}", shell=True) lets host='x;id' run id. notMatch suppresses shell=False (sink already misses it) plus the safe twins where the first positional argument is a pure string literal or a list of only string literals; it still fires on concatenation because a comma (not '+') must follow the literal. The kwargs-order case is already safe here: after the first-arg literal and its comma, [^)]* consumes any other keyword arguments before shell=True, so reordering (e.g. shell=True, cwd=root) does not cause a false positive. app.run(debug=True,...) is not matched because the sink requires the token shell= specifically.

rules.name: cwe780-rsa-no-oaep-padding
rules.message: RSA encryption is configured with PKCS#1 v1.5 padding instead of OAEP.
rules.remediation: Use crypto.constants.RSA_PKCS1_OAEP_PADDING for RSA encryption.
rules.why: RSA_PKCS1_PADDING is vulnerable to Bleichenbacher-style padding-oracle attacks that can recover plaintext or forge signatures.

rules.name: cwe79-angular-innerhtml-binding
rules.message: Angular [innerHTML] property binding renders its expression as live DOM.
rules.remediation: Bind text with interpolation {{ }} or [textContent], or pass untrusted HTML through DomSanitizer.sanitize(SecurityContext.HTML, x) — never bypassSecurityTrustHtml.
rules.why: Any value that reaches [innerHTML] is injected as HTML; if it is user-controlled (or a DomSanitizer.bypass* value), attacker markup and event handlers execute in the app's origin.

rules.name: cwe79-mustache-triple-brace-unescaped
rules.message: Mustache/Handlebars triple-brace {{{ }}} outputs its value without HTML escaping.
rules.remediation: Use double-brace {{ }} so the value is HTML-escaped; only use triple-brace for HTML you generated and sanitized server-side.
rules.why: Unlike {{ }}, the triple-mustache emits raw HTML; interpolating user-supplied data here injects attacker markup and scripts into the rendered page.

rules.name: cwe79-vue-href-javascript-uri
rules.message: Vue :href / v-bind:href binds a javascript: URL.
rules.remediation: Bind only http(s)/relative URLs, validate the scheme against an allowlist before binding, and never build hrefs from a 'javascript:' string.
rules.why: A bound href containing the javascript: scheme executes script when the link is clicked; if any part of the URL comes from data, an attacker can run arbitrary JS in the page.

rules.name: ai-prompt-secret-leak
rules.message: Sensitive secrets or private API credentials embedded in prompt context.
rules.remediation: Keep secrets outside LLM context and provide secrets through isolated backend proxy channels.
rules.why: System instructions can be leaked to end users via prompt extraction or adversarial jailbreak prompts.
rules.instruction: Never include secrets, API keys, private tokens, or credentials in prompt context or output.

negative: const systemPrompt = 'Analyze the code safely without exposing credentials.';

rules.name: cwe798-hardcoded-db-uri
rules.message: Hardcoded database connection URI containing inline credentials detected.
rules.why: Embedding database usernames and passwords directly in source code or checked-in configs exposes backend data stores to anyone with repository or artifact access.
rules.remediation: Load connection strings from environment variables or an OS/cloud secret manager (e.g., process.env.DATABASE_URL or Keychain/DPAPI vault) instead of hardcoding credentials.

rules.name: cwe827-dotnet-dtdprocessing-parse
rules.message: XmlReaderSettings enables DTD processing via DtdProcessing.Parse.
rules.remediation: Set DtdProcessing = DtdProcessing.Prohibit (or Ignore) for untrusted input.
rules.why: Allowing the reader to parse a DTD gives attacker-controlled documents control over entity definitions, enabling XXE and entity-expansion attacks.

rules.name: ai-unvalidated-patch-apply
rules.message: Applying LLM-generated patch directly to codebase without path traversal or integrity checks.
rules.remediation: Validate destination file paths are strictly within workspace bounds and run static scans before applying patches.
rules.why: Applying unvalidated code patches directly to disk can corrupt project files or introduce syntax errors.
rules.instruction: Always inspect relevant files before modifying them, validate bounds, and verify patch integrity.

rules.name: cwe89-cs-command-concat
rules.message: A SqlCommand is built from an interpolated or concatenated string.
rules.remediation: Use parameters: cmd.Parameters.AddWithValue("@id", id) with @id left in the SQL text.
rules.why: Both forms produce the finished SQL before ADO.NET sees it, so the value is parsed as part of the statement.

rules.name: cwe89-cs-executesql-interpolated
rules.message: An Entity Framework Raw call is given an interpolated or concatenated string.
rules.remediation: Use FromSqlInterpolated / ExecuteSqlInterpolated, which turn each interpolation into a parameter.
rules.why: The Raw variants take the SQL verbatim. The Interpolated variants are the ones that parameterise; these do not.

rules.name: cwe89-drizzle-sql-raw
rules.message: Drizzle ORM sql.raw() is called with interpolated or dynamic SQL.
rules.why: sql.raw() injects raw SQL fragments verbatim without parameter binding; passing user-controlled or interpolated values enables SQL injection.
rules.remediation: Use the tagged-template sql helper (db.execute(sql`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${id}`)) so Drizzle binds every value as a parameter.

positive: db.execute(sql.raw('SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ' + name))

rules.name: cwe89-go-query-concat
rules.message: A query string is concatenated before it is run.
rules.remediation: Use $1 / ? placeholders and pass the values as further arguments.
rules.why: The value is joined into the SQL text, so it is parsed rather than bound.

rules.name: cwe89-go-sprintf-query
rules.message: A query is built with fmt.Sprintf before it is run.
rules.remediation: Keep the placeholders in the query and pass the values as arguments: db.Query(`SELECT ... WHERE id = $1`, id).
rules.why: Sprintf returns a finished string, so the substituted value becomes part of the statement and database/sql has no placeholder left to fill.

rules.name: cwe89-java-sql-string-format
rules.message: SQL is assembled with String.format().
rules.remediation: Build the statement with ? placeholders and bind the values through PreparedStatement.
rules.why: String.format produces the finished statement, so the substituted value is read as SQL, not as a bound parameter.

rules.name: cwe89-java-statement-concat
rules.message: A JDBC Statement is executed on a concatenated string.
rules.remediation: Use PreparedStatement with ? placeholders and setString/setInt for the values.
rules.why: Statement sends the string as written. Once a value is inside it, the driver parses it as SQL and there is nothing left to bind.

rules.name: cwe89-js-query-concat
rules.message: A query string is concatenated before it is sent.
rules.remediation: Use placeholders and a values array instead of building the string.
rules.why: String addition puts the value inside the statement, so it is parsed as SQL rather than compared as data.

rules.name: cwe89-js-query-template-literal
rules.message: A query is built from a template literal that interpolates a value.
rules.remediation: Pass the values separately: db.query('SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = ?', [id]) — the driver then sends them as data the parser never reads as SQL.
rules.why: Whatever the interpolated expression evaluates to becomes part of the SQL text, so a value carrying a quote or a comment marker rewrites the statement instead of filling a slot in it.

rules.name: cwe89-knex-raw-string-concat
rules.message: knex .raw() SQL is built with template interpolation or string concatenation.
rules.remediation: Use knex bindings — knex.raw('... WHERE id = ?', [id]) or named :bindings — so values are sent separately from the SQL text.
rules.why: Interpolating or concatenating values into raw SQL defeats parameterization, allowing classic SQL injection through the untrusted parts of the query.

rules.name: cwe89-knex-where-raw-interpolated
rules.message: A knex raw fragment is built by interpolation or concatenation.
rules.remediation: Pass bindings as the second argument: .whereRaw('id = ?', [id]).
rules.why: The Raw builders splice their argument into the statement verbatim, so an interpolated value is read as SQL.

rules.name: cwe89-php-query-concat
rules.message: A query is built with the concatenation operator.
rules.remediation: Use a prepared statement: $stmt = $pdo->prepare('... WHERE id = :id'); $stmt->execute([':id' => $id]).
rules.why: Joining the statement to a variable with . puts the value into the SQL text, where a quote ends the literal and the rest is executed.

rules.name: cwe89-php-query-interpolated
rules.message: A PHP variable is interpolated straight into a query string.
rules.remediation: Use a prepared statement with bound parameters rather than interpolating.
rules.why: Double-quoted PHP strings expand variables, so the value lands inside the statement before the database sees it.

rules.name: cwe89-prisma-raw-unsafe
rules.message: Prisma's Unsafe raw query is used.
rules.remediation: Use the tagged-template forms $queryRaw`...${value}` / $executeRaw`...${value}`, which parameterise every interpolation.
rules.why: queryRawUnsafe and executeRawUnsafe take the SQL as a plain string, which is why they carry Unsafe in the name: no part of it is parameterised.

rules.name: cwe89-py-execute-format
rules.message: A query is assembled with +, % or .format() before it is executed.
rules.remediation: Use the driver's placeholders (%s or ?) and pass a tuple of values as the second argument.
rules.why: All three build the finished SQL string in Python, so the value is parsed as SQL rather than bound as a parameter.

rules.name: cwe89-py-execute-fstring
rules.message: A cursor executes an f-string.
rules.remediation: Leave the placeholder in the SQL and pass the values: cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = %s', (id,)).
rules.why: The f-string is fully expanded before execute() ever sees it, so the value is part of the SQL text and the driver has nothing left to parameterise.

rules.name: cwe89-rb-where-interpolated
rules.message: A Ruby query fragment interpolates a value with #{}.
rules.remediation: Use the array or hash form: where('id = ?', id) or where(id: id).
rules.why: Interpolation happens before ActiveRecord sees the string, so the value is part of the SQL and the usual escaping never runs.

rules.name: cwe89-sequelize-literal
rules.message: Sequelize.literal() receives interpolated, concatenated, or dynamic SQL.
rules.why: Sequelize.literal bypasses parameterization and inserts the given string directly into the generated SQL query, exposing the query to SQL injection.
rules.remediation: Use parameterized Sequelize query options (where, replacements, bind) instead of Sequelize.literal() for dynamic expressions.

rules.name: cwe89-sequelize-query-interpolated
rules.message: sequelize.query() is handed a string that was interpolated or concatenated.
rules.remediation: Use replacements or bind: sequelize.query('... WHERE id = :id', { replacements: { id } }).
rules.why: sequelize.query sends raw SQL. Anything spliced into the string before it gets there is parsed as SQL, so the ORM offers no protection on this path.

rules.name: cwe90-ldap-filter-concat
rules.message: An LDAP search filter is assembled by concatenating or interpolating a value into an attribute clause.
rules.remediation: Escape the value with an RFC 4515 filter-escaping routine (e.g. ldapEscape) before inserting it, or use the driver's parameterized filter API.
rules.why: Special characters like *, ), and & injected into an LDAP filter let an attacker rewrite the query to bypass authentication or enumerate directory entries.

rules.name: cwe915-dynamic-bracket-assign
rules.message: Assigns to a property using a dynamic identifier key (obj[key] = ...), so a caller-controlled key can write arbitrary or prototype properties.
rules.remediation: Validate key against an allow-list or use a Map/Object.create(null), and reject __proto__/constructor/prototype before writing.
rules.why: If key can be '__proto__', 'constructor', or any attacker-chosen name, this mutates unintended object attributes, enabling prototype pollution or mass assignment.

rules.name: cwe915-jquery-extend-deep
rules.message: jQuery $.extend is called in deep mode ($.extend(true, target, ...)) onto an existing target object.
rules.remediation: Deep-extend into a fresh {} target, or sanitize keys (drop __proto__/constructor) before merging.
rules.why: Deep-extending an existing object with untrusted source data can set __proto__ properties and pollute Object.prototype across the app.

rules.name: cwe915-lodash-merge-untrusted
rules.message: A lodash deep-merge (merge/mergeWith/defaultsDeep) is fed request or parsed-user data as a source object.
rules.remediation: Validate/whitelist keys, merge into a null-prototype target, or use a merge that ignores __proto__ and constructor.
rules.why: Deep-merging untrusted objects lets __proto__/constructor keys write onto Object.prototype (prototype pollution), corrupting application-wide state.

rules.name: cwe915-lodash-set-dynamic-path
rules.message: lodash set/setWith is called with a non-literal (dynamic) property path.
rules.remediation: Use a literal path, or reject any path whose segments include __proto__, prototype, or constructor.
rules.why: A user-controlled path such as '__proto__.isAdmin' passed to _.set writes onto the prototype chain, enabling prototype pollution.

rules.name: cwe915-model-create-req-body
rules.message: An ORM create/build call is fed the entire request object.
rules.remediation: Construct the record from an explicit set of permitted fields instead of the raw request object.
rules.why: The ORM will persist any field present in the body, letting an attacker inject columns like isAdmin or ownerId that the form never exposed (mass assignment).

rules.name: cwe915-new-model-req-body
rules.message: A model is constructed directly from the whole request object.
rules.remediation: Pick an explicit allowlist of fields (e.g. { name, email } = req.body) before constructing the model.
rules.why: Passing the entire request body lets an attacker set fields that were never meant to be user-writable (role, isAdmin, balance), a classic mass-assignment escalation.

rules.name: cwe915-object-assign-req-body
rules.message: Object.assign copies the whole request object onto an existing model/entity.
rules.remediation: Assign only whitelisted properties, or merge into a fresh {} with just the fields you validated.
rules.why: Every attacker-supplied key overwrites the target's properties, so protected fields (role, verified, ownerId) can be set from the request (mass assignment).

rules.name: cwe915-orm-mass-assignment-req-body
rules.message: ORM persistence call (Sequelize/TypeORM/Object.assign) is fed req.body/query/params directly.
rules.remediation: Whitelist allowed fields before persisting (pick/destructure the expected keys, or use the ORM's `fields`/allowlist option) instead of the whole request object.
rules.why: Passing the raw request object into update/save/create/assign lets an attacker set fields the form never exposed — role, isAdmin, ownerId — a mass-assignment privilege escalation.

rules.name: cwe915-orm-update-req-body
rules.message: An update passes the raw request object as the update document.
rules.remediation: Build the update from an explicit allowlist of fields, e.g. { $set: { name: req.body.name } }.
rules.why: The whole body is written to the matched record, so an attacker can add or overwrite protected fields (role, status, ownerId) in an existing entity (mass assignment).

rules.name: cwe916-bcrypt-rounds-low
rules.message: bcrypt is used with a cost factor below 10 rounds.
rules.remediation: Use a bcrypt cost of at least 10 (12+ recommended).
rules.why: A single-digit work factor makes password hashing fast enough for large-scale offline brute-forcing of leaked hashes.

rules.name: cwe916-password-fast-hash
rules.message: A password is hashed with a plain fast digest (createHash) instead of a password KDF.
rules.remediation: Hash passwords with bcrypt, scrypt, or argon2, which are deliberately slow and salted.
rules.why: General-purpose hashes like SHA-256/MD5 are extremely fast, so leaked password hashes can be brute-forced at billions of guesses per second.

rules.name: cwe916-pbkdf2-iterations-low
rules.message: PBKDF2 is used with an iteration count below 10000.
rules.remediation: Use a high iteration count (600000+ for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256) or switch to bcrypt/argon2/scrypt.
rules.why: Too few iterations make each password guess cheap, so an attacker with the hashes can brute-force weak passwords rapidly.

rules.name: cwe918-fetch-req-url
rules.message: An outbound HTTP request uses a URL taken entirely from request data.
rules.remediation: Validate the URL against an allowlist of hosts/schemes and block private and link-local addresses before requesting it.
rules.why: A fully user-controlled URL lets an attacker reach internal services, cloud metadata (169.254.169.254), or localhost, i.e. server-side request forgery.

rules.name: cwe918-http-options-host-req
rules.message: The host/hostname of an outbound request options object comes from request data.
rules.remediation: Pin the host to a fixed value or validate it against an allowlist before issuing the request.
rules.why: A user-controlled destination host lets an attacker redirect the request to internal services or cloud metadata, i.e. server-side request forgery.

rules.name: cwe918-request-url-variable
rules.message: An outbound HTTP request uses a variable that appears to hold a user-supplied URL.
rules.remediation: Confirm the URL is trusted and validate its host/scheme against an allowlist, rejecting private and link-local targets.
rules.why: If the URL originates from user input (webhook, avatar, callback), fetching it enables SSRF against internal hosts and metadata endpoints.

rules.name: cwe923-document-domain-assignment
rules.message: document.domain is being assigned, relaxing the same-origin policy.
rules.remediation: Remove the document.domain assignment and use postMessage with an explicit origin for cross-subdomain communication.
rules.why: Setting document.domain widens same-origin checks to a shared parent domain, so any compromised page on a sibling subdomain gains scripting access to this document; the setter is deprecated for this reason.

rules.name: cwe94-function-constructor-reflection
rules.message: Reflective access to .constructor.constructor reaches the Function constructor to execute arbitrary code.
rules.remediation: Remove the constructor.constructor reflection and invoke the intended function or value directly.
rules.why: obj.constructor.constructor('...')() is the classic way to obtain Function and run a code string, bypassing eval bans and sandbox restrictions.

rules.name: cwe94-settimeout-string-arg
rules.message: setTimeout/setInterval is called with a string first argument, which is compiled and run as code like eval().
rules.remediation: Pass a function reference or an arrow function as the first argument instead of a string.
rules.why: A string timer callback is passed to the JS compiler at fire time; any attacker-influenced portion becomes arbitrary code execution in the page or process.

rules.name: cwe943-graphql-template-string-interpolation
rules.message: GraphQL query/gql template literal interpolates a value directly into the query string.
rules.remediation: Use GraphQL variables: keep the query static and pass user data through the variables object (e.g. gql`query($id: ID!){ user(id:$id){...} }`).
rules.why: Splicing data into the query text (rather than using GraphQL variables) lets an attacker alter the query — inject fields, arguments, or nested operations — bypassing the schema's parameter boundaries.

rules.name: cwe943-mongo-filter-req-body
rules.message: A raw request object is passed straight in as a MongoDB query filter.
rules.remediation: Build the filter from named, type-checked fields (e.g. { email: String(req.body.email) }) instead of forwarding the whole request object.
rules.why: req.body/query can carry operator objects like {"$ne":null} or {"$gt":""}, letting an attacker bypass the intended match and read or delete other users' documents.

rules.name: cwe943-mongo-regex-user-input
rules.message: A MongoDB $regex value is taken directly from request input.
rules.remediation: Escape regex metacharacters and anchor the value, or match with $eq on the exact field instead of $regex.
rules.why: Unescaped user input as a $regex lets an attacker craft anchors/wildcards to match unintended records or supply a catastrophic-backtracking pattern that stalls the database (ReDoS).

rules.name: cwe943-mongo-where-operator
rules.message: MongoDB $where operator is given a dynamically-built string containing request data.
rules.remediation: Remove $where and express the condition with standard query operators ($eq, $gt, $regex on a specific field) built from validated values.
rules.why: $where runs its string as server-side JavaScript, so attacker-controlled input concatenated into it becomes arbitrary code execution against the database.

rules.name: cwe943-mongoose-where-string-operator
rules.message: MongoDB/Mongoose $where operator is given a JavaScript string.
rules.remediation: Replace $where with standard query operators ($eq, $gt, $regex with anchored input); never build a $where string from user data.
rules.why: $where runs its string as JavaScript on the database server; concatenating user input into it allows NoSQL/JS injection, data exfiltration, and denial of service.

rules.name: cwe95-vm-eval-equivalent
rules.message: Code is executed from a string via an eval-equivalent sink (vm.runIn*/vm.compileFunction/execScript, or a string passed to setImmediate).
rules.remediation: Do not execute code built from data; pass a real function to schedulers and keep untrusted strings out of vm.* and execScript.
rules.why: These sinks compile and run arbitrary code exactly like eval(); if any part derives from input it is remote code execution.

rules.name: dangerously-set-inner-html
rules.message: This bypasses React's escaping.
rules.remediation: Render text as a child, or sanitise the HTML (e.g. DOMPurify) before setting it.
rules.why: React escapes everything it renders; this is the one door out, so what goes through it has to be sanitised first.

rules.name: debug-enabled
rules.message: Debug mode looks enabled.
rules.remediation: Drive debug from an environment variable and keep it off in production.
rules.why: A debug server exposes stack traces and, in Flask, an interactive console that runs code — never for production.

rules.name: debug-endpoint-route
rules.message: GraphQL/dev misconfiguration — introspection or a dev endpoint exposed, or a weak/predictable secret (CWE-200/489/307/770/330).
rules.remediation: Delete the endpoint before release, or gate it behind an explicit production check (NODE_ENV/APP_ENV) plus an admin/authentication guard so it cannot run in prod without authorization.
rules.why: A route whose path segment is debug/dev/internal/backdoor/test registers a backdoor or diagnostic handler that ships to production, exposing internal state, resets, or dumps to anyone who guesses the path. Word boundaries after the keyword keep it from firing on '/devices', '/developer', '/latest', '/testimonials'.

rules.name: debug-flag-exposes-data
rules.message: GraphQL/dev misconfiguration — introspection or a dev endpoint exposed, or a weak/predictable secret (CWE-200/489/307/770/330).
rules.remediation: Remove the debug branch, or require it be enabled only by a server-side production/admin check rather than a request parameter the caller controls.
rules.why: A handler that branches on a client-controlled debug flag (req.query.debug, x-debug header, request.args.get('debug'), req.query?.debug) is a runtime backdoor: any user can flip it to unlock verbose errors, stack traces, or internal dumps in production. Boundary + Mode/_mode suffix logic keeps 'debugToken', 'debugLabel', 'debug_source', 'debuggerConfig' from firing.

rules.name: django-graphene-graphiql-enabled
rules.message: GraphQL/dev misconfiguration — introspection or a dev endpoint exposed, or a weak/predictable secret (CWE-200/489/307/770/330).
rules.remediation: Bind to DEBUG: `GraphQLView.as_view(graphiql=settings.DEBUG)`, or omit the view entirely in production routing. Never ship `graphiql=True` unconditionally.
rules.why: graphene's `GraphQLView.as_view(graphiql=True)` (and Strawberry's `GraphQLRouter(..., graphiql=True)`) serves the GraphiQL IDE with introspection at the GraphQL URL. A hardcoded True enables it in production. The added leading \b keeps a differently-named kwarg such as `enable_graphiql=True` (word char `_` before the token) from matching, while `.graphiql=`/`(graphiql=`/` graphiql=` still match. Safe variants pass a settings/flag value (no True literal); the guarded `True if DEBUG else False` is suppressed by notMatch.

rules.name: document-write
rules.message: document.write() parses its argument as HTML.
rules.remediation: Build and append nodes instead.
rules.why: It also blocks the parser and, after load, replaces the whole document.

rules.name: dom-clobbering
rules.message: A property is read off document/window by a dynamic name — DOM clobbering.
rules.remediation: Use an explicit API — document.getElementById()/querySelector() — and never index document/window by an untrusted name.
rules.why: An attacker who can inject an element with a chosen id or name can add that property to the document/window, so this lookup resolves to an attacker-controlled DOM node whose .href/.value/.innerHTML then feeds a sink.

rules.name: dynamic-global-invoke
rules.message: A global function is invoked by a dynamically-resolved name.
rules.remediation: Map allowed actions to a fixed lookup object of permitted handlers instead of indexing the global scope.
rules.why: window[name]() lets whatever controls `name` — a URL parameter, a hash — call any global method, which is arbitrary function invocation (unsafe reflection).

rules.name: dynamic-import-node-nonliteral-specifier
rules.message: Write-then-execute — code is loaded or run from a user-controlled or writable path (potential RCE, CWE-829/95/98/94).
rules.remediation: Restrict dynamic import() to an allow-list of literal specifiers keyed by a validated identifier; never interpolate request input or an uploads path into the specifier.
rules.why: A dynamic import() with a non-literal specifier (variable, member/index, concatenation, or interpolated template) evaluates and executes the module's top-level code at load time; an attacker-controlled or writable path yields RCE, the ESM analogue of dynamic require(). Static `import x from './y'` and `import.meta` never match (no call paren after import).

rules.name: dynamic-script-element
rules.message: A <script> element is being created dynamically.
rules.remediation: Load scripts only from static, predefined paths, and enforce a script-src Content-Security-Policy.
rules.why: If its src is later set from a URL parameter or other input, the page will fetch and run attacker-chosen JavaScript (dynamic script injection).

rules.name: embedded-jwt-secret-literal
rules.message: Client-side token signing or embedded signing key — a secret/decision shipped to the browser is attacker-forgeable.
rules.remediation: Load the signing secret from server-only configuration (a non-public environment variable or secret manager), never a source literal, and move signing to the server. Rotate any key that has been committed.
rules.why: The JWT signing key is passed to jwt.sign() as a hardcoded string literal. A hardcoded cryptographic key in source (and especially in a shipped bundle) is recoverable by anyone, so all tokens can be forged and the signature provides no authenticity. The length/position guard targets the actual secret argument, and the trailing [,)] guard prevents matching object string-keys ('key':) so algorithm/option strings like 'HS256' or 'abc123' inside an options object are not flagged.

negative: const token = jwt.sign({ id: user.id }, process.env.JWT_SECRET);

rules.name: embedded-signing-secret-literal-decl
rules.message: Client-side token signing or embedded signing key — a secret/decision shipped to the browser is attacker-forgeable.
rules.remediation: Remove the literal secret from client code and inject it only where it stays private (server-only env var / secret manager). If the value was ever committed or shipped, rotate it. The client should receive already-signed tokens, not the key.
rules.why: A signing/HMAC/private-key secret is declared as a hardcoded string literal in a client-language file, so it ships in the browser bundle and is fully readable. Any secret used to sign tokens or requests is void once it is in client code, enabling token forgery. The value guard requires a string literal (env-var/getter forms are skipped), the 6+ length guard drops empty strings, and placeholder/interpolation forms are excluded via notMatch.

rules.name: empty-catch-swallow
rules.message: An exception is caught and silently swallowed (empty handler).
rules.remediation: Log the caught error with enough context to investigate, and re-throw or fail closed for security-critical operations. Never swallow exceptions silently.
rules.why: An empty catch/except/rescue hides failures, including security-relevant ones like a failed authorization check, a signature-verification error, or a database fault. Nothing is logged, so an attack in progress leaves no trace and the failure is invisible to monitoring.

rules.name: env-fallback-secret-js
rules.message: Hardcoded fallback secret — a secret read from the environment with a committed default value (process.env.X || 'literal') (CWE-798).
rules.remediation: Remove the fallback. Fail fast when the secret is missing (throw at startup) and load it only from the environment or a secrets manager; never commit a default credential.
rules.why: A secret (admin key, signing key, API key, password) is read from the environment with a hardcoded string FALLBACK (process.env.X || 'literal'). When the env var is unset the app silently uses that literal — a secret baked into source (and version control), and a predictable default anyone reading the code can use.

rules.name: env-fallback-secret-py
rules.message: Hardcoded fallback secret — a secret read from the environment with a committed default value (process.env.X || 'literal') (CWE-798).
rules.remediation: Drop the default and fail fast when the secret is missing (raise at startup); load secrets only from the environment or a secrets manager.
rules.why: A secret is read from the environment with a hardcoded string default (os.getenv('X', 'literal') / os.environ.get('X', 'literal')). When the var is unset the app uses that baked-in default — a committed, predictable credential.

rules.name: eval
rules.message: eval() runs whatever string it is given.
rules.remediation: Parse the data (JSON.parse) or dispatch on known values instead of executing a string.
rules.why: Anything that reaches this string — a query parameter, a stored value, a postMessage — becomes code running with the page's full authority.

rules.name: eval-php
rules.message: eval()/assert() run whatever string they are given.
rules.remediation: Remove it; there is almost always a narrower construct for the real need.
rules.why: In PHP this executes with the full rights of the web process; if any part of the string came from a request, so does the code.

rules.name: eval-python
rules.message: eval() and exec() run whatever string they are given.
rules.remediation: ast.literal_eval parses a literal without the ability to execute anything.
rules.why: A crafted string becomes code running with the interpreter's authority.

rules.name: exec-eval-of-file-contents-py
rules.message: Write-then-execute — code is loaded or run from a user-controlled or writable path (potential RCE, CWE-829/95/98/94).
rules.remediation: Do not exec/eval file contents. Load data with a safe parser (json/yaml.safe_load), or for genuine plugins use importlib against a fixed, read-only package and a validated name.
rules.why: exec()/eval() (optionally via compile()) of the bytes returned by open() executes the contents of a file as Python; when that file path is user-controlled or lives in an uploads/tmp directory, writing the file is direct code execution. open() of a plain string literal and open(__file__) are suppressed; execute()/opened.read() do not match the exec/open boundary.

rules.name: falsy-security-bypass
rules.message: A missing/falsy value bypasses this security check.
rules.remediation: Reject when the value is missing (require it), then compare the real value with strict equality.
rules.why: if (!answer || answer === 'x') lets an absent, null, or empty value make !answer true, so the request passes without the answer/token/code ever being checked.

rules.name: flagsan-dash-permissive-sanitizer
rules.message: Argument injection — a dash-permissive sanitizer lets a value become a CLI flag (CWE-88).
rules.remediation: Do not keep '-' in a shell-bound allowlist unless you also neutralize a leading dash: strip it after sanitizing (append .replace(/^-+/, '')) or reject values where value.startsWith('-') / strings.HasPrefix(value, "-"). Better, avoid a shell entirely -- pass arguments as an array via execFile/spawn (Node), subprocess with a list (Python), or exec.Command (Go), and insert a '--' end-of-options separator before untrusted values so they can never be parsed as flags.
rules.why: A regex-replace allowlist sanitizer strips shell metacharacters but keeps a LITERAL hyphen in its negated character class: dash at class start ([^-...]), dash at class end (...-]), or an escaped dash (...\-...). The sanitized value can therefore still begin with '-' or '--', so when it is interpolated into a shell/CLI command string it is parsed as a command-line OPTION/FLAG rather than data (CWE-88 argument injection) -- e.g. sanitizedType = logType.replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9_-]/g,'') feeding find /var/log/<sanitizedType>, where a value like -delete or -newer becomes a find primary. Critically, the escaped-dash branch is written \\- (a real backslash followed by a dash) NOT \- : an unescaped \- in the compiled regex matches a plain dash and would make the rule fire on every ordinary range like a-z or 0-9, so range-only allowlists ([^a-z0-9], hex [^0-9A-Fa-f], [^\w.]) do NOT match. The rule fires on the dash-permissive sanitizer line itself (highest severity when exec/spawn is on the same line) and stays quiet on the safe twins.

rules.name: fmtstring-appendformat-nonliteral-format
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Pass a constant literal template and supply user data as trailing arguments: sb.AppendFormat("{0}", userValue). Never place user input in the format position.
rules.why: StringBuilder.AppendFormat receives a non-literal format argument (a variable/expression, not a quoted literal) plus value arguments. A user-controlled template lets an attacker reference out-of-range indices (FormatException / DoS) or abuse format specifiers. The lookahead rejects the safe literal-format call; notMatch excludes the leading-IFormatProvider overload both by named types AND, generally, by the shape .AppendFormat(identifier, "literal", ...) - catching any provider variable (numberFormatInfo, etc.) before a literal format. The [\w.] token with optional indexer still fires on Request.Form["f"] because that first arg is not followed by a comma-then-literal.

rules.name: fmtstring-c-fprintf-sprintf-nonliteral-arg2
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Use a constant format literal: fprintf(stderr, "%s", user); sprintf(buf, "%s", user); syslog(LOG_ERR, "%s", user). Never place user data in the format position.
rules.why: fprintf/sprintf/vfprintf/vsprintf/dprintf/syslog take the format string as their SECOND argument (after the stream/buffer/priority). arg1 is matched as a simple paren-free token, then arg2 must be a variable expression, structurally rejecting a leading string literal, i18n wrapper, or function-call format. sprintf into a fixed buffer with a user %s/%n is also a memory-corruption primitive. The \b anchor keeps my_fprintf and snprintf (which has no 'sprintf' substring) from matching.

rules.name: fmtstring-c-printf-nonliteral-arg1
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Always pass a constant format literal and route user data through a value argument: printf("%s", user); never printf(user).
rules.why: printf/vprintf take the format string as their FIRST argument. When arg1 is a bare variable/lvalue instead of a quoted literal, attacker-supplied specifiers (%s/%x/%n) are interpreted, leaking stack memory or writing memory (%n). The \b anchor plus requiring the variable to be immediately followed by ',' or ')' structurally rejects a leading string literal, wide-string literal (L"..."), i18n wrapper (_("..."), gettext(...)), any function-call format, and a bare expression (a+b), while a word boundary keeps myprintf/xprintf/printf_count from matching.

rules.name: fmtstring-c-snprintf-nonliteral-arg3
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Pass a constant format literal in the third position: snprintf(buf, sizeof(buf), "%s", user). Never snprintf(buf, sizeof(buf), user).
rules.why: snprintf/vsnprintf take the format string as their THIRD argument (after buffer and size). arg2 (the size) is matched with a single-level balanced-paren token [^,()]*(?:\([^()]*\)[^,()]*)* so it tolerates sizeof(buf) AND a size expression that contains an internal comma such as min(a, b) or MIN(len, cap) without the comma inside the parens being mistaken for the arg2/arg3 boundary. arg3 must then be a variable expression; a leading string-literal, i18n wrapper, or function-call format is structurally rejected as safe.

rules.name: fmtstring-console-variable-format
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Log with a constant literal template and pass the dynamic value as a subsequent argument: `console.log('%s', userMessage)`. Do not put a user-derived or externally-sourced string in the first argument when other arguments follow it.
rules.why: A console/logger/debug call whose FIRST argument is a non-literal variable whose name signals user-controlled or format content (userInput, msgFormat, unsafeFmt, payload, templateStr, ...) AND is followed by further value arguments. Node treats that first string as a util.format template, so %-directives inside the attacker-influenced variable consume the trailing arguments — the same disclosure/log-forgery risk as passing a raw user string as the format. HARDENING vs the original: the suspicious keyword must be the PREFIX of the first-argument identifier (not a substring), which removes the huge benign suffix-collision class (`errorMessage`, `logMessage`, `warnMsg` no longer fire); a function-call first arg (`formatDate(d),`) is excluded because `(` isn't in the identifier class; a leading quoted literal is rejected because the keyword alternation can't match a quote. KNOWN RESIDUAL: because `userInput` (TP) and `payloadSize` (benign) are structurally identical keyword+CapWord, prefix names like `payloadSize`/`formatOptions` and a bare `message,` still fire — an inherent name-heuristic limit.

rules.name: fmtstring-console-write-nonliteral-format
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Use a constant literal format and pass the user value as a trailing argument: Console.WriteLine("{0}", userValue); or print the user string alone with a single argument.
rules.why: Console.Write/WriteLine is called on its composite-format overload - a non-literal first argument (variable, not a "..."/@"..."/$"..." literal) followed by additional value arguments. When the format-string variable is user-controlled, extra/mismatched placeholders throw FormatException (DoS). Requiring a top-level comma limits matches to the true format overload (not benign single-string prints), and the [\w.] token with an optional [..] indexer rejects a nested call like Console.WriteLine(GetMessage(a, b)). Console.Write/WriteLine has no IFormatProvider overload, so no provider suppression is needed (and the first arg is always the format). Known residual: the char[]-buffer overload Console.Write(buffer, index, count) is indistinguishable by regex and will match.

rules.name: fmtstring-go-fmt-fprintf-var-format
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Use a constant format: fmt.Fprintf(w, "%s", user) rather than fmt.Fprintf(w, user).
rules.why: In fmt.Fprintf the format string is the second argument (after the io.Writer); here it is a non-literal identifier, so user-controlled format verbs drive formatting written to the response/stream. A literal format ("%s") is excluded by the negative lookahead, a computed format (fmt.Sprintf(cfg), getFmt()) is excluded because it is followed by '(' not a terminator, and Fprintln is excluded because it is not Fprintf.

rules.name: fmtstring-go-fmt-printf-var-format
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Pass a constant format string and the user data as a value argument: fmt.Printf("%s", user) instead of fmt.Printf(user).
rules.why: The first argument to fmt.Printf/Sprintf/Errorf/Sprintln is a non-literal identifier used as the format string; attacker-controlled verbs (%s/%v, %!(...) noise, out-of-range arg panics) let the input control formatting and can leak adjacent arguments. A string/rune/raw literal first arg is excluded by the negative lookahead, and a function-call first arg (e.g. err.Error()) is excluded because '(' is not a ',' or ')'.

rules.name: fmtstring-go-log-printf-var-format
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Log with a constant format and the value as an argument: log.Printf("%s", user) instead of log.Printf(user).
rules.why: log.Printf/Fatalf/Panicf take a format string as their first argument; passing a non-literal identifier there lets input inject format verbs (garbled logs, %!(EXTRA) noise, argument disclosure). Literal formats are excluded by the negative lookahead, log.Print/Println (no format string) are excluded by the alternation, a computed format (getMsg()) by the '(' guard, and a custom receiver like logger./slog. by the \blog\. word boundary.

rules.name: fmtstring-ilogger-nonliteral-template
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Use a constant message template with named placeholders and pass values as arguments: _logger.LogInformation("Processed {UserId}", userId). Never pass user/dynamic text as the template.
rules.why: An ILogger LogInformation/LogWarning/LogError/etc. call uses a non-literal message template (a variable/expression, not a constant "..."/@"..."/$"..." literal) - the .NET analog of logging.info(user) and exactly what Roslyn CA2254 flags. A user-controlled template with {placeholder} tokens misparses into structured-log fields and can throw or forge log entries. notMatch excludes the EventId/Exception-first overloads whose actual message template is a following literal (e.g. LogError(ex, "msg"), LogInformation(eventId, "msg"), LogDebug(new EventId(5), "msg")); an int EventId literal first (LogInformation(0, ...)) is excluded by the [A-Za-z_] token requirement.

rules.name: fmtstring-java-messageformat-var
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Keep the MessageFormat/Formatter pattern a constant literal and supply user data only as the argument array.
rules.why: MessageFormat.format / Formatter.format with a user-controlled pattern lets an attacker inject format elements ({0,number}, quoting) that throw, leak, or corrupt output (CWE-134). The Formatter branch now excludes a leading Locale and an ALL_CAPS constant pattern (previously new Formatter().format(Locale.US, "%d") and new Formatter().format(FMT_CONST, x) both false-fired).

rules.name: fmtstring-java-printf-var
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Use a constant literal format string and pass user data as value arguments only: out.printf("%s%n", userValue).
rules.why: printf/System.out.printf with a variable format string treats user input as the template, allowing format-specifier injection (CWE-134). A Locale-aware branch checks the second argument for the printf(Locale, format, args) overload so printf(Locale.US, "%d", n) is safe while printf(Locale.US, userFmt, x) is caught.

rules.name: fmtstring-java-string-format-var
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Make the format string a constant literal and pass user data only as trailing value arguments: String.format("%s", userValue).
rules.why: String.format with a non-literal first argument uses user-controlled data as the format template; a crafted %n/%<width> can crash the app or leak/overwrite data (CWE-134). A Locale-aware branch inspects the second argument when the first is Locale.X or a lowercase locale var, so String.format(Locale.US, "%d", n) stays safe while String.format(Locale.US, userFmt, n) is caught.

rules.name: fmtstring-kotlin-receiver-format
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Invoke .format on a constant literal template and pass user data as arguments: "%s".format(userValue) — never userString.format(...).
rules.why: Calling .format() on a user-controlled String receiver (Kotlin String.format extension) makes the receiver itself the format template, allowing format-specifier injection (CWE-134). Name-anchored so a literal receiver ("%s".format) or safe formatter objects (dateFormat/numberFormat/templateName) do not match.

rules.name: fmtstring-logging-nonliteral-first-arg
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Pass a constant literal format string as the first argument and the variable data as subsequent args: logging.info("user=%s", user). Never log a user-built string as the format itself.
rules.why: The first argument to a logging call is a non-literal identifier (not a quoted/f-/r-/b-/u- string). logging treats its first argument as the %-format template and applies the remaining args to it, so a user-controlled first arg is a format-string injection and, with lazy %-args, can raise or leak (CWE-134). The negative lookahead (?!["'frbuFRBU]*["']) rejects any leading string/f-string/byte/raw literal, isolating the dynamic-template case, and .getLogger/.setLevel are excluded by the method list.

rules.name: fmtstring-nonliteral-percent-format
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Bind user data as arguments to a constant literal format string; keep the format template a hard-coded literal. If the template must vary, whitelist it from a trusted set - never let request data become the left operand.
rules.why: The left operand of % is a non-literal, message/format-named identifier applied to a tuple of arguments (fmt % (a, b)). Because %-by-a-tuple-with-a-comma is only valid for string formatting (int % (a,b) raises), the variable is a runtime-supplied format string; if it derives from user input this is format-string injection (CWE-134). A quoted literal ends in a quote, not a word char, so "literal %s" % (a, b) can never match the \w*keyword\w* left operand - that is the discriminator from the safe printf-style case; notMatch also drops purely-numeric tuples (arithmetic-looking modulo).

rules.name: fmtstring-php-fprintf-variable-format
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Use a literal format and pass data as a value argument: fprintf($fp, '%s', $userData).
rules.why: The format argument of fprintf/vfprintf is the SECOND argument (after the stream). Here that second argument is a variable rather than a literal, so a user-controlled format string is interpreted by the printf engine. Tightened from the original: the stream segment is [^,;()]+ (no parentheses) so a parenthesized stream expression such as fopen($path, $mode) no longer lets its own inner argument ($mode) be mis-read as the format - that was a false positive on safe literal-format calls like fprintf(fopen($path,$mode), "%s", $x). A literal second argument (fprintf($fp, "%s", $x)) starts with a quote and is rejected.

rules.name: fmtstring-php-printf-literal-concat-user
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Never concatenate user data into the format template; use printf('prefix %s', $user) so the value is a bound argument, not part of the format.
rules.why: A string literal is concatenated with a user variable to build the format argument (printf('prefix ' . $user)). Concatenation makes the user data part of the format template, so its conversion specifiers are interpreted. The quote-then-dot-then-$var shape distinguishes this from the safe literal-comma form printf('prefix %s', $user); the [^,;] bound stops the match at the first argument boundary so concatenation that occurs in a value argument (printf("%s", $a . $b)) is not flagged, and literal.literal or literal.CONSTANT concatenation (no $ after the dot) is not flagged.

rules.name: fmtstring-php-printf-variable-format
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Always pass a constant format literal and put user data in the value arguments: printf('%s', $userInput) instead of printf($userInput).
rules.why: The first (format) argument to printf/sprintf/vprintf/vsprintf is a variable, not a quoted literal. If it is user-controlled, embedded conversion specifiers are interpreted - causing argument-count crashes, information disclosure, or output corruption. The literal-format safe form printf("%s", $x) starts with a quote and is not matched; gettext wrappers _(...) / __(...) and constant formats (MSG_TEMPLATE) start with _ or a letter and are not matched; fprintf/vfprintf are excluded by the word boundary (covered by the fprintf rule).

rules.name: fmtstring-php-syslog-variable-message
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Format with a literal template first: syslog(LOG_ERR, sprintf('%s', $userData)); never pass raw user input as the message.
rules.why: The syslog message argument (2nd arg, after the priority) is a non-literal, user-controlled variable. Passing untrusted data as the message risks format-specifier handling (%m) and log injection; the safe form uses a constant template with data supplied separately. Tightened from the original: the priority segment is [^,;()]+ (no parentheses) so a parenthesized priority expression like get_priority($lvl, $fac) can no longer have its inner argument mistaken for the message on an otherwise safe literal-message call.

rules.name: fmtstring-req-input-as-format
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Keep the format string a constant literal and pass user data only as a trailing value argument: `console.log('%s', req.query.msg)` or `util.format('%s', userValue)`. Never place user-controlled data in the first (template) position.
rules.why: Request input (req.query/params/body/headers/cookies) is passed as the FIRST argument of util.format / console.* / a logger call — i.e. as the FORMAT TEMPLATE. Node's util.format interprets %s/%d/%j/%o in that first argument, so attacker-controlled specifiers can consume/mis-render later arguments (disclosing objects via %j/%o), corrupt structured logs, or cause type confusion. The user token must sit immediately after `(`, so a literal-format-then-user-value call (`console.log('%s', req.query.msg)`, `console.log('x', req.query)`) is not flagged, and `console.table`/`res.json` are outside the sink.

rules.name: fmtstring-request-percent-format
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Use a constant literal format string with the user value as an argument, or f-strings/str.format with a fixed template. Never place user input on the left of the % operator.
rules.why: A request attribute is the LEFT operand of the %-formatting operator with a tuple or list on the right (request.args[...] % (a, b) / % [x]), so the user controls the format string while trusted values are the arguments - classic %-format-string injection (CWE-134). Requiring the right operand to be a list ('% [') or a comma-bearing parenthesis ('% (a, b)' / '% (x,)') is the fix for the original rule's false positive on arithmetic modulo with a parenthesised expression: 'request.args[n] % (base * 2)' has no comma and no longer matches.

rules.name: fmtstring-ruby-kernel-format
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Keep the format string a constant literal and pass user data only as trailing value arguments: format("%s", user).
rules.why: format()/sprintf()/Kernel.format is called with a NON-LITERAL first argument, so user-controlled text is used as the format template (crash, info disclosure via mismatched specifiers). Added a targeted def-guard so a method DEFINITION `def format(...)`/`def sprintf(...)` is not flagged, while a one-line `def x; format(user_fmt); end` still fires (the guard only matches `def` immediately naming format/sprintf).

rules.name: fmtstring-ruby-percent-operator
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Make the template a constant literal ("%s" % user) or sanitise/whitelist the template; never let user input be the left operand of %.
rules.why: A user-controlled / format-named variable is the LEFT operand of the % operator, i.e. the template is attacker-controlled while the values are on the right. Kept as-is: requiring the bracket/paren after % (a Ruby format-array/tuple) means integer modulo (page % 2) is not flagged, and a string-LITERAL left operand ("%s" % [x]) never matches because a format-named identifier does not abut the % operator.

rules.name: fmtstring-ruby-printf
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Use a constant literal format and pass user values as arguments: printf("%s\n", user).
rules.why: printf is called with a non-literal format argument, letting user input act as the format string. The IO-first-arg branch still suppresses printf($stdout, "%d", n); added a def-guard so `def printf(...)` is not flagged while `def run; printf(user_fmt); end` still fires. sprintf and myprinter.printf are already excluded by the preceding-char class.

rules.name: fmtstring-ruby-syslog
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Pass a constant format literal and user data as arguments: Syslog.log(pri, "%s", user).
rules.why: Syslog.log receives a non-literal format argument after the priority, so user data is interpreted as a C-style format string. Kept as-is: the (?!["']) lookahead suppresses literal second args, and the leading \b means MySyslog.log does not match.

rules.name: fmtstring-sprintf-variable-format
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Make the format string a hardcoded constant literal and bind all dynamic data as value arguments after it: `sprintf('%s', userValue)`. If a template must be selected at runtime, pick it from a fixed server-side map of trusted literal templates keyed by an allowlisted identifier — never let its text be user-derived.
rules.why: A printf/sprintf/vsprintf/util.format call whose FIRST argument (the format template) is a NON-LITERAL — a variable or member/index expression — followed by additional value arguments. When the template itself is dynamic, attacker-controlled %-directives are interpreted, consuming the following arguments and enabling information disclosure, log injection, or crashes. The leading negative lookahead `(?![\s"'`])` plus an identifier-start requirement structurally rejects a quoted/backtick literal format (`printf("literal %s", x)`, `util.format(`tpl`, y)`) and a numeric first arg (`printf(3, y)`), which are the safe forms; `String.format(...)`/`myFormat(...)` are outside the sink.

rules.name: fmtstring-string-format-nonliteral-format
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Make the format string a constant literal and pass user data only as trailing value arguments: String.Format("{0}", userValue). Never pass user input in the format-string position.
rules.why: String.Format is called with a non-literal first argument (a variable/expression, not a quoted "...", @"...", or $"..." literal). If the template is user-controlled it becomes a composite-format-string injection: an out-of-range index throws FormatException (DoS) and format/alignment specifiers can be abused. The negative lookahead structurally rejects the safe literal-format call. notMatch excludes the IFormatProvider overload two ways: by named provider types AND, generally, by the shape String.Format(identifier, "literal", ...) - which reliably catches any provider variable (numberFormatInfo, fmtProvider, custom casings) that precedes a literal format, killing the top false-positive class.

rules.name: fmtstring-user-format-receiver-named
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Treat user strings only as .format() arguments, never as the template/receiver. Use a fixed literal template, or string.Template().safe_substitute for user-provided templates.
rules.why: A variable whose name marks it user-controlled (user*, request*, untrusted*, payload*, attacker*, malicious*) is the RECEIVER of .format()/.format_map(), meaning the attacker supplies the format template. Field-access payloads ({0.__init__.__globals__[...]}, {x[SECRET]}) then leak internals (CWE-134). The receiver is a bare identifier immediately before .format(, never a quoted literal, so "literal {}".format(user_name) and "{user}".format(user=data) do not fire.

rules.name: fmtstring-user-format-receiver-request
rules.message: Format string injection — user input used as the format/template string (CWE-134).
rules.remediation: Never call .format() on user-controlled strings. Use a fixed template with the user data as an argument ("...{}".format(user_value)), or string.Template with safe_substitute, or an explicit mapping you control.
rules.why: A request attribute is the RECEIVER of str.format()/format_map() - the user controls the format template. Via {0.__class__...} / {config[SECRET]} field access this leaks attributes and globals and can disclose secrets (CWE-134). The discriminator is that request.* is immediately followed by .format( (it is the template), not sitting inside the parentheses as an argument to a literal template, so "...{}".format(request.args[...]) and dict-lookup templates[request.args[k]].format(x) do not fire.

rules.name: form-api-clobbering
rules.message: A native form property/method is accessed on a form element (DOM-clobbering risk).
rules.remediation: Call the prototype directly: HTMLFormElement.prototype.submit.call(form).
rules.why: An injected <input name="submit"> or name="elements" shadows form.submit / form.elements with the element node, so this reference resolves to the input, not the native API — breaking or hijacking submission.

rules.name: go-plugin-open-user-path
rules.message: Write-then-execute — code is loaded or run from a user-controlled or writable path (potential RCE, CWE-829/95/98/94).
rules.remediation: Open only a fixed literal plugin path shipped with the application; if the name is dynamic, validate it against an allow-list and require it under a read-only directory that no request handler can write to.
rules.why: plugin.Open() loads a Go shared object and runs its init() functions; a non-literal path lets an attacker point it at an uploaded or writable .so and execute code in-process. A literal path is suppressed, a leading word-boundary stops matching inside otherplugin.Open(...), and pluginManager.Opened(...)/myplugin.OpenConn(...) fail the .Open( boundary.

rules.name: go-reflected-html-response-request
