rules.message: Reflected / context-mismatched XSS — user input reaches HTML or JS output without proper contextual encoding (CWE-79/116).
rules.remediation: Render with the auto-escaping html/template package, or apply template.HTMLEscapeString / html.EscapeString (or bluemonday for rich HTML) to the value before writing it.
rules.why: HTML written to the http.ResponseWriter (via fmt.Fprint/Fprintf/Fprintln, w.Write, or io.WriteString) is built from r.URL.Query()/r.FormValue/r.PostFormValue/r.Header with no escaping, reflecting attacker markup -> reflected XSS.

rules.name: graphiql-ide-enabled-js
rules.message: GraphQL/dev misconfiguration — introspection or a dev endpoint exposed, or a weak/predictable secret (CWE-200/489/307/770/330).
rules.remediation: Guard by environment: `graphiql: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production'`. For graphql-yoga set `graphiql: false` in prod and disable introspection with `useDisableIntrospection`.
rules.why: express-graphql, graphql-yoga, graphql-http and mercurius expose the GraphiQL in-browser IDE via a `graphiql` option. A literal true (or mercurius 'playground'/'graphiql' string) serves an interactive query console with introspection on the production endpoint. Env-guarded values place a variable/ternary after the colon and match neither the literal nor the string alternatives; a comparison like `process.env.GRAPHIQL === 'true'` puts the literal far from the separator so it is not matched.

rules.name: graphql-batch-link-enabled
rules.message: GraphQL/dev misconfiguration — introspection or a dev endpoint exposed, or a weak/predictable secret (CWE-200/489/307/770/330).
rules.remediation: Set a small batchMax bound and ensure the server enforces per-operation rate limiting and query cost limits; use a non-batching HttpLink for sensitive mutations.
rules.why: Apollo BatchHttpLink / batch:true coalesces multiple GraphQL operations into a single HTTP request; against an unprotected server this enables request-count rate-limit bypass and amplification.

rules.name: graphql-batched-http-requests-enabled
rules.message: GraphQL/dev misconfiguration — introspection or a dev endpoint exposed, or a weak/predictable secret (CWE-200/489/307/770/330).
rules.remediation: Set allowBatchedHttpRequests:false, or cap the batch length and enforce per-operation rate limiting plus query cost/complexity limits.
rules.why: Apollo Server with allowBatchedHttpRequests:true accepts an array of operations in one HTTP request, so an attacker can pack many login/OTP mutations into a single request and bypass per-request rate limiting and brute-force throttles.

rules.name: graphql-formaterror-stacktrace-exposed
rules.message: GraphQL/dev misconfiguration — introspection or a dev endpoint exposed, or a weak/predictable secret (CWE-200/489/307/770/330).
rules.remediation: Return only client-safe fields: `formatError: (err) => ({ message: err.message, extensions: { code: err.extensions?.code } })`. Strip stack/stacktrace before returning, and include them only behind a dev-only guard.
rules.why: A GraphQL error formatter (formatError / customFormatErrorFn / formatErrorFn) that returns an object with a `stack` / `stacktrace` / `stackTrace` KEY ships raw stack traces to clients, leaking source paths and internals. Tightened from the original (`...[^\n]*\bstack`, which fired on read-for-logging like `const s = err.stack` and on unrelated keys like `stackId`): the sink now requires the stack token to be an object key (immediately followed by a colon), so `stackId:`/`stackFrame:` and value-only reads no longer match. notMatch clears the sanitizing cases (`delete err.stack`, `stack: undefined/null`, `omit(err,['stack'])`), comments, and env/isDev/isProd-guarded dev-only exposure.

rules.name: graphql-introspection-enabled
rules.message: GraphQL/dev misconfiguration — introspection or a dev endpoint exposed, or a weak/predictable secret (CWE-200/489/307/770/330).
rules.remediation: Gate on environment: `introspection: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production'` (Apollo) or `introspection=not settings.IS_PRODUCTION` (Python). For graphql-yoga/envelop add `useDisableIntrospection` in prod. Off by default; enable only in non-production.
rules.why: Schema introspection lets any client download the full type graph (types, fields, args, deprecations), mapping the entire API surface. A hardcoded literal (Apollo `introspection: true`, ariadne/Strawberry `introspection=True`) leaves it on in production. The leading \b keeps safe `disableIntrospection: true` and `shouldEnableIntrospection: true` (word char before the token) from matching, and env-guarded values (`NODE_ENV !== 'production'`, `!isProd`, a ternary) place a variable after the separator so no literal true/True follows; the guarded `True if ... else` form is killed by notMatch.

rules.name: graphql-playground-option-enabled
rules.message: GraphQL/dev misconfiguration — introspection or a dev endpoint exposed, or a weak/predictable secret (CWE-200/489/307/770/330).
rules.remediation: Disable in production: `playground: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production'`, or migrate to Apollo Server 3/4 and use the environment-aware landing-page plugins. Prefer `playground: false` for prod builds.
rules.why: Apollo Server 2's `playground: true` (and equivalent configs) turns on the embedded GraphQL Playground IDE, exposing an interactive schema explorer and introspection to anyone hitting the endpoint. A hardcoded true means on in every environment. Env-guarded values put a variable/ternary after the colon, so no literal true follows; `optionsPlayground` / `playgroundEnabled:` require a separator that the boundary+colon prevents from matching.

rules.name: hardcoded-secret
rules.message: This looks like a real credential written into the file.
rules.remediation: Read it from the environment or a secret store instead of hard-coding it.
rules.why: A key committed to a repository is a key that has leaked, and rotating it later does not un-publish it.

rules.name: hardcoded-signing-secret-assignment
rules.message: Client-side token signing or embedded signing key — a secret/decision shipped to the browser is attacker-forgeable.
rules.remediation: Read the secret from a non-public secret source at runtime (server-only env var, KMS, Vault, secrets manager) and remove the literal from source. Rotate any secret that was ever committed. Public keys and non-secret identifiers can stay literal.
rules.why: A variable or property named for a signing secret (JWT_SECRET, signingKey, hmacSecret, clientSecret, privateKey, ...) is assigned a hardcoded string literal. In a client bundle this is a shipped credential: it is trivially extracted and lets an attacker sign or impersonate. Even in server code it is a hardcoded-credential smell.

rules.name: header-value-crlf-injection
rules.message: HTTP response splitting / header injection — user input placed into a response header without stripping CRLF (CWE-113).
rules.remediation: Never place raw request data into a header value. Strip CR/LF (value.replace(/[\r\n]/g, '')) or validate against a strict allowlist/enum, and for filenames use encodeURIComponent or a sanitized basename that is actually the value written. Prefer library helpers (e.g. res.attachment/res.download) that encode header values.
rules.why: A response-header setter (res.setHeader/header/set/append/writeHead/putHeader/addHeader, or PHP header()) receives a value argument built from raw request input (req./request./query/body/params/headers/$_GET/getParameter) via concatenation or a backtick template. Because CR/LF are not stripped, an attacker can embed %0d%0a to inject additional headers or split the response (CWE-113). The classic critical sample applies path.basename to a decoy variable while the header template still embeds the raw req.query.filename.

rules.name: header-value-var-interpolation
rules.message: User input in a response header value or a CLI argument array (header injection / argument injection).
rules.remediation: Strip CR/LF from any user-derived header value (or reject it), and prefer a library that encodes header values; for filenames use encodeURIComponent and the RFC 5987 filename* form.
rules.why: A response header value is built from a template literal or concatenation that interpolates a variable (often derived from request input, e.g. a filename in Content-Disposition). If the value contains CR/LF, an attacker splits the response and injects headers or a body (HTTP response splitting / header injection). Broadens the req.*-direct rule to the common one-hop-removed variable case.

rules.name: hmac-public-key
rules.message: A public key is used as the HMAC secret (algorithm-confusion).
rules.remediation: Verify RS/ES tokens with the asymmetric verify (public key), and pin the algorithm; never feed a public key to HMAC.
rules.why: If tokens are verified with HMAC keyed by the RSA public key, an attacker who has that public key (it is public) can forge a valid HS256 token for any user.

rules.name: hpp-c-querystring-var-into-url
rules.message: HTTP parameter pollution — raw/duplicated request parameters forwarded so layers disagree (CWE-235).
rules.remediation: Do not append the raw query string to a downstream URL. Rebuild the query from validated, canonicalised single values before forwarding.
rules.why: A variable clearly holding the raw query string (query_string/raw_query/raw_qs/...) is concatenated into a downstream URL (scheme, ?%s/&%s trailer, or CURLOPT_URL) without re-serialisation, so a duplicated parameter is re-interpreted downstream — HTTP Parameter Pollution. The regex requires BOTH a URL indicator and a raw-query-named variable on the same statement; the \b anchor prevents sink substring matches; the notMatch guard clears encode/canonicalise/validate/reserialise wrappers, and a cleaned name (escaped_query, canonical_qs, clean_query) is not in the raw-query name set. Residual edge: a ?%s appearing in non-URL prose on the same line alongside a raw-query variable could still fire.

rules.name: hpp-c-raw-querystring-forwarded
rules.message: HTTP parameter pollution — raw/duplicated request parameters forwarded so layers disagree (CWE-235).
rules.remediation: Parse the query string into typed parameters, validate each, and re-serialise a canonical single-value-per-key query for the downstream request rather than forwarding the raw string.
rules.why: The raw CGI QUERY_STRING (getenv("QUERY_STRING")) is concatenated/formatted directly into an outbound URL or handed to curl on the same statement without re-parsing. A duplicated parameter (?id=1&id=2) the gateway read one way is re-parsed differently downstream — HTTP Parameter Pollution. The regex requires a string-builder/curl sink AND the raw getenv("QUERY_STRING") on the same statement; the \b anchor prevents substring matches (xsprintf/myasprintf); the notMatch guard clears lines that first URL-encode / canonicalise / validate / parse it.

rules.name: hpp-forward-raw-body
rules.message: HTTP parameter pollution — raw/duplicated request parameters forwarded so layers disagree (CWE-235).
rules.remediation: Parse and validate the body, then re-serialise a canonical payload (a clean dict via data=/json=). Do not pipe request.body/request.data straight to the outbound call.
rules.why: The raw request body (request.body / data / get_data() / stream, or awaited request.body()) is forwarded verbatim as the body of a downstream request. Duplicate keys in a urlencoded body are re-parsed downstream and may resolve differently than upstream - HTTP Parameter Pollution (CWE-235). The data=/content=/body= kwarg must be bound directly to request.body/data/get_data/stream, so re-serialised payloads (json.dumps, serialize(), a clean dict) and request.form/request.POST do not fire.

rules.name: hpp-forward-raw-body-stream
rules.message: HTTP parameter pollution — raw/duplicated request parameters forwarded so layers disagree (CWE-235).
rules.remediation: Deserialise and validate the body into a typed object, then re-serialise only the validated fields for the downstream request instead of forwarding the raw stream.
rules.why: Piping the raw request body/stream/parameter-map straight into a downstream request re-parses duplicated parameters at the backend, enabling HTTP Parameter Pollution and validation bypass. Requires a forwarding sink AND a raw request accessor on the same statement, so getParameter("x") (single value) and plain reads that only store the body do not fire.

rules.name: hpp-forward-raw-form-collection
rules.message: HTTP parameter pollution — raw/duplicated request parameters forwarded so layers disagree (CWE-235).
rules.remediation: Build the downstream content from an explicit allowlist of expected keys with single canonical values, not by re-emitting the raw request collection.
rules.why: The entire incoming form/query collection (Request.Form / Request.Query) is re-wrapped into a FormUrlEncodedContent and forwarded downstream verbatim. Every submitted key - including duplicates and attacker-injected extras - is replayed to the backend, which may parse duplicate keys differently (HPP) or honor injected privileged fields. Added (?!\s*\[) so a single-parameter read Request.Form["id"] (not a whole-collection forward) does not match.

rules.name: hpp-forward-raw-query-string
rules.message: HTTP parameter pollution — raw/duplicated request parameters forwarded so layers disagree (CWE-235).
rules.remediation: Do not concatenate request.getQueryString() into a downstream URL; re-build the query from individually validated, canonicalised single values.
rules.why: Forwarding the raw request query string into a downstream URL lets a duplicated parameter (e.g. ?id=1&id=2) be re-parsed differently by the backend than by the front-end, bypassing validation via HTTP Parameter Pollution. The url-var branch now requires string concatenation (+) so that merely storing or validating getQueryString() into a url-named variable does not fire.

rules.name: hpp-forward-raw-querystring-downstream
rules.message: HTTP parameter pollution — raw/duplicated request parameters forwarded so layers disagree (CWE-235).
rules.remediation: Do not forward the raw query string. Parse the parameters, validate/allowlist each expected key to a single canonical value, and re-serialise (e.g. QueryHelpers.AddQueryString with a validated dictionary) before building the downstream URL.
rules.why: The RAW incoming query string (Request.QueryString as a whole, Request.Url.Query, or Request.RawUrl) is concatenated into a downstream request URL. Because the duplicated-parameter string is re-parsed by a different framework downstream, an attacker can supply ?role=user&role=admin so the tiers disagree on which value wins (HPP). Tightened lookahead (?!\s*\[|\s*\.Get) excludes the single-value indexed form Request.QueryString["x"] AND the single-value accessor Request.QueryString.Get("x")/GetValues("x"), which are not raw-forwarding.

rules.name: hpp-go-duplicate-param-first-index
rules.message: HTTP parameter pollution — raw/duplicated request parameters forwarded so layers disagree (CWE-235).
rules.remediation: Use r.FormValue / q.Get for a single canonical value, or explicitly reject requests that supply the parameter more than once.
rules.why: Indexing the raw multi-value slice (r.Form["x"][0] or [len-1]) manually picks first-vs-last for a duplicated parameter; if a downstream component picks the opposite occurrence, the two views of the same request disagree (HTTP parameter pollution). The map-index-then-slice-index shape distinguishes it from r.FormValue("x")[0] (a string byte index) and r.URL.Query().Get("x")[0].

rules.name: hpp-go-rawbody-forward
rules.message: HTTP parameter pollution — raw/duplicated request parameters forwarded so layers disagree (CWE-235).
rules.remediation: Parse and validate the body, then re-serialize a canonical body (e.g. bytes.NewReader(json.Marshal(v))) for the downstream request rather than forwarding r.Body verbatim.
rules.why: The raw inbound request body (r.Body) is streamed unmodified into an outbound request; if it carries duplicated form parameters, the downstream service re-parses them with different precedence than the frontend, enabling parameter pollution. The body must appear as a real argument of the outbound call (balanced-paren match), optionally wrapped in one no-op adaptor like io.NopCloser, so an r.Body mentioned in a trailing comment or a separate statement on the same line no longer matches.

rules.name: hpp-go-rawquery-forward
rules.message: HTTP parameter pollution — raw/duplicated request parameters forwarded so layers disagree (CWE-235).
rules.remediation: Re-serialize a validated url.Values (q.Encode()) built from canonicalised single values instead of forwarding the raw query string.
rules.why: The raw inbound query string (r.URL.RawQuery) is concatenated/formatted straight into a downstream URL, so a duplicated parameter (?a=1&a=2) is re-parsed by the backend with different first/last semantics than the gateway used, enabling parameter pollution. The sprintf branch now requires a query-position verb ([?&]%s) so a plain log format like "state=%s" no longer matches.

rules.name: hpp-go-requesturi-forward
rules.message: HTTP parameter pollution — raw/duplicated request parameters forwarded so layers disagree (CWE-235).
rules.remediation: Build the downstream URL from validated, canonicalised path and url.Values rather than concatenating the raw RequestURI.
rules.why: r.RequestURI carries the raw, unparsed path+query exactly as sent; concatenating it into a downstream URL forwards duplicated parameters verbatim so the backend can resolve them differently than the proxy did (HTTP parameter pollution). Matching is restricted to string concatenation and a URL-context sprintf verb, so an http.Get to a fixed backend followed by an unrelated log of r.RequestURI, or any plain log line, no longer matches.

rules.name: hpp-manual-first-vs-last-duplicate
rules.message: HTTP parameter pollution — raw/duplicated request parameters forwarded so layers disagree (CWE-235).
rules.remediation: Reject requests that contain the parameter more than once, or canonicalise to a single documented value and use that everywhere; never let first-vs-last selection differ between tiers.
rules.why: Code explicitly picks one of several values for a specific, possibly-duplicated request parameter: it names the parameter (Request.Query["x"] or .GetValues("x")) and then selects First/Last/FirstOrDefault/LastOrDefault() or [index]. When one tier selects the first occurrence and another (WAF/proxy/backend) selects the last, a duplicated parameter is interpreted inconsistently - the classic HPP primitive. Tightened from the original: it now requires a named parameter access immediately before the first/last selection, so Request.Query.Keys.First() / Request.Query.First() (collection iteration, not value selection) no longer match, and .First(predicate) is excluded by requiring empty parens.

rules.name: hpp-php-raw-body-forward-postfields
rules.message: HTTP parameter pollution — raw/duplicated request parameters forwarded so layers disagree (CWE-235).
rules.remediation: Decode the body, validate and canonicalize each field, then re-serialize with http_build_query or json_encode before forwarding rather than piping php://input straight through.
rules.why: The raw request body (php://input / HTTP_RAW_POST_DATA) is forwarded as CURLOPT_POSTFIELDS without re-parsing, so duplicated body parameters reach the backend unchanged and can be parsed differently downstream - the raw-body HPP shape as a precise same-line sink. The [^;]* guard keeps a php://input read from an earlier statement on the same line from being joined; notMatch suppresses re-serialized bodies (http_build_query/json_encode).

rules.name: hpp-php-raw-querystring-forward
rules.message: HTTP parameter pollution — raw/duplicated request parameters forwarded so layers disagree (CWE-235).
rules.remediation: Parse the incoming query with parse_str, keep only validated single canonical values, then rebuild the downstream query string with http_build_query instead of forwarding the raw QUERY_STRING.
rules.why: The raw $_SERVER['QUERY_STRING'] is concatenated verbatim into a downstream request URL passed to a curl/stream sink. Duplicated parameters (?id=1&id=2) are forwarded unparsed and may be resolved differently by the backend than by this app - HTTP Parameter Pollution. This is the precise same-line forwarding shape; the sink function is required, so bare reads/logging of QUERY_STRING do not match. notMatch suppresses validated rebuilds via http_build_query.

rules.name: hpp-php-request-uri-concat-outbound
rules.message: HTTP parameter pollution — raw/duplicated request parameters forwarded so layers disagree (CWE-235).
rules.remediation: Extract only the needed, validated parameters from the parsed request and reconstruct the downstream URL with http_build_query rather than concatenating the raw REQUEST_URI.
rules.why: A downstream URL is built by concatenating the raw $_SERVER['REQUEST_URI'] (path plus raw query string) into an outbound curl/stream request. Duplicate/encoded parameters pass through unnormalized, enabling parameter pollution on the backend. The sink function is required, so header()/logging/echo of REQUEST_URI does not match; notMatch suppresses sanitized/reconstructed forms (http_build_query, rawurlencode, urlencode, parse_url, basename).

rules.name: hpp-querystring-stringify-forward
rules.message: HTTP parameter pollution — raw/duplicated request parameters forwarded so layers disagree (CWE-235).
rules.remediation: Build the downstream query from an explicit allowlist of keys with single validated values (e.g. `new URLSearchParams({ id: String(value) })`) rather than re-stringifying the entire user-parsed object. Decide and enforce one policy for duplicate keys before forwarding.
rules.why: The whole parsed request query/body/params object is re-serialised with qs.stringify / querystring.stringify (or .encode) and forwarded downstream. `qs` expands duplicated keys into arrays, so the re-encoded string no longer matches the wire form the downstream parser expects and a duplicated parameter can be re-interpreted differently, enabling HPP. The sink requires req.query/body/params to be the DIRECT first argument (immediately after `(`), so a wrapped/validated object (`pick(req.query, ...)`, `sanitize(req.query)`, `{ id: req.query.id }`) is not flagged; `\b` on the object keyword rejects `myqs.stringify(...)` and `qs.stringify(reqData)`.

rules.name: hpp-raw-request-url-forward
rules.message: HTTP parameter pollution — raw/duplicated request parameters forwarded so layers disagree (CWE-235).
rules.remediation: Do not forward the raw query string. Parse inbound parameters into a validated object, select the single intended value per expected key (rejecting or canonicalising duplicates), and re-serialise only allowlisted keys via URLSearchParams before building the downstream URL so upstream and downstream agree on parameter semantics.
rules.why: The RAW inbound request URL/query string (req.originalUrl / req._parsedUrl / req.rawQuery / req.rawUrl) is passed verbatim into a downstream outbound request, so duplicated parameters (?role=user&role=admin) survive untouched and the downstream service may pick a different occurrence than the gateway did — the core HTTP Parameter Pollution primitive for authz/filter bypass. Requires an outbound-client call on the same line, so `res.redirect(req.originalUrl)`, `logger.info(... req.originalUrl)`, and bare assignments (no client keyword) are not flagged; notMatch suppresses an encodeURIComponent-wrapped value.

rules.name: hpp-ruby-manual-dup-parse
rules.message: HTTP parameter pollution — raw/duplicated request parameters forwarded so layers disagree (CWE-235).
rules.remediation: Use Rack::Utils.parse_nested_query / the framework params parser and decide duplicate handling explicitly; do not hand-split the raw query string.
rules.why: The query string is split manually on & instead of using a real parser, so first-vs-last duplicate handling diverges from the framework and downstream services (HPP). Kept as-is: the split-on-& literal keys the pattern tightly, so splits on '/', ',', '=' or a real parser do not match.

rules.name: hpp-ruby-raw-body-forward
rules.message: HTTP parameter pollution — raw/duplicated request parameters forwarded so layers disagree (CWE-235).
rules.remediation: Deserialize, validate and re-encode the body from a canonical object rather than forwarding request.raw_post/request.body.read.
rules.why: The raw request body is proxied unchanged to a downstream service, allowing duplicate-parameter pollution between the two parsers. Added \b (MyRestClient); narrowed bare request.body to request.body.(read|string) so guard uses like request.body.present?/.rewind stop firing; added JSON.parse suppression for the parse-then-forward safe case.

rules.name: hpp-ruby-raw-query-forward
rules.message: HTTP parameter pollution — raw/duplicated request parameters forwarded so layers disagree (CWE-235).
rules.remediation: Parse, validate and re-serialise only the parameters you need (e.g. URI.encode_www_form on a permitted hash) instead of forwarding the raw query string.
rules.why: The raw query string is forwarded verbatim into a downstream request, so duplicated parameters can be re-parsed differently by the backend (HTTP Parameter Pollution). Added \b (MyHTTParty) and generalised parse_nested_query to parse(?:_nested)?_query so a safe Rack::Utils.parse_query re-parse is suppressed.

rules.name: iac-docker-curl-pipe-shell
rules.message: Remote script piped directly into a shell interpreter without checksum verification.
rules.remediation: Download the artifact, verify its SHA-256 digest against a pinned checksum, and then execute it.

negative: RUN curl -fsSL https://example.com/tool.tgz -o tool.tgz && sha256sum -c tool.sha256

rules.name: iac-docker-user-root
rules.message: Container configuration explicitly sets the runtime user to root.
rules.remediation: Drop privileges before container startup using a non-root USER (for example USER 10001:10001).

rules.name: iac-iam-wildcard-admin
rules.message: IAM policy grants wildcard Action permissions (*).
rules.remediation: Scope IAM policies to the exact least-privilege actions and specific resource ARNs required.

rules.name: iac-k8s-privileged-container
rules.message: Container or Kubernetes pod enables privileged execution or host namespace sharing.
rules.remediation: Set privileged: false, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, and avoid hostNetwork/hostPID/hostIPC sharing.

rules.name: iac-terraform-public-ingress
rules.message: Infrastructure configuration exposes resources or ingress rules to public access (0.0.0.0/0 or public-read ACL).
rules.remediation: Restrict security group ingress CIDRs to trusted internal or VPN ranges and keep storage buckets private.

rules.name: identity-from-raw-request-value-csharp
rules.message: Broken session management — identity/role from an unverified client value or a writable store (CWE-807/302).
rules.remediation: Use the authenticated principal (User.Identity / HttpContext.User) or a validated token (TokenValidationParameters). Protect any identity cookie with the Data Protection API.
rules.why: The acting user or role is read straight from Request.Cookies/Headers/Query/Form. These are client-controlled, so relying on them for session identity or authorization is a bypass. Fixed a real gap: snake_case user_id was missed (word boundary fails before underscore); added user[-_]?id. User.Identity / HttpContext.User are excluded (not Request.<source>).

rules.name: identity-from-raw-request-value-go
rules.message: Broken session management — identity/role from an unverified client value or a writable store (CWE-807/302).
rules.remediation: Resolve identity from a verified session (a random session id in a server store) or a validated token (jwt.Parse with verification / securecookie.Decode).
rules.why: Identity/role is read from a spoofable request source (r.Header.Get("X-User"), r.Cookie("user"), Query().Get("user_id")) and trusted as the acting user. Fixed a real gap: the original alternation missed snake_case user_id (no word boundary before an underscore) so Query().Get("user_id")/Cookie("user_id") slipped through; added user[-_]?id.

rules.name: identity-from-raw-request-value-py
rules.message: Broken session management — identity/role from an unverified client value or a writable store (CWE-807/302).
rules.remediation: Derive identity from Django request.session / Flask server-side session, or from a verified token (jwt.decode with verification, itsdangerous signed cookie).
rules.why: A user identifier is read from a raw request cookie/header/query/form (Flask request.cookies/headers/args, Django request.COOKIES/GET/META) and used as identity. These values are attacker-controlled. request.session is excluded (not a raw source), and lines carrying jwt.decode/itsdangerous/signer.unsign/verify=True are suppressed as verified.

rules.name: identity-from-superglobal-cookie-php
rules.message: Broken session management — identity/role from an unverified client value or a writable store (CWE-807/302).
rules.remediation: Store identity in $_SESSION (server-side session) after authenticating, or verify a signed token (hash_hmac/hash_equals, JWT).
rules.why: Identity or role is taken from a raw PHP superglobal ($_COOKIE/$_GET/$_REQUEST/$_POST user/role) with no integrity check. Because the rule spans query/post inputs (not just cookies) the accurate mapping is untrusted-input-in-security-decision (CWE-807). $_SESSION and lines with jwt/hash_hmac/hash_equals are excluded.

rules.name: identity-from-trusted-request-header-java
rules.message: Broken session management — identity/role from an unverified client value or a writable store (CWE-807/302).
rules.remediation: Authenticate via the container/framework principal (SecurityContextHolder / getUserPrincipal) or a verified token. If a trusted upstream proxy injects the header, strip/verify it at the edge.
rules.why: The acting user identity is read from a request header (X-User, X-Remote-User, ...). Any client can send an arbitrary header, so trusting this assumed-immutable data as authenticated identity is an authentication bypass by header spoofing (CWE-302). User-Agent is explicitly excluded.

rules.name: identity-from-unsigned-cookie-rb
rules.message: Broken session management — identity/role from an unverified client value or a writable store (CWE-807/302).
rules.remediation: Use cookies.signed[...] / cookies.encrypted[...] or the Rails session (session[:user_id]), which are tamper-protected.
rules.why: A plain (unsigned) Rails cookie holding a user identifier is used as identity. cookies[:user] is fully client-writable with no integrity checking, so it can be forged to any account. This is authentication by assumed-immutable data (CWE-302). cookies.signed/cookies.encrypted and session[...] are excluded.

rules.name: identity-var-assigned-from-raw-client-value-js
rules.message: Broken session management — identity/role from an unverified client value or a writable store (CWE-807/302).
rules.remediation: Populate identity/role from trusted state only: a verified JWT claim, req.signedCookies, or the authenticated server-side session (req.session).
rules.why: An identity or authorization variable (currentUser, userId, role, isAdmin, req.user, ...) is assigned directly from a raw client value (req.cookies/headers/query/body). The client fully controls its own identity and privilege state. RHS must be a raw req.<source> read, so req.session/req.signedCookies/req.user and getRole(jwt.verify(...)) are excluded.

rules.name: idor-ar-find-by-params
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Anchor the finder to the owner: current_user.documents.find_by(id: params[:id]), or add the owning key to the finder itself: Model.find_by(id: params[:id], user_id: current_user.id), or gate with authorize/Pundit policy after loading.
rules.why: Model.find_by(attr: params[...]) and the dynamic Model.find_by_<attr>(params[...]) finders resolve a single record from a client-controlled reference (id, token, uuid, number) on the global class scope with no ownership constraint; an attacker enumerates or guesses the value to reach records they do not own. The \w*!? tail covers find_by, find_by!, and dynamic find_by_id / find_by_uuid variants. The argument bridge was tightened from [^\n]* to [^\n)]* so the finder cannot reach across a closing paren into an unrelated params[...] later on the same line (cross-call false positive).

rules.name: idor-ar-find-params
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Scope the query to the current principal instead of the global class: current_user.documents.find(params[:id]) (raises RecordNotFound for records you don't own), or add an explicit authorization gate (Pundit authorize @document / CanCan authorize! :read, @document) on the same statement.
rules.why: Model.find(params[:id]) performs a primary-key lookup on a class-level scope using a client-supplied id with no ownership/authorization predicate co-located, so any authenticated user can read another user's record by changing the id. The uppercase [A-Z]\w* receiver distinguishes an unscoped Model.find from the safe current_user.things.find (lowercase association receiver), which the regex intentionally does not match. notMatch was broadened to cover more Rails/Pundit/CanCan principal helpers (current_tenant/shop/site/workspace/project/owner, signed/encrypted cookies, policy(...)) and a full-line-comment guard was added so commented-out sinks do not fire.

rules.name: idor-ar-where-id-params
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Add the ownership column to the same where (Model.where(id: params[:id], user_id: current_user.id)) or start from the scoped association (current_user.posts.where(id: params[:id])); alternatively apply policy_scope / accessible_by(current_ability).
rules.why: Model.where(id: params[:id]) / where(post_id: params[:post_id]) selects a record by a client-supplied reference key on the global class scope with no owner column in the same filter, so the resulting record is not constrained to the requester. The key alternation (id|_id|\w+_id) targets reference-lookup shapes; presence of an ownership predicate or auth gate on the line suppresses. notMatch broadened with more principal helpers and a comment guard.

rules.name: idor-django-orm-findbyid-request
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Constrain the query to the current principal, e.g. Model.objects.get(pk=request.GET['id'], user=request.user), or use get_object_or_404(Model.objects.filter(user=request.user), pk=...), or enforce an object-level permission check.
rules.why: A Django/MongoEngine object is fetched by a primary-key/slug taken straight from the request, with no ownership column constraining the lookup — any authenticated user can read another user's row by changing the id.

rules.name: idor-doctrine-repo-find-req
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Use findOneBy(['id' => $request->id, 'owner' => $this->getUser()]) or run a voter/policy check ($this->denyAccessUnlessGranted('view', $entity)) after loading. A scoped fetch through the owner ($this->getUser()->getPosts()->find(...)) is also suppressed.
rules.why: A repository/entity-manager find() fetches an entity by identifier taken from the request, with no ownership or authorization gate on the statement — the classic broken-object-level-authorization pattern. Critically, Symfony's ownership idioms $this->getUser()/isGranted()/denyAccessUnlessGranted() are NOT matched by the Laravel-style ->user token, so they were added explicitly; this is the top FP source for this broad ->find rule.

rules.name: idor-efcore-find-request
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Scope the load to the caller: after Find, verify ownership (if (doc.OwnerId != _userManager.GetUserId(User)) return Forbid();), or query by owner directly with _context.Documents.FirstOrDefault(d => d.Id == id && d.OwnerId == currentUserId).
rules.why: EF Core Find/FindAsync resolves a row by primary key. When that key is read straight from Request.Query/Form/RouteValues/Cookies/Headers or RouteData with no co-located ownership predicate or authorization gate, any authenticated user can enumerate other users' records by changing the id (CWE-639). The negative lookahead (?![^;]*=>) keeps this to scalar-key Find and excludes MongoDB lambda Find. notMatch drops lines that also carry an ownership term (UserId/OwnerId/TenantId/...), a post-fetch guard (Forbid/Unauthorized/Challenge), an [Authorize]/GetUserId/User.Identity/NameIdentifier check, or that are fully commented out (^\s*//).

rules.name: idor-efcore-lambda-request
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Add an ownership term to the same predicate (=> d.Id == id && d.OwnerId == currentUserId) or apply resource-based authorization before returning the entity.
rules.why: EF Core SingleOrDefault/FirstOrDefault/Single/First/Where builds a predicate that compares an entity key to a client-supplied value (Request.*/RouteData) with no ownership constraint in the same statement, selecting arbitrary rows by client id (CWE-639). notMatch suppresses predicates that also constrain the row to the caller (&& d.OwnerId == currentUserId, TenantId, ...), carry an authorization gate, or are commented out.

rules.name: idor-eloquent-findbyid-req
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Scope the lookup to the owner instead of a bare primary-key fetch, e.g. auth()->user()->documents()->findOrFail($request->id) (which uses instance ->find, not the static ::find this rule flags), or add a policy check: $this->authorize('view', $doc).
rules.why: Model::find()/findOrFail() fetches a row solely by its primary key. When the key comes straight from the request ($request->id, $_GET['id'], request('id')) and no ownership/authorization predicate appears on the statement, any authenticated user can read another user's record by changing the id.

rules.name: idor-eloquent-where-id-req
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Add an ownership constraint to the same query — ->where('user_id', auth()->id()), ->whereBelongsTo(auth()->user()), a tenant scope — or authorize via a policy after loading.
rules.why: Model::where('id', $request->id)->first() looks a record up by an id column driven by client input with no second predicate binding it to the current user, so an attacker can enumerate other users' rows. The ownership twin chains a second where('user_id', auth()->id()) / whereBelongsTo / a tenant column, which notMatch drops. The id-key was tightened to (\w+_)?id so columns like 'paid'/'valid'/'uuid' no longer match by ending in 'id'.

rules.name: idor-file-access-params
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Strip the path with File.basename(params[:file]) and confine to a per-user directory (File.join(current_user.folder, File.basename(params[:file]))), map the request to an allow-list of permitted files, or look the file up through an owner-scoped model and authorize it before serving.
rules.why: send_file / send_data / File.read(lines) / File.open / File.binread / File.new / IO.read fed a client-controlled path or filename (params[:file], upload_dir + params[:name]) returns an arbitrary file: an attacker substitutes another user's document id/name, or traverses with ../ to read files outside the intended directory, with no ownership check on which file may be served. File.readlines was added to the sink set (the read\b boundary was excluding it) and a full-line-comment guard added.

rules.name: idor-file-access-request
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Scope the file to the owner and sanitise: send_from_directory(user_dir(current_user.id), secure_filename(request.args['file'])).
rules.why: A file is served or opened using a name/path taken from the request without scoping it to the caller (or sanitising it), letting an attacker read another user's or an arbitrary file by id/path.

rules.name: idor-fs-path-traversal
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Reduce the input to a bare name with path.basename, resolve against a fixed base dir, and verify the resolved path still startsWith that base (or map the input through an allowlist) before touching the filesystem; for res.sendFile pass a fixed { root }.
rules.why: A filesystem path or download target is built from a client-supplied filename with no containment check, so ../ sequences or absolute paths let the caller read or write files outside the intended directory (path-traversal IDOR over files).

rules.name: idor-gorm-first-req-param
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Scope the lookup to the requester: db.Where("owner_id = ?", currentUser.ID).First(&doc, id), or verify ownership after loading before returning the record.
rules.why: gorm First/Take/Last/Find loads a row by primary key from its second positional argument. When that argument is a client-supplied reference (c.Param/c.Query/mux.Vars/URLParam/FormValue, plus fiber c.Params and echo c.QueryParam) and no co-located ownership predicate is present, any authenticated user can read another user's record by changing the id (classic IDOR).

rules.name: idor-gorm-where-concat-req
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Never concatenate request input into a Where condition. Use placeholders: db.Where("id = ? AND owner_id = ?", id, currentUser.ID), and let gorm bind the values.
rules.why: A gorm .Where() built by string-concatenating client input into the condition (double-quote or backtick fragment). This is both an IDOR (record addressed by a client reference) and an outright SQL injection, since the input is spliced into the SQL text rather than bound as a parameter. Note: the shared ownership notMatch here suppresses concatenations that also carry an owner term to honor the IDOR corpus, but any concatenation of request input into Where is still a SQLi and should be caught by a dedicated SQLi rule.

rules.name: idor-gorm-where-id-req
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Add an ownership term to the same query: .Where("id = ? AND user_id = ?", id, currentUser.ID), or apply a gorm Scope that always injects the tenant/owner filter.
rules.why: A parameterized gorm .Where() (double-quote or backtick condition) keyed only on an id/_id/xxxId column with a client-supplied value filters by the object reference alone. The placeholder stops SQL injection but not IDOR: with no ownership column (user_id/owner_id/org_id/...) in the predicate or a gorm Scope, the requester can address any record.

rules.name: idor-jdbc-sql-concat-id
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Use a bound parameter (WHERE id = ?) AND add an ownership predicate (AND owner_id = ?) bound to the authenticated user, rather than concatenating a client-supplied id into the query.
rules.why: A raw SQL / JPQL string that filters a record by an id column via string concatenation of a request value, with no ownership column also present in the WHERE clause, both exposes an insecure direct object reference and opens SQL injection. The string must begin with SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE (so prose and log messages that merely mention 'WHERE id =' are excluded), and lines routed through a logger are suppressed.

rules.name: idor-jpa-repo-findbyid-req
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Scope the lookup to the caller: use a derived query such as findByIdAndOwnerId(id, principal.getId()), add an ownership check after loading, or gate the handler with @PreAuthorize/@PostAuthorize(returnObject.owner == principal).
rules.why: A Spring Data repository fetch (findById/getReferenceById/getOne/findOneById) whose key argument is taken straight from the HTTP request (getParameter, path/query param, Ktor call.parameters) with no co-located ownership or authorization predicate lets any authenticated user read another user's record by changing the id. Owner-scoped derived methods (findByIdAndOwnerId, findByIdAndUserId) are naturally excluded because 'findById' is no longer immediately followed by '('.

rules.name: idor-mongo-findone-bson-req
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Include the owner in the filter: bson.M{"_id": objID, "userId": claims.UserID}, and convert the id with primitive.ObjectIDFromHex; reject the request if the ownership-scoped query matches nothing.
rules.why: A mongo-go-driver Find/FindOne/FindOneAnd*/UpdateOne/DeleteOne/ReplaceOne whose bson.M/bson.D filter embeds a client-supplied reference inline (c.Param/c.Query/mux.Vars/URLParam/FormValue) fetches or mutates the document by id with no ownership key in the same filter, so any user can target another user's document.

rules.name: idor-mongo-findone-id-filter
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Add an ownership constraint to the same filter object, e.g. findOne({ _id: req.params.id, userId: req.user.id }), so a non-owned id simply returns null instead of another user's record.
rules.why: A Mongo filter keys on { _id: <client value> } with no additional ownership field (userId/ownerId/tenantId/etc. co-present in the same filter object), so the document is fetched or mutated purely by a client-chosen id.

rules.name: idor-mongo-idfilter-req
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Add an owner discriminator to the filter, e.g. ['_id' => new ObjectId($request->id), 'userId' => (string) auth()->id()], or authorize the loaded document with a policy/voter.
rules.why: A Mongo/ODM filter selects a document by _id taken directly from the request, with no owner key (userId/owner/tenant) in the same filter array, so any user can read another's document by supplying its _id. notMatch now also covers Symfony ownership idioms (getUser, isGranted, denyAccessUnlessGranted) and the tenant vocabulary so scoped filters are not flagged.

rules.name: idor-mongodb-filter-request
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Combine an owner filter: Builders<Doc>.Filter.And(Filter.Eq(d => d.Id, id), Filter.Eq(d => d.OwnerId, uid)), or authorize the returned document against the current principal before use.
rules.why: MongoDB.Driver Find with a lambda predicate, a Builders<T>.Filter expression, or a new BsonDocument filter keyed on a client-supplied _id/reference (Request.*/RouteData) and no owner predicate returns documents chosen entirely by the client (CWE-639). Requiring one of =>/Builders</BsonDocument keeps this to real Mongo filters. notMatch drops filters that also constrain by owner/tenant, carry an authorization gate or post-fetch guard, or are commented out.

rules.name: idor-mongoengine-objects-callable-request
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Filter by owner too: Document.objects(id=request.args['id'], owner=current_user).first(), returning 404 on empty.
rules.why: MongoEngine's callable manager Model.objects(id=...) is queried with a request-supplied id and no ownership filter, exposing any document by id.

rules.name: idor-mongoid-objectid-params
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Query from an owner-scoped criteria (current_user.documents.find(params[:id])) or include the owner in the selector (Model.where(_id: BSON::ObjectId(params[:id]), owner_id: current_user.id)); or authorize the loaded document.
rules.why: In Mongoid a document is fetched by casting a client-supplied value to an ObjectId (Model.find(BSON::ObjectId(params[:id])) or where(_id: BSON::ObjectId(params[:id]))) with no owner field in the query. The ObjectId cast defeats the Class.find(params[:id]) rule (argument is not literally params), so this rule catches the wrapped form; it is still IDOR because no ownership is enforced. The pre-cast bridge was tightened to [^\n)]* to prevent matching an ObjectId cast belonging to a different call later on the line.

rules.name: idor-mongotemplate-criteria-id-no-owner
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Chain an ownership constraint onto the Criteria, e.g. Criteria.where("_id").is(id).and("ownerId").is(principal.getId()), or verify the returned document's owner before use.
rules.why: A MongoTemplate Criteria that matches a document solely by _id (Criteria.where("_id").is(...)) with no chained ownership constraint (.and("ownerId")..., .andOperator(...owner...)) fetches/mutates any document by id regardless of who owns it. This is a per-line heuristic: an ownership .and(...) on a separate line cannot be seen, so it carries a strong notMatch and accepts some false positives.

rules.name: idor-orm-findbyid-req
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Scope the lookup to the requester: findOne({ _id: req.params.id, userId: req.user.id }) or add an explicit ownership/authorization check after the fetch (compare doc.owner to the session user, or gate the route with a policy/guard).
rules.why: A record is loaded/mutated by primary key taken straight from the client (req.params/query/body) as the direct first argument, with no co-located ownership or session predicate, so any authenticated user can substitute another user's id and read or modify that record.

rules.name: idor-orm-where-id-req
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Add the owner constraint to the where object, e.g. where: { id: req.params.id, userId: req.user.id }, or enforce a route guard/policy that verifies the fetched row belongs to the requester.
rules.why: A TypeORM/Prisma/Sequelize where clause keys on { id: <client value> } (findOne/findUnique/findOneBy/update/delete) with no ownership column in the same where object, so records are addressed purely by a client-chosen id.

rules.name: idor-pdo-sql-where-id-req
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Include an ownership column bound to the session in the WHERE clause (AND user_id = :uid with auth()->id()), and use a bound parameter for the id rather than string interpolation.
rules.why: A raw SQL statement selects/updates/deletes a resource by an id column concatenated or interpolated from request input, with no owner/tenant column in the WHERE clause. Besides the SQLi risk (unbound interpolation of $_GET/$request into the string), any user can target another user's row by supplying a different id. notMatch now covers the full tenant vocabulary (org/team/account/company/group/customer) so multi-tenant scoping predicates are not flagged; table names like 'accounts'/'orders' still fire because the guards require the *_id suffix.

rules.name: idor-pymongo-findone-id-request
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Include the owner in the filter: db.docs.find_one({'_id': ObjectId(request.args['id']), 'user_id': session['uid']}), and treat a None result as not-found.
rules.why: A Mongo document is fetched/mutated by _id taken from the request with no ownership key in the filter; even wrapped in ObjectId() this is a direct object reference an attacker can point at anyone's document.

rules.name: idor-raw-sql-id-request
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Use a parameterised query with an ownership clause: cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM docs WHERE id=%s AND user_id=%s', (doc_id, current_user.id)).
rules.why: A record is selected/updated by id built into a raw SQL string via f-string or concatenation from request input, with no owner predicate — a direct object reference (and a SQL-injection sink to boot).

rules.name: idor-spring-controller-pathvar-access
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Add @PreAuthorize/@PostAuthorize on the handler, switch to an owner-scoped repository method (findByIdAndOwnerId), or verify the loaded entity belongs to the authenticated principal before returning/deleting it.
rules.why: A terse Spring controller handler that binds an id from @PathVariable/@RequestParam and immediately fetches or deletes by that id in the same expression, with no method-security annotation or ownership variant, is a direct object reference an attacker can enumerate. @AuthenticationPrincipal / Authentication params, @Secured/@RolesAllowed admin routes, and owner-scoped derived methods are suppressed.

rules.name: idor-sql-query-id-req
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Add an ownership predicate bound to the session user: WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2, passing the authenticated user id as the second parameter; treat an empty result as not-authorized.
rules.why: A database/sql, pgx or sqlx Query/QueryRow/Get/Select whose SELECT ... WHERE id = ?/$1 is parameterized with a client-supplied value (double-quote or backtick SQL). The placeholder blocks SQL injection but the row is still addressed by object id alone, with no owner_id/user_id term in the WHERE clause, so it is an IDOR.

positive: row := db.QueryRow("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1", c.Param("id"))
negative: row := db.QueryRow("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $2", c.Param("id"), userId)

rules.name: idor-sql-where-id-req
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Use a parameterized query AND include an ownership column, e.g. WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2 bound to [id, req.user.id]; never string-concat request values into the WHERE clause.
rules.why: A SQL statement concatenates/interpolates a client-supplied id directly into a WHERE id = ... clause with no owner predicate, letting the caller read or change any row by id (and, secondarily, inject SQL).

rules.name: idor-sqlalchemy-get-request
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Add the ownership column to the query: session.query(Doc).filter_by(id=request.args['id'], user_id=current_user.id).first(), and 404 when it returns None.
rules.why: A SQLAlchemy row is loaded by primary key straight from request input (Query.get / Session.get / filter_by(id=...)) without an owner predicate, so an attacker can enumerate other users' records.

rules.name: idor-versioned-api-id
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Confirm the handler enforces ownership; attach the standard auth/authorization middleware or guard (requireAuth, @UseGuards(OwnerGuard), a policy check) to the versioned route, or retire the deprecated endpoint.
rules.why: Aggravator, not a bug by itself: a route under a versioned/legacy path (/v1/, /api/v2/) exposes an :id parameter with no auth middleware or guard named on the same line. Old versioned endpoints are a common place ownership checks were never back-ported, so these are worth an audit.

rules.name: idor-versioned-api-id-param
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Confirm the handler enforces resource-based ownership/authorization for the id; retire deprecated/legacy versions or gate them behind [Authorize] with a resource policy (e.g. IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(User, resource, "Owner")).
rules.why: Aggravator (info): a route mapped under a versioned (/v1/, /v2/) or deprecated/legacy path segment that binds an {id}-style route parameter is a frequent home for un-refactored, weakly-authorized direct object access. It flags the attack surface for manual per-object authorization review. The version token is now anchored to a path segment ((?:[^"]*/)?) so incidental substrings like srv2/ do not match; notMatch drops routes that carry an explicit [Authorize] gate on the same line or are commented out.

rules.name: idor-versioned-api-id-route
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Confirm the controller action for this versioned route scopes the lookup to the current principal and/or authorizes the object (Pundit/CanCan). Retire deprecated API versions and ensure every versioned member route enforces the same ownership checks as the current version.
rules.why: Aggravator (informational): a route under a versioned API path (/api/v1, /v2, ...) that takes an :id (or :*_id) member parameter is a high-surface IDOR target and older/deprecated versions often lag on authorization. This flags the exposure for review; it does not by itself prove the handler is missing an ownership check. The member-param match was tightened from :\w*id to :(?:id|\w+_id) so it matches the documented :id / :*_id intent and stops flagging incidental params ending in 'id' such as :valid, :uuid, :paid.

rules.name: idor-versioned-route-id-param
rules.message: Possible IDOR — a resource is accessed by a client-supplied id with no ownership check (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Audit versioned/deprecated handlers for the same ownership/authorization checks as the current API; retire or gate legacy versions rather than leaving object-by-id endpoints unscoped.
rules.why: Aggravator, not a standalone bug: a route registered under a versioned path (/v1/, /api/v2/, ...) that takes an id-style path parameter (:id, {fileId}). Versioned/legacy endpoints are frequently the ones missing the ownership checks their newer replacements added, so any IDOR here is higher-risk and worth a targeted look. Comment lines are excluded.

rules.name: importlib-import-module-user-name
rules.message: Write-then-execute — code is loaded or run from a user-controlled or writable path (potential RCE, CWE-829/95/98/94).
rules.remediation: Map a validated key to a fixed module via an explicit dict of imports, or check the resolved name against an allow-list set before importing; do not import a name built from request data.
rules.why: importlib.import_module()/__import__() with a variable, a call result, a concatenated string, or an f-string imports and executes whatever module name is computed; if the name or a package search path is attacker-influenced (or points at a writable plugins dir), a planted module runs on import. The identifier branch now also matches a following call-paren so import_module(resolve_name(x)) is caught, while '.'.join(...) and plain literals stay inert.

rules.name: importmap-runtime
rules.message: An import map is referenced/created from JavaScript at runtime.
rules.remediation: Define the import map statically in HTML before any module loads; never build it from input at runtime.
rules.why: If a bare-module alias in the import map is set from input, every subsequent bare import is redirected to an attacker-controlled module URL — total code control (module hijacking).

rules.name: incrementing-counter-as-session-js
rules.message: Predictable session/token identifier — a security id from a non-CSPRNG or observable source (CWE-330/340).
rules.remediation: Assign the identifier from a CSPRNG (crypto.randomUUID / crypto.randomBytes); never use a monotonically increasing counter as a session id or token.
rules.why: A session id or token taken from an incrementing counter (++counter, counter++, lastId + 1) is sequential and trivially predictable: an attacker who holds one valid id can guess every other by adding or subtracting 1.

rules.name: inner-html
rules.message: Assigning to innerHTML parses the value as HTML.
rules.remediation: Use textContent to write characters without parsing, or sanitise the HTML first.
rules.why: Any markup in the value becomes real elements, including a script-bearing attribute.

rules.name: insecure-cookie
rules.message: A cookie flag weakens the cookie's protection.
rules.remediation: Prefer httpOnly: true, secure: true, and a SameSite of Lax or Strict.
rules.why: Without HttpOnly a script can read the cookie; without Secure it can travel over http; SameSite=None permits cross-site sending.

rules.name: insecure-random
rules.message: This random number is not unpredictable.
rules.remediation: Use a CSPRNG: crypto.randomBytes / crypto.getRandomValues / secrets / random_bytes.
rules.why: Math.random / rand / mt_rand are for simulation, not secrecy — their output can be predicted, so a token built from them can be guessed.

rules.name: insecure-url
rules.message: This address is plain http.
rules.remediation: Use https:// for anything that leaves the machine (loopback is exempt).
rules.why: The request and its answer travel in the clear and can be read or rewritten in transit.

rules.name: insert-adjacent-html
rules.message: insertAdjacentHTML parses its argument as HTML.
rules.remediation: Build nodes with the DOM API, or sanitise before inserting.
rules.why: Like innerHTML, any markup in the value is turned into live elements.

rules.name: internal-secret-return
rules.message: An endpoint returns a secret from the environment.
rules.remediation: Authenticate the caller in this service too (API key, mTLS, or a signed internal header).
rules.why: If this internal service trusts an upstream proxy for auth, anyone who reaches it directly gets the secret — a broken trust boundary.

rules.name: java-class-forname-user-controlled
rules.message: Write-then-execute — code is loaded or run from a user-controlled or writable path (potential RCE, CWE-829/95/98/94).
rules.remediation: Resolve a validated key to a fixed Class via an explicit allow-list map instead of forName(userInput); never reflectively load a class named by request data.
rules.why: Class.forName() with a non-literal name selects a class from externally-controlled input (unsafe reflection); combined with newInstance()/getConstructor() it instantiates and runs attacker-chosen code, including gadget classes on the classpath or loaded from a writable location. A single string-literal name (one- or three-arg) is suppressed; a leading word-boundary stops it matching myClass.forName(...).

rules.name: java-reflected-html-writer-getparameter
rules.message: Reflected / context-mismatched XSS — user input reaches HTML or JS output without proper contextual encoding (CWE-79/116).
rules.remediation: Encode for the output context with OWASP Java Encoder (Encode.forHtml), Apache Commons StringEscapeUtils.escapeHtml4, or Spring HtmlUtils.htmlEscape; sanitize rich HTML with Jsoup.clean; cast numeric params with Integer.parseInt.
rules.why: A servlet response writer emits an HTML fragment concatenated with request.getParameter/getHeader/getQueryString with no output encoding, reflecting attacker markup -> reflected XSS.

rules.name: java-runtime-exec-script-from-upload-dir
rules.message: Write-then-execute — code is loaded or run from a user-controlled or writable path (potential RCE, CWE-829/95/98/94).
rules.remediation: Execute only fixed, non-writable program paths; never build the command or first argument from request input or an uploads directory, and validate any dynamic component against an allow-list.
rules.why: Runtime.exec()/ProcessBuilder running an interpreter or script whose path comes from an uploads/tmp/writable directory or a request parameter executes attacker-supplied code; the file-write primitive becomes RCE through the spawned process. The keyword set was tightened to variable-shaped upload tokens (Dir/Path/File suffix) plus getParameter/tmpdir/writableDir/'/tmp/', so a benign 'uploads' data argument to cp/tar no longer fires.

rules.name: java-scriptengine-groovy-eval-file-contents
rules.message: Write-then-execute — code is loaded or run from a user-controlled or writable path (potential RCE, CWE-829/95/98/94).
rules.remediation: Do not evaluate script files sourced from untrusted or writable locations; if scripting is required, run only fixed trusted scripts and sandbox the engine (SecureASTCustomizer / restricted bindings).
rules.why: GroovyShell.evaluate()/ScriptEngine.eval() over a File, FileReader, or Files.read* result executes the script contents; when that file is an upload or lives in a writable path, writing the file is RCE. A File/FileReader built from a plain string literal is suppressed, and evaluateExpression(...)/logger.eval(...) fail the eval-open boundary.

rules.name: java-urlclassloader-from-upload-dir
rules.message: Write-then-execute — code is loaded or run from a user-controlled or writable path (potential RCE, CWE-829/95/98/94).
rules.remediation: Load classes only from fixed, application-controlled, non-writable locations; do not build classloader URLs from request input or an uploads directory, and verify any dynamic URL is contained within a trusted base.
rules.why: Constructing a URLClassLoader over a URL/File derived from an uploads/tmp/writable directory or a request parameter lets an attacker who can place a JAR/class there have it loaded and executed, turning a file upload into code execution. The keyword set now includes the uppercase UPLOAD form so new File(UPLOAD_DIR, jar) is caught; the sink is anchored to the URLClassLoader constructor so fixed-URL loaders do not match.

rules.name: jquery-html
rules.message: jQuery .html() with a variable parses it as HTML.
rules.remediation: Use .text() for text, or sanitise the HTML first.
rules.why: Passing anything but a constant string to .html() turns markup in the value into live elements.

rules.name: js-html-content-type-send-bare-var
rules.message: Reflected XSS — an unescaped variable is interpolated into an HTML response (CWE-79).
rules.remediation: Escape or sanitise the variable before sending it as HTML (escapeHtml/he.encode/DOMPurify), send structured data with res.json, or serve static markup with res.sendFile; only label a response text/html when its body is trusted or already encoded.
rules.why: The response is explicitly declared text/html (a Content-Type header set to a quoted 'text/html', or res.type('html')) and, on the same statement, a bare variable is handed to .send/.end/.write with no HTML-tag literal on the line to key on. Sending an unescaped string variable as text/html is reflected/stored XSS even when the markup is assembled elsewhere. Kept precise: the content-type must be a real quoted 'text/html'/type('html') (a quote must sit adjacent to text/html, so a coincidental comment mention like 'returned text/html' does not match) AND the sent argument must be a single identifier/member/index expression that closes with ) -- not a string literal, not res.json, and not a function call (escapeHtml(x)/he.escape(x)/DOMPurify.sanitize(x)/sendFile(x)/readFileSync(x)/renderString(x)), because an identifier followed by ( never reaches the required ). notMatch additionally drops escaped/sanitised sends, sendFile/readFile(Sync), res.json, obviously-numeric variables, and comments. A lone res.setHeader('Content-Type','text/html') with no bare-variable send on the line does not match, and a template-literal body (Rule 1's job) does not match here.

rules.name: js-numeric-isnan-money-no-bound
rules.message: Unsafe numeric validation — isNaN/Number accepts Infinity and negatives without a range guard (CWE-1284).
rules.remediation: Do not validate money/quantity with isNaN() alone. Require finiteness and a sign bound: `if (!Number.isFinite(x) || x < 0) reject()` (or x > 0), clamp with `Math.max(0, x)`, or enforce a schema bound such as zod `z.number().finite().nonnegative()` / `.positive()` or `Joi.number().min(0)`.
rules.why: isNaN() only rejects NaN; it returns false for Infinity (isNaN(Infinity) === false) and for every negative number. When it is the sole validator for a money/quantity value (price, amount, discount, qty/quantity, total, balance, cost, credit, points, refund), an attacker can submit a negative value or Infinity that passes the check, enabling negative-total abuse, credited/free purchases, and downstream overflow. This is CWE-1284 (Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input). The rule fires on isNaN(<money-ish var>) only when the SAME line carries no Number.isFinite() check, no 0-bound comparison (<0/<=0/>=0/>0), no Math.max(0,...) clamp, and no zod/Joi .positive()/.min()/.nonnegative() schema, and it is not a comment line.

rules.name: js-redos-ambiguous-alternation-quantified
rules.message: ReDoS — a regex with nested or overlapping quantifiers can backtrack catastrophically on crafted input, freezing the process (CWE-1333).
rules.remediation: Make the alternatives mutually exclusive (remove the duplicate branch, or reorder/anchor so they cannot both match the same prefix), or match with a linear-time engine (RE2/node-re2); always bound input length for user-supplied data.
rules.why: A quantified alternation whose branches overlap — (a|a)*, (foo|foo)+, (a|ab)+, (\w|\w)* — lets the engine match the same text through multiple branches, so a long repeated-token input explodes into exponential backtracking. The sink uses a backreference \1 to require one alternative to be a literal duplicate or prefix of the next, inside a group that is immediately quantified by + or *, so disjoint alternations ((cat|dog)+, (GET|POST)+), logical/bitwise x || y and (a | ab) & mask, and unquantified ambiguous groups ((foo|foobar)) are all left alone. Case-sensitive (ignoreCase false) so the duplicate must be exact.

rules.name: js-redos-quantified-group-within-quantified-group
rules.message: ReDoS — a regex with nested or overlapping quantifiers can backtrack catastrophically on crafted input, freezing the process (CWE-1333).
rules.remediation: Collapse the nested quantifiers into one (anchor the pattern and use a single bounded, non-overlapping subpattern for each label/segment), validate and length-limit the input before matching, or run the pattern through a linear-time engine (RE2/node-re2).
rules.why: Two stacked quantified groups — an inner (...)+/(...)* nested inside an outer (...)+/(...)*, separated only by a short literal delimiter — is the canonical catastrophic shape (the email/hostname (([...])+\.)+ and (([...])*_)* forms). Ambiguous partitioning of a long near-match drives exponential backtracking; feeding it request data is a single-request DoS. The sink flags a quantified group close )+ or )* followed, with no intervening parenthesis, by another )+ / )*. The separator between the two closes is restricted to non-alphanumeric chars ([^()a-zA-Z0-9]*): real ReDoS separators are punctuation/escapes (\. - _ @ / :), whereas nested arithmetic such as ((a+b)*c)*d or ((x+1)*2)+3 puts an operand (word char) between the two )*/)+ and is therefore not flagged.

rules.name: js-reflected-html-res-send-concat
rules.message: Reflected / context-mismatched XSS — user input reaches HTML or JS output without proper contextual encoding (CWE-79/116).
rules.remediation: HTML-escape the value for text context (escapeHtml/he.encode) or run it through a sanitizer (DOMPurify/sanitize-html) before concatenation, or render via an auto-escaping template instead of string building.
rules.why: Express handler concatenates user input (req.query/body/params/cookies/headers) into an HTML fragment emitted by res.send/write/end (optionally via a res.status(...).send() chain) with no HTML-entity encoding, so tags and attributes in the input are reflected verbatim -> reflected XSS.

rules.name: js-reflected-html-send-unescaped-var
rules.message: Reflected XSS — an unescaped variable is interpolated into an HTML response (CWE-79).
rules.remediation: HTML-entity-encode the value for its context (escapeHtml/he.encode) or run it through a sanitiser (DOMPurify/sanitize-html) before it enters the markup, or render via an auto-escaping template engine instead of hand-building HTML; never interpolate or concatenate a raw string variable directly into a tag. Send structured data with res.json when the client expects data, not HTML.
rules.why: res.send/write/end (or reply.send, incl. a res.status(...).send() / res.type('text/html').send() chain) emits a backtick template OR a string concatenation that both contains an HTML tag (a '<' followed by a letter or slash) AND interpolates/concatenates a bare, un-escaped variable into element/attribute context. Both facts are required by two lookaheads, so it does not fire on a literal-only body or a bare non-HTML value. Broadens the req.*-only reflected-XSS rule: the tainted value is commonly one hop removed from the request (e.g. `replaced`, built by templateStr.replace(token, req.query.x)), which a literal-req.* match misses. Any unescaped string variable placed inside a tag is reflected/stored XSS. The concat branch anchors a string-literal quote adjacent to the + so it matches 'variable spliced into HTML', not a bare var+var expression. notMatch drops escaped/sanitised values (escapeHtml/htmlEscape/encodeHTML/he.encode/he.escape/DOMPurify/sanitize/xss()/a .replace or .replaceAll that encodes <>& via a regex, char-class, or string literal), encodeURI(Component), the deprecated escape(), res.json, obviously-numeric interpolations or concatenations (count/length/id/index/total/idx/size/num/offset/limit, covered in both the ${...} and + var forms), auto-escaping template renders ({{ }} is not ${}), and comment lines.

rules.name: js-reflected-html-template-literal-text
rules.message: Reflected / context-mismatched XSS — user input reaches HTML or JS output without proper contextual encoding (CWE-79/116).
rules.remediation: Escape the interpolated value for HTML text context (escapeHtml/he.encode) or sanitize with DOMPurify/sanitize-html; prefer an auto-escaping template engine over hand-built HTML template literals.
rules.why: A template-literal HTML string interpolates ${req.*} directly into element/text (or attribute) context with no encoding, so injected markup is reflected into the response -> reflected XSS. The tag-open must sit at the template start or follow a delimiter (whitespace/>/quote/}/etc.), which excludes TypeScript generics (Array<string>) and bare comparison operators that are not real tags.

rules.name: js-replace-user-replacement-token
rules.message: Replacement-token injection — user input used as a replace() replacement or preg_replace /e is interpreted, not literal (CWE-116/94).
rules.remediation: Pass a replacer FUNCTION instead of a raw string, e.g. str.replace(pattern, () => userValue), so no token expansion occurs. If a string replacement is required, first escape dollar signs in the user value with a global replace of the dollar sign by a doubled dollar. Never bind untrusted input directly as the replacement argument.
rules.why: The second argument of String#replace / #replaceAll is a REPLACEMENT string, not literal text: the dollar tokens expand to the whole match, the pre-match text, the post-match text, a numbered capture group, or a literal dollar. When that argument is a bare user-controlled identifier/member (or a concatenation led by one) rather than a function or a fixed literal, an attacker can embed those tokens to splice adjacent buffer content into the output. The sink fires only when arg1 is a regex/string/identifier pattern and arg2 is an identifier/member (optionally subscripted) closed by ) or +, so string-literal replacements, inline function replacements (function/async/paren-wrapped, and single-param arrows because `id =>` is followed by = not )/+), CALL replacements like escapeHtml(x) / JSON.stringify(x) / schema.parse(x) (a ( follows the callee), and optional-chaining members like req?.query?.name (the ? is outside [\w$.]) are all excluded by construction; notMatch drops comment lines and lines that globally escape the dollar sign (/\$/g). Verified precise: no regex change was required and it does not fire on any safe twin tested.

rules.name: js-unhandled-json-parse-request-noguard
rules.message: Unvalidated request input may throw an unhandled exception (robustness / DoS, CWE-20/248).
rules.remediation: Wrap the parse in try/catch and respond 400 on failure, e.g. `let data; try { data = JSON.parse(req.body); } catch { return res.status(400).end(); }`, or validate with a schema (zod/Joi) first. If a body parser already ran, use req.body directly instead of re-parsing. Note `|| '{}'` / `?? '{}'` is not a fix — it does not catch malformed JSON.
rules.why: JSON.parse called directly on a request-derived value throws an uncaught SyntaxError when the client sends malformed JSON (and `|| '{}'` / `?? '{}'` defaults do NOT help, since they only patch null/undefined, not an invalid string). With no try/catch on the line the exception escapes the handler and, absent a global error boundary, 500s or crashes the process. Refinement vs. the original: the sink's property was narrowed from `(?:req|request|ctx|event)\.<anything>` to an input-bearing property allowlist (body/query/params/headers/cookies/rawBody/payload/data/request/files/...). The original broad form fired on `JSON.parse(req.app.get('cfg'))` — parsing a server-side config off the Express app handle, not user input — a verified false positive now suppressed by the sink. The try/catch, comment, and schema/validate suppressors keep it off guarded parses; requiring the property-access form (not JSON.parse(localVar)) keeps it off non-request parses.

rules.name: js-url-attr-fully-user-controlled
rules.message: Reflected / context-mismatched XSS — user input reaches HTML or JS output without proper contextual encoding (CWE-79/116).
