rules.remediation: Validate and normalize the URL with new URL()/sanitize-url and enforce a scheme allowlist (http/https/mailto/relative) before emitting it into the attribute.
rules.why: The entire href/src value begins with user input (${req.*} or ""+req.* right after the attribute quote), so an attacker can supply a javascript: or data: URL that executes -> XSS. A fixed prefix (host/#/path) before the interpolation is not matched, so only fully attacker-controlled URLs fire. HTML-entity escaping does not neutralize a dangerous URL scheme, making this a context-mismatch when only escaped.

rules.name: js-wrong-context-event-handler
rules.message: Reflected / context-mismatched XSS — user input reaches HTML or JS output without proper contextual encoding (CWE-79/116).
rules.remediation: Do not put user data in inline handlers; attach behavior via addEventListener reading a data-* attribute, or JSON.stringify the value into the handler. HTML escaping alone is insufficient for this context.
rules.why: User data is placed inside an inline event-handler attribute (onclick=, onerror=, ...) and appears before the tag's closing >, which is a JavaScript execution context. HTML-entity escaping is the wrong encoder and does not stop breakout, so the value runs as script -> context-mismatched-encoding XSS. The lookbehind excludes data-onclick-style attribute names and the [^>] bound stops an unrelated req later on the line from matching; lowercase handler names avoid React's camelCase onClick={} JSX.

rules.name: js-wrong-context-javascript-uri
rules.message: Reflected / context-mismatched XSS — user input reaches HTML or JS output without proper contextual encoding (CWE-79/116).
rules.remediation: Never build javascript: URLs from user input. Use a normal http(s)/relative URL and validate the scheme against an allowlist; bind dynamic behavior through JS event listeners instead.
rules.why: User data is appended into a javascript: URL in an href/src/action attribute and stays within the attribute's double-quoted value; the value runs as script when the link/form is activated. HTML-entity escaping is the wrong context and does not prevent execution -> XSS. The [^"] bound prevents a static javascript:void(0) href plus a separate data-* attribute carrying req from matching.

rules.name: js-wrong-context-script-block
rules.message: Reflected / context-mismatched XSS — user input reaches HTML or JS output without proper contextual encoding (CWE-79/116).
rules.remediation: Serialize the value with JSON.stringify() (and additionally escape < as < to defeat </script>), or emit it as a data-* attribute and read it via JS; never rely on HTML escaping inside <script>.
rules.why: User data is spliced into the body of a server-built <script> block (the req must appear after the opening tag's >, so <script src/data-* attribute lines are excluded). HTML-entity escaping is the wrong context here and cannot neutralize a JS string breakout or a literal </script> sequence, so the value executes -> context-mismatched-encoding XSS. Note htmlEscape() inside a script tag is still vulnerable.

rules.name: jwt-decode-noverify
rules.message: jwt.decode() does not verify the signature.
rules.remediation: Use jwt.verify() with the key so a forged token is rejected.
rules.why: decode() reads the claims without checking they were signed, so the values cannot be trusted for a security decision.

rules.name: jwt-long-lived-token
rules.message: A token or session is issued with a very long lifetime.
rules.remediation: Keep access tokens short-lived (minutes to hours) and use a revocable refresh token or server-side session for longer sessions.
rules.why: A JWT or session that lives for months or years cannot be revoked in practice: a stolen token stays valid long after the breach, and there is no natural point to re-check the user's status or permissions.

rules.name: jwt-missing-expiry
rules.message: jwt.sign is called without an expiry (expiresIn).
rules.remediation: Always pass an expiry, e.g. jwt.sign(payload, key, { expiresIn: '15m' }), and set exp explicitly if you build the payload yourself.
rules.why: A JWT with no exp claim never expires: once issued it is valid forever, so a leaked token grants permanent access and cannot be aged out.

rules.name: jwt-none
rules.message: A JWT is accepted with algorithm 'none'.
rules.remediation: Pin a real algorithm (e.g. RS256/HS256) and never allow 'none'.
rules.why: The 'none' algorithm means no signature, so anyone can forge a token the server will trust.

rules.name: lfi-md-html-inline-image-user-src
rules.message: Renderer resource embedding — a document/PDF/image converter resolves a user-controlled resource, enabling LFI or SSRF (CWE-918/73/611).
rules.remediation: Resolve the attribute against a fixed asset root and enforce containment (path.resolve + startsWith(baseDir) or basename-only), reject absolute/traversal/file:// values, and allowlist permitted directories.
rules.why: A Markdown/HTML renderer that inlines images/assets reads a local file whose path is the src/href attribute parsed from user content (to base64-embed it); an attacker sets src to /etc/passwd or a traversal path, yielding local file inclusion (LFI). Added PHP fopen/readfile to the read-sink set; containment/realpath/basename/allowlist guards and window.open are suppressed.

rules.name: lfi-mpdf-writehtml-user
rules.message: Renderer resource embedding — a document/PDF/image converter resolves a user-controlled resource, enabling LFI or SSRF (CWE-918/73/611).
rules.remediation: Render only trusted/templated HTML, restrict allowed image roots, and disable remote resource loading; do not pass raw request input to WriteHTML.
rules.why: mPDF $mpdf->WriteHTML($userHtml) embeds images/stylesheets/backgrounds referenced by attacker markup; a local path in an /CSS url() causes local file inclusion (LFI), and remote refs cause outbound fetches (SSRF). SetHTMLHeader/SetHTMLFooter are excluded because the sink requires the exact method WriteHTML.

rules.name: lfi-nbconvert-untrusted-notebook
rules.message: Renderer resource embedding — a document/PDF/image converter resolves a user-controlled resource, enabling LFI or SSRF (CWE-918/73/611).
rules.remediation: Never nbconvert untrusted notebooks with --execute; sanitize/strip attachments and custom templates, run in an isolated sandbox, and validate the notebook path against an allowlist.
rules.why: jupyter nbconvert on an untrusted .ipynb renders attacker-controlled cell/attachment/template content; templates and outputs can reference local files (LFI), and --execute additionally runs embedded code. Log lines are suppressed to avoid status-logging noise.

rules.name: lfi-pandoc-no-sandbox-user-input
rules.message: Renderer resource embedding — a document/PDF/image converter resolves a user-controlled resource, enabling LFI or SSRF (CWE-918/73/611).
rules.remediation: Run pandoc with --sandbox on untrusted input, restrict --resource-path to a safe directory, and disable raw HTML/TeX; avoid concatenating request data that selects the input file.
rules.why: pandoc converting user-supplied documents can read arbitrary local files through include directives, raw LaTeX \input, and embedded image/resource paths, giving local file inclusion (LFI) when run without --sandbox. Taint gate now covers Ruby #{} and PHP '. $var'; literal-only invocations with a trailing keyword arg (e.g. check=True) and log lines no longer fire.

rules.name: lfi-puppeteer-allow-file-access-flag
rules.message: Renderer resource embedding — a document/PDF/image converter resolves a user-controlled resource, enabling LFI or SSRF (CWE-918/73/611).
rules.remediation: Remove these flags; keep default web-security and no local-file access, and gate remote fetches with request interception.
rules.why: Launching the headless-Chrome converter with --allow-file-access-from-files or --disable-web-security lets user-supplied HTML read local files via file:// (LFI) and bypass same-origin protections when rendered to PDF/image. Prose mentions without the leading '--' do not match.

rules.name: lfi-xhtml2pdf-pisa-createpdf
rules.message: Renderer resource embedding — a document/PDF/image converter resolves a user-controlled resource, enabling LFI or SSRF (CWE-918/73/611).
rules.remediation: Supply a link_callback that maps only allowlisted static/media directories and rejects absolute/traversal paths and file:// URIs; render fixed sources where possible.
rules.why: xhtml2pdf/pisa CreatePDF/pisaDocument on user-controlled HTML resolves image/link resources through its resource resolver; without a restricting link_callback an attacker references local files (LFI) via the src/href in the supplied markup.

rules.name: logging-disabled
rules.message: Logging is turned off or discarded.
rules.remediation: Keep security-relevant logging enabled in production (auth successes/failures, access-control denials, input-validation failures) and forward it to monitoring; only reduce verbosity, never silence it.
rules.why: Disabling logging or routing it to a null sink removes the audit trail: authentication failures, authorization denials, and errors that reveal an attack in progress are never recorded, so incidents go undetected and cannot be investigated afterwards.

rules.name: logic-client-price-trust
rules.message: Client-controlled price, discount, total, or privilege field is trusted directly from request payload.
rules.remediation: Recompute pricing and discounts server-side from authoritative catalog records and never accept client-supplied roles or privilege flags.

positive: await orders.create({ itemId: req.body.itemId, price: req.body.price });
negative: await orders.create({ itemId: item.id, price: catalogItem.price });

rules.name: logic-jwt-unverified-decode
rules.message: JWT decoded or configured without cryptographic signature verification (alg=none or unverified decode).
rules.remediation: Always use jwt.verify / verify_signature=True with an explicit asymmetric or HMAC algorithm allowlist excluding 'none'.

rules.name: logic-race-non-atomic-balance
rules.message: Non-atomic read-modify-write update on balance, credits, or inventory risks race-condition double spending.
rules.remediation: Perform balance or inventory deductions inside a database transaction with conditional atomic updates (UPDATE ... SET balance = balance - $1 WHERE id = $2 AND balance >= $1).

rules.name: logic-webhook-missing-timestamp
rules.message: Webhook signature read without visible timestamp or replay-window validation.
rules.remediation: Enforce timestamp tolerance checks alongside HMAC signature verification (or use provider SDK constructEvent helpers) to block webhook replay attacks.

negative: const sig = req.headers['x-webhook-signature']; verifyWithTimestamp(sig, req.headers['x-webhook-timestamp'], tolerance);

rules.name: loose-equality-secret
rules.message: A secret/code/role is compared with loose == (type coercion) instead of ===.
rules.remediation: Use strict === / !==, and compare secrets with a constant-time equality.
rules.why: With ==, {"resetCode": 0} or false coerces so that resetCode == 0 or resetCode == "" is true — an attacker passes a falsy value and bypasses the check without knowing the real code.

rules.name: mass-assign-object-assign-constraint-override
rules.message: Mass-assignment override (BOLA) — a user object merged after a security constraint can override it (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Apply the ownership/tenant constraint LAST so it always wins: Object.assign({}, req.body, { tenantId }). Better, never merge raw request input into a query or record - derive tenantId/userId from the authenticated session and allow-list the client fields with pick/omit or a schema (zod/joi/yup) so ownership keys can never be supplied by the client.
rules.why: Object.assign and the lodash assign/assignIn/extend/merge/mergeWith family, jQuery/$.extend, and angular.extend copy properties left-to-right so the RIGHTMOST source wins. The rule fires only when a fixed ownership/tenant constraint object literal ({ tenantId }, { userId }, { orgId }, { isAdmin: false }, ...) is NOT the last argument, enforced by the trailing \}\s*, (a comma must follow the constraint object). A later source is typically user-controlled (req.body/req.query, or a variable holding them such as queryFilter = req.body.filter), so the client can send its own tenantId/userId, override the server-set restriction, and read or mutate another tenant's/owner's records - CWE-639 authorization bypass through a user-controlled key, the classic multi-tenant BOLA. The critical sample Object.assign({}, { tenantId }, queryFilter) is caught because { tenantId } is followed by another argument. The safe twin Object.assign({}, req.body, { tenantId }) does NOT fire: the constraint is last, followed by ) not a comma. _.defaults is deliberately excluded from the sink because it fills only undefined keys (leftmost wins, safe).

rules.name: mass-assign-spread-constraint-override
rules.message: Mass-assignment override (BOLA) — a user object merged after a security constraint can override it (CWE-639).
rules.remediation: Put the constraint AFTER the user object so it wins - { ...req.body, tenantId } or { ...req.body, ...{ tenantId } } - or set it as the final literal property. Do not spread req.body/req.query over a scoped base object. Prefer building the object from session-derived ownership values plus an allow-list (pick/omit or a zod/joi/yup schema) of the client-writable fields.
rules.why: Object spread applies properties left-to-right and LATER keys overwrite earlier ones, so a constraint appearing before a user-controlled spread is silently overridden. Three shapes are matched, each now requiring the overriding source to be req.body/query/params for precision: (1) inline constraint-literal spread followed by a user spread - { ...{ tenantId }, ...req.body } (optionally parenthesized/cast, e.g. ...(req.body as object)); (2) a constraint property followed by a user spread - { tenantId, ...req.body }, { userId: session.userId, ...req.body }; and (3) a constraint-scope VARIABLE spread followed by a user spread - { ...tenantScope, ...req.body }, { ...constraint, ...req.query }. Branch (3) was tightened from the original '...anyVar, ...req.body' (which fired on the ubiquitous safe pattern { ...defaults, ...req.body }) to require the variable name to carry an ownership token (tenant/owner/org/account/scope/constraint, either case), so defaults/baseSettings/pagination no longer match. In every matched case the client can supply tenantId/userId/ownerId in req.* and break tenant/owner isolation (CWE-639). Safe twins do not fire: { ...req.body, ...{ tenantId } } and { ...req.body, tenantId } (constraint wins, placed last), { ...{ label:'x' }, ...req.body } (non-constraint literal), and destructuring rest const { tenantId, ...rest } = req.body (spread is ...rest, not ...req).

rules.name: math-rand-time-as-session-go
rules.message: Predictable session/token identifier — a security id from a non-CSPRNG or observable source (CWE-330/340).
rules.remediation: Use crypto/rand (rand.Read into a byte slice, then hex/base64 encode) or a v4 UUID for session ids and tokens; math/rand and time are unsuitable.
rules.why: Go's math/rand (rand.Intn, rand.Int63, rand.Uint64, ...) is a deterministic PRNG and time.Now().Unix()/UnixNano() is an observable clock; these functions do not exist on crypto/rand, so matching them signals a predictable session id or token.

rules.name: math-random-as-session-token-js
rules.message: Predictable session/token identifier — a security id from a non-CSPRNG or observable source (CWE-330/340).
rules.remediation: Replace Math.random() with a CSPRNG: crypto.randomBytes / crypto.randomUUID in Node, or crypto.getRandomValues in the browser.
rules.why: Math.random() is a non-cryptographic PRNG whose internal state can be recovered from a few outputs, so tokens or session ids built from it are predictable and forgeable.

rules.name: mutation-xss
rules.message: Re-serialising SVG/MathML content can produce mutation XSS (mXSS).
rules.remediation: Never hand-serialise inside SVG/MathML; sanitise with a namespace-aware parser such as DOMPurify.
rules.why: When the parser crosses the SVG/MathML namespace boundary during re-serialisation, a payload in <annotation-xml> or a style element can mutate into an executable script attribute on insertion.

rules.name: netauthz-forwardable-header-as-auth-cs
rules.message: Broken access control — authorization based on network location or a spoofable client header (CWE-346/290).
rules.remediation: Do not authorize on X-* request headers; use ASP.NET auth (cookie/JWT, [Authorize]). If a trusted reverse proxy sets the header, strip it at ingress and verify a signed proxy secret rather than a presence/equality check.
rules.why: ASP.NET Request.Headers["X-Forwarded-For"|"X-Internal"|"X-Admin"|...] compared with ==/.Equals to a value (or .Contains gating a grant) authorizes on a client-settable header. With or without ForwardedHeaders these X-* values pass through non-stripping proxies and are forgeable, so an attacker gains privilege. notMatch excludes logging, IP-splitting, and existing real auth checks.

rules.name: netauthz-forwardable-header-as-auth-go
rules.message: Broken access control — authorization based on network location or a spoofable client header (CWE-346/290).
rules.remediation: Do not authorize on X-* request headers. Use a verified token/session. If a trusted proxy sets the header, strip it at ingress and verify a signed proxy secret rather than a plain equality/non-empty check.
rules.why: r.Header.Get("X-Forwarded-For"|"X-Internal"|"X-Admin"|...) compared to a value, or a non-empty presence check (!= "") gating grant/allow/authorize/isAdmin, authorizes on a client-settable header. These survive non-stripping proxies, so an external client forges one for privilege. notMatch excludes logging, IP-splitting, and rate-limit uses.

rules.name: netauthz-forwardable-header-as-auth-java-kt
rules.message: Broken access control — authorization based on network location or a spoofable client header (CWE-346/290).
rules.remediation: Do not trust X-* request headers for authorization; use Spring Security / a verified token. If a trusted proxy sets the header, strip it at the edge and verify a signed proxy value instead of a presence/equality check.
rules.why: request.getHeader("X-Forwarded-For"|"X-Internal"|"X-Admin"|...) compared with equals/==, or a != null presence check gating grant/allow/authorize/isAdmin, authorizes on a client-settable header. These pass through non-stripping proxies, so an attacker forges one. notMatch excludes logging, IP-extraction, and rate-limit uses.

rules.name: netauthz-forwardable-header-as-auth-js
rules.message: Broken access control — authorization based on network location or a spoofable client header (CWE-346/290).
rules.remediation: Never trust X-Forwarded-* or custom X-* headers for access control. Authenticate with a verified token/session. If a trusted proxy injects such a header, have the proxy strip it on ingress and validate a proxy-signed secret, not a plain presence/equality check.
rules.why: A forwardable/custom request header (X-Forwarded-For, X-Internal, X-Admin, X-User-Role, X-Auth-Token, etc.) is compared to a value, or its mere presence gates grant/allow/authorize/next(). These headers are fully client-settable and pass untouched through proxies that do not strip them, so any external client forges one to gain privilege. X-Forwarded-Proto was removed from the header list because its === 'https' compare drives HTTPS-redirect logic, not auth; notMatch also excludes IP-extraction, logging, rate-limiting, and redirect lines.

rules.name: netauthz-forwardable-header-as-auth-php
rules.message: Broken access control — authorization based on network location or a spoofable client header (CWE-346/290).
rules.remediation: Never authorize on HTTP_X_* request headers. Use a real session ($_SESSION after login) or verified token. If a trusted proxy injects the header, strip and re-set it at the edge and verify a signed proxy secret.
rules.why: $_SERVER['HTTP_X_FORWARDED_FOR'|'HTTP_X_ADMIN'|'HTTP_X_INTERNAL'|...] compared to a value, or isset()/!empty() gating grant/allow/authorize/$admin=, authorizes on a client-settable header (PHP maps X-* request headers into HTTP_X_*). These headers pass through non-stripping proxies, so an external client forges one. notMatch excludes logging/rate-limit/IP-extraction.

rules.name: netauthz-forwardable-header-as-auth-py
rules.message: Broken access control — authorization based on network location or a spoofable client header (CWE-346/290).
rules.remediation: Do not authorize on X-Forwarded-* or custom X-* headers. Use Flask-Login/session or a verified token. If a trusted proxy sets the header, strip it at the edge and verify a proxy-signed value rather than trusting presence/equality.
rules.why: Flask request.headers X-Forwarded-For / X-Internal / X-Admin / X-User-Role compared to a value, or present and gating grant/allow/authorize/is_admin, authorizes on a client-settable header. Such headers survive non-stripping proxies, so an attacker forges one for privilege. X-Forwarded-Proto was removed from the list (its != 'https' compare is redirect logic, not auth); notMatch excludes IP-extraction, logging, rate-limit, and redirect uses.

rules.name: netauthz-forwardable-header-as-auth-rb
rules.message: Broken access control — authorization based on network location or a spoofable client header (CWE-346/290).
rules.remediation: Do not authorize on X-* request headers. Use Devise/session or a verified token. If a trusted proxy sets the header, strip and re-inject it at the edge and verify a signed proxy value.
rules.why: Rails request.headers['X-Forwarded-For'|'X-Admin'|'X-Internal'|...] (or get_header('HTTP_X_*')) compared to a value drives an access decision (the grant keyword precedes it in a postfix `if`). These headers are client-settable and survive non-stripping proxies, so an attacker forges one. notMatch excludes logging, IP-extraction, and rate-limit uses.

rules.name: netauthz-loopback-internal-ip-as-auth-js
rules.message: Broken access control — authorization based on network location or a spoofable client header (CWE-346/290).
rules.remediation: Do not authenticate by source IP. Require a real credential (session, signed/verified token, mTLS). If a localhost-only surface is genuinely needed, enforce it by binding to 127.0.0.1 at the network layer, not with an in-request IP comparison.
rules.why: Comparing req.ip / connection|socket.remoteAddress to a loopback (127.0.0.1, ::1) or private-range literal (10., 192.168., 172.16-31) treats network position as identity. Any client behind the same reverse proxy/NAT, or one that can influence the derived IP (e.g. via X-Forwarded-For when trust_proxy is set), reaches the privileged branch.

rules.name: netauthz-origin-referer-as-auth-cs
rules.message: Broken access control — authorization based on network location or a spoofable client header (CWE-346/290).
rules.remediation: Use ASP.NET authentication/authorization (cookie/JWT, [Authorize]) rather than the Origin/Referer header. Use Origin only for CORS and antiforgery-token CSRF defense.
rules.why: ASP.NET Request.Headers["Origin"|"Referer"] equals/StartsWith/Equals a trusted value to decide access. These are client-controlled headers, forgeable off-browser, so an attacker supplies the expected value to bypass the gate. CORS Append/Add and logging are excluded by notMatch.

rules.name: netauthz-origin-referer-as-auth-go
rules.message: Broken access control — authorization based on network location or a spoofable client header (CWE-346/290).
rules.remediation: Do not authorize on Origin/Referer. Use a verified token/session for identity; use Origin only for CORS responses and add CSRF protection.
rules.why: r.Header.Get("Origin"|"Referer") equals or HasPrefix-matches a trusted value to decide access. Both headers are client-set and forgeable, so an attacker supplies the expected Origin/Referer to reach the privileged branch. CORS Set/Add and logging are excluded by notMatch.

rules.name: netauthz-origin-referer-as-auth-java-kt
rules.message: Broken access control — authorization based on network location or a spoofable client header (CWE-346/290).
rules.remediation: Authorize with Spring Security / a verified token, not the Origin/Referer header. Use Origin only when building CORS responses; defend CSRF with tokens and SameSite cookies.
rules.why: request.getHeader("Origin"|"Referer") equals/startsWith a trusted string and that grants access. These headers are client-controlled and forgeable off-browser, so an attacker supplies the expected value to bypass the gate. CORS setHeader/addHeader and logging are excluded by notMatch.

rules.name: netauthz-origin-referer-as-auth-js
rules.message: Broken access control — authorization based on network location or a spoofable client header (CWE-346/290).
rules.remediation: Never use Origin/Referer as an authentication or authorization signal. Use a session or verified token for identity; use Origin only for CORS response headers and CSRF defenses (alongside SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens).
rules.why: The Origin/Referer request header equals or startsWith a trusted value and that decides access. Both headers are set by the client (or absent/forgeable off-browser), so treating them as identity lets an attacker send the expected Origin/Referer and take the privileged path. Distinct from CORS header-setting, which the notMatch excludes.

rules.name: netauthz-origin-referer-as-auth-php
rules.message: Broken access control — authorization based on network location or a spoofable client header (CWE-346/290).
rules.remediation: Authorize on a session ($_SESSION with a real login) or verified token, not HTTP_ORIGIN/HTTP_REFERER. Use Origin only for CORS headers and add proper CSRF tokens.
rules.why: $_SERVER['HTTP_ORIGIN']/HTTP_REFERER compared to (or strpos-prefixed against) a trusted value to decide access treats a client-controlled header as identity. Both are forgeable outside a browser, so the check is bypassable. CORS/logging lines are excluded by notMatch.

rules.name: netauthz-origin-referer-as-auth-py
rules.message: Broken access control — authorization based on network location or a spoofable client header (CWE-346/290).
rules.remediation: Do not authorize on Origin/Referer. Use Flask-Login/session or a verified token for identity; reserve Origin for CORS config and pair CSRF tokens with SameSite cookies.
rules.why: Flask request.headers Origin/Referer (or request.referrer) equals/startsWith a trusted value to decide access. These headers are client-supplied and forgeable, so an attacker sends the expected value to reach the privileged branch. CORS/logging/analytics uses are excluded by notMatch.

rules.name: netauthz-origin-referer-as-auth-rb
rules.message: Broken access control — authorization based on network location or a spoofable client header (CWE-346/290).
rules.remediation: Authorize with Devise/session or a verified token, not the Origin/Referer header. Reserve Origin for CORS and rely on Rails CSRF protection with SameSite cookies.
rules.why: Rails request.origin/referer (or headers['Origin'/'Referer']) equals/start_with? a trusted value to authorize. These headers are client-supplied and forgeable, so an attacker sends the expected value to bypass the gate. CORS/logging lines are excluded by notMatch.

rules.name: netauthz-remote-addr-as-auth-go
rules.message: Broken access control — authorization based on network location or a spoofable client header (CWE-346/290).
rules.remediation: Authorize with a verified token/session. For internal-only services rely on network segmentation or a 127.0.0.1 listen address, not an r.RemoteAddr comparison in the handler.
rules.why: r.RemoteAddr compared to (or HasPrefix-matched against) a loopback/private literal, or net.IP.IsLoopback()/IsPrivate() gating a branch, authorizes by network position. RemoteAddr is the TCP peer (the proxy behind a load balancer) and any forwarded-header-derived IP is client-controlled, so the gate is spoofable.

rules.name: netauthz-remote-addr-as-auth-java-kt
rules.message: Broken access control — authorization based on network location or a spoofable client header (CWE-346/290).
rules.remediation: Use Spring Security / a verified token or session for authorization. If an endpoint must be internal-only, enforce it via network ACLs or a bind address, not an in-servlet remote-address comparison.
rules.why: request.getRemoteAddr()/getRemoteHost() equals or startsWith a loopback/private literal, or InetAddress.isLoopbackAddress()/isSiteLocalAddress() gating privilege, authorizes by network location. Behind a load balancer getRemoteAddr() returns the proxy address and forwarded headers are attacker-controlled, so the check is bypassable.

rules.name: netauthz-remote-addr-as-auth-php
rules.message: Broken access control — authorization based on network location or a spoofable client header (CWE-346/290).
rules.remediation: Gate privilege on a verified session/token, not on REMOTE_ADDR. Restrict admin surfaces at the web-server/firewall layer if network isolation is required.
rules.why: $_SERVER['REMOTE_ADDR'] (or Symfony getClientIp()/ip()) compared to a loopback/private literal, or strpos() prefix-matched against a private range, uses source IP as an authorization credential. Behind a proxy REMOTE_ADDR is the proxy, and getClientIp() honors forwarded headers when trusted proxies are configured, so this is spoofable.

rules.name: netauthz-remote-addr-as-auth-py
rules.message: Broken access control — authorization based on network location or a spoofable client header (CWE-346/290).
rules.remediation: Authenticate with a session or verified token, not the client IP. If localhost-only access is required, bind the socket to 127.0.0.1; never gate privilege on remote_addr / access_route.
rules.why: Flask/WSGI request.remote_addr, access_route[0], or environ['REMOTE_ADDR'] compared to a loopback/private literal makes authorization depend on network location. remote_addr is trivially spoofed when a proxy sets it from a forwarded header, and access_route derives from X-Forwarded-For which is fully client-controlled.

rules.name: netauthz-remote-ip-as-auth-cs
rules.message: Broken access control — authorization based on network location or a spoofable client header (CWE-346/290).
rules.remediation: Use ASP.NET authentication/authorization ([Authorize], a verified token, or cookie auth). Restrict internal endpoints with Kestrel bind address or network policy, not a RemoteIpAddress comparison.
rules.why: ASP.NET Connection.RemoteIpAddress compared to a loopback/private literal, prefix-matched, or checked via IPAddress.IsLoopback / Equals(IPAddress.Loopback) authorizes by network location. With ForwardedHeaders middleware the RemoteIpAddress is derived from X-Forwarded-For and is spoofable.

rules.name: netauthz-remote-ip-as-auth-rb
rules.message: Broken access control — authorization based on network location or a spoofable client header (CWE-346/290).
rules.remediation: Gate privilege on Devise/session or a verified token, never on request.remote_ip. Enforce internal-only endpoints at the infrastructure layer.
rules.why: Rails request.remote_ip / request.ip compared to a loopback or private-range literal makes authorization depend on network location. remote_ip is computed from X-Forwarded-For / Client-IP headers, which are client-settable, so an attacker can forge a trusted value and reach the privileged action.

rules.name: network-graphql-introspection-enabled
rules.message: GraphQL schema introspection is unconditionally enabled, exposing all queries, mutations, and internal types.
rules.remediation: Disable GraphQL introspection in production (introspection: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production') and enforce query depth/complexity limits.

positive: const server = new ApolloServer({ typeDefs, resolvers, introspection: true });
negative: const server = new ApolloServer({ typeDefs, resolvers, introspection: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development' });

rules.name: network-http-smuggling-te-cl
rules.message: Lenient HTTP parser or conflicting Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length headers risk HTTP request smuggling.
rules.remediation: Reject requests containing both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length and disable insecureHTTPParser in Node.js HTTP servers/clients.

rules.name: new-function
rules.message: new Function() compiles a string into code.
rules.remediation: Use a real function, a lookup table, or JSON.parse for data.
rules.why: It is eval() by another name: the body is executed with the caller's authority.

rules.name: node-childprocess-exec-script-from-upload-dir
rules.message: Write-then-execute — code is loaded or run from a user-controlled or writable path (potential RCE, CWE-829/95/98/94).
rules.remediation: Only spawn interpreters/scripts from fixed, non-writable application paths; never pass an uploads/tmp path or req.file.path as the command or first argument, and validate any dynamic segment against an allow-list.
rules.why: child_process exec/spawn/fork of a program or script located in an uploads/tmp/writable directory (or taken from req.file) runs whatever an attacker uploaded there, converting a file-write into code execution. The keyword set was tightened from bare 'upload'/'writable' to variable-shaped tokens (upload*/writable* with Dir/Path suffix, uploaded*, os.tmpdir, req.file(s)., /tmp/), so benign data-path args in quoted literals (exec('rsync uploads/ backup/'), a script named 'upload_report.js') no longer flood.

rules.name: nosqli-basicquery-document-parse-dynamic
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Never parse raw request JSON into a query. Build the filter from explicitly typed, coerced fields (Criteria/Filters.eq with String.valueOf/parseInt), or validate the input against a schema/allowlist before use.
rules.why: Building a Mongo query from a dynamic value via new BasicQuery(...) or Document.parse(...) (argument begins with an identifier/expression/cast, not a fixed " string literal and not an UPPER_CASE constant) lets attacker-controlled JSON define query operators ($where, $ne, $gt, $regex), i.e. NoSQL/operator injection. Guard idioms are matched as stems so camelCase wrappers (schemaValidate, sanitizeJson, escapeMongo) suppress.

rules.name: nosqli-doctrine-findby-whole-request
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Pass a criteria array built from validated, type-cast scalars — findOneBy(['email' => (string) $data['email']]) — rather than $request->all()/$_POST.
rules.why: A Doctrine ODM repository findBy/findOneBy receives the whole request array as its criteria. With the MongoDB driver the nested-array input becomes query operators, so an attacker can bypass the intended criteria ({field: {$ne: null}}) or dump collections. Like the driver twin, the sink requires the request bag as the immediate first argument, so wrapped/validated forms dodge it.

rules.name: nosqli-koa-ctx-filter
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Coerce ctx values to scalars (String(ctx.request.body.x)) or validate the body with a schema (koa-joi-router / zod) before querying; never hand a raw ctx.query or ctx.request.body to a find/update filter.
rules.why: Koa exposes user input as ctx.query / ctx.params / ctx.request.body; here it flows into a Mongo filter either as the whole object or as an uncoerced field value, allowing operator injection ({ $ne: ... }, { $gt: ... }) exactly as with Express req.*.

rules.name: nosqli-mongo-filter-decoded-map
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Decode request input into a typed struct, or coerce each field to the expected scalar before use (body["user"].(string), strconv.Atoi, fmt.Sprint, cast.ToString). Reject non-string values instead of passing the raw interface{} into the filter.
rules.why: A mongo filter that reads a value straight out of a JSON-decoded request map (body["x"], payload["x"], req["x"], form/query values) whose values are interface{}. An attacker can send {"password": {"$ne": null}} so the value becomes a query operator object rather than a scalar, bypassing auth or matching arbitrary documents. Covers Find/FindOne/FindOneAnd*/UpdateOne/DeleteOne/ReplaceOne filters.

rules.name: nosqli-mongo-filter-raw-value
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Cast every user value to the expected scalar type inside the filter — (string) $request->username, (int) $_GET['id'], $request->string('name') — or validate against a schema before querying.
rules.why: A filter field is set to a raw request value ('username' => $request->username, 'name' => $_POST['name']) with no scalar coercion. Because PHP query strings can carry nested arrays, the value may arrive as {"$ne": null} or {"$regex": ".*"}, injecting operators into the field predicate (e.g. login bypass on password). notMatch adds Laravel typed accessors (->string()/->integer()/->boolean()/->float()) which return coerced values; note a coercer anywhere on the line suppresses the whole line (accepted recall trade-off for precision). Any cast placed before the value also breaks the sink itself, since the token right after => is then '(' rather than '$'.

rules.name: nosqli-mongo-filter-request-map
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Never use the raw request map as a filter. Construct the Document field-by-field with typed keys and coerced scalar values (new Document("user", String.valueOf(body.get("user")))) or validate against a schema first.
rules.why: Passing a deserialized request map (a @RequestBody Map / params map, optionally wrapped in a Document/BasicDBObject) straight into a Mongo query lets the client supply operator keys ($ne, $gt, $regex, $where) inside field values, bypassing intended equality filters. The 'new' keyword is optional so Kotlin's Document(body) is caught; a Document built field-by-field with a literal key ('username', ...) is excluded because the raw map name never sits right after the paren.

rules.name: nosqli-mongo-operator-injection
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Avoid $where/$function on user input entirely. Coerce operands to scalars, and for $regex escape the pattern (escapeStringRegexp) or replace it with an anchored, validated value; prefer exact-match queries over user-controlled operators.
rules.why: A Mongo query operator ($where, $regex, $ne, $gt, $in, ...) is driven directly by request input. $where and $function evaluate attacker JavaScript (RCE / blind extraction); $regex enables ReDoS and enumeration; comparison operators leak or over-select data.

rules.name: nosqli-mongo-operator-injection-request
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Coerce the input to the expected scalar (or re.escape a $regex), and avoid $where entirely with user input: {'age': {'$gt': int(request.args['min'])}}.
rules.why: A Mongo query operator ($where/$regex/$ne/$gt/$in/…) is fed a request value directly. $where enables server-side JS injection; $regex enables ReDoS/bypass; comparison operators let an attacker widen the match set.

rules.name: nosqli-mongo-operator-req-input
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Escape regex input with regexp.QuoteMeta before building the $regex operand (or use an anchored, validated pattern), and avoid $where/$function on user data. Prefer typed field equality over operator objects driven by request values.
rules.why: Client input is placed directly as the operand of a dangerous mongo operator ($where JS, $regex, $expr, $function) read from a request accessor. Unescaped input in $regex enables regex injection / ReDoS, and in $where/$expr/$function it enables query or code injection.

rules.name: nosqli-mongo-where-concat
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Avoid $where entirely; express the condition with native operators over typed fields (bson.M{"field": value}). If a computed match is unavoidable, use $expr with typed operands, never a concatenated JS string.
rules.why: A bson $where filter whose JavaScript body is built by string concatenation (double-quote or backtick) or fmt.Sprintf. $where executes server-side JS, so any unescaped user value spliced into the string is arbitrary code / query injection (data exfiltration, DoS).

rules.name: nosqli-mongo-where-js-concat
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Avoid $where entirely; express the predicate with typed Criteria operators. If a numeric bound is needed, coerce the input (Long.parseLong/Integer.parseInt/.toInt()) and never concatenate raw strings into the JS body.
rules.why: A Mongo $where clause whose server-side JavaScript is built by string-concatenating user input allows JavaScript/operator injection into the query engine. The '+' must be followed by an identifier or quote (a numeric literal concatenation like '"..." + 5' is naturally excluded), and both Java (Integer.parseInt/Long.valueOf) and Kotlin (.toInt/.toLong/.toBigDecimal) numeric coercions suppress.

rules.name: nosqli-mongo-where-js-injection
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Avoid $where with user data entirely; express the condition with normal operators ($gt, $eq). If unavoidable, coerce interpolated values to numbers (intval/(int)) and never build the JS string from raw request input.
rules.why: A $where clause concatenates request input into server-side JavaScript. An attacker closes the expression and injects arbitrary JS (0;return true, sleep loops), yielding data exfiltration or denial of service. Note (string) casting does NOT prevent this (attacker breaks out of quotes), so only numeric coercers (intval/(int)/(float)) and preg_quote/number_format appear in notMatch — string casts are deliberately excluded.

rules.name: nosqli-mongo-whole-request-filter
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Never pass a raw request array as a filter. Validate to a typed shape first ($request->validate([...]) / ->safe()) and build the filter from scalars you cast yourself, e.g. ['email' => (string) $data['email']].
rules.why: The entire request bag ($request->all(), $request->query(), $_POST, $_GET) is passed as a Mongo query filter. PHP decodes user[$ne]=1 style input into nested arrays, so an attacker injects operators ({"$ne": null}, {"$gt": ""}) turning the filter into an auth bypass or full dump. The sink deliberately requires the request bag as the FIRST argument, so wrapped/validated variants (collect(...), array_map(...), $request->safe()) naturally dodge it and are also caught by notMatch.

rules.name: nosqli-mongodb-bsondocument-parse-request
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Bind the request to a typed DTO and build the filter from scalar fields via Builders<T>.Filter.Eq(x => x.Field, dto.Field). Never parse user-controlled JSON directly into a filter document.
rules.why: BsonDocument.Parse or BsonSerializer.Deserialize into an untyped BsonDocument/BsonValue/object/dynamic turns a raw user string into an operator-bearing filter document. The attacker supplies {"$where":"..."} or {"pwd":{"$ne":null}} and injects query operators (CWE-943). Deserializing into a typed DTO is excluded. notMatch drops input validated/whitelisted/schema-checked before use, or commented-out calls.

rules.name: nosqli-mongodb-json-string-concat
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Never assemble filter JSON from input. Use the typed Builders<T>.Filter API with scalar values (Builders<Doc>.Filter.Eq(d => d.Name, name)).
rules.why: MongoDB.Driver implicitly converts a JSON string to a FilterDefinition. Building that JSON by string concatenation ("{ ... " + input) or interpolation with a placeholder ($"{{ ... {input} }}") lets an attacker inject query operators or extra clauses (CWE-943). The concat branch now requires a closing quote before the + ("\{[^;]*"\s*\+) so a literal + inside a value ("{ expr: 'a+b' }") no longer false-fires, and the interpolation branch requires an actual placeholder (\$"\{\{[^;]*\{[^{]) so a placeholder-less interpolated constant ($"{{ status: 'active' }}") no longer fires. notMatch drops values numerically coerced before insertion, and commented-out lines. Regex.Escape was removed from notMatch: it does not escape the JSON string-terminating quote and so does not stop this injection.

rules.name: nosqli-mongodb-jsonfilterdefinition-request
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Construct filters from typed, validated fields via Builders<T>.Filter.Eq(...). Do not feed request strings into JsonFilterDefinition.
rules.why: new JsonFilterDefinition<T>(userInput) wraps a raw user-controlled JSON string as the query filter, allowing operator injection identical to BsonDocument.Parse: the attacker supplies {"$ne":null} or {"$where":"..."} to subvert the query (CWE-943). \s* was added around the generic angle bracket to tolerate spacing. notMatch drops input validated/whitelisted/sanitized before use, or commented-out calls.

rules.name: nosqli-mongodb-where-injection
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Do not use $where. Express the condition with typed comparison filters (Builders<T>.Filter). If $where is truly required, use a constant function with bound scope variables and never concatenate request input.
rules.why: A MongoDB $where clause evaluates a server-side JavaScript string. Concatenating or interpolating user input into that string is direct code injection: an attacker breaks out of the predicate to run arbitrary JS or force full-collection scans (CWE-943). The concat trigger is tightened to a + adjacent to a string quote ("\s*\+ or \+\s*"), so a constant JS expression that merely contains arithmetic ("this.a + this.b") no longer false-fires; interpolation ($") and String.Format/Concat are still caught. notMatch drops values coerced to a number ((int)/int.Parse/Convert.To*) before use, or commented-out lines. Regex.Escape was removed from notMatch because escaping regex metacharacters does not neutralize JavaScript $where injection and would mask real bugs.

rules.name: nosqli-mongoengine-raw-request
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Do not build __raw__ from request data; validate/coerce fields first, or express the query with typed MongoEngine field lookups instead of __raw__.
rules.why: MongoEngine's __raw__ escape hatch passes a request-controlled dict straight to the driver, so injected operators reach the query unchecked — the same operator-injection bypass as raw PyMongo.

rules.name: nosqli-mongoid-params-hash-filter
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Whitelist and coerce before querying: build the selector from strong params with explicit scalar keys (Model.where(status: params[:status].to_s)), or params.permit(:status).to_h / params.slice(:state); never pass an unfiltered hash as a Mongo selector.
rules.why: Passing the raw params hash (or a params sub-hash) straight into a Mongoid criteria method (.where(params), .where(params[:filter]), .or(params[:query])) hands the attacker control of the whole selector. Because Rails parses query/body into nested hashes, a request like filter[age][$gt]=0 injects Mongo operators ($gt, $ne, $regex, $where), enabling filter bypass and data exposure with no key whitelisting or scalar coercion. The params\b boundary already excludes local vars named params_hash/parameters; strong-params and coercion idioms plus full-line comments are suppressed.

rules.name: nosqli-mongoid-where-js-string
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Never build a $where/JS string from input. Use a field criterion with a coerced scalar (Model.where(:age.gt => params[:min].to_i)) or a plain equality hash (Model.where(name: params[:name].to_s)); if a numeric threshold is unavoidable, wrap it in Integer(...) / .to_i.
rules.why: Passing a String to Mongoid's .where sends it to MongoDB as a $where JavaScript predicate that is eval'd server-side. Interpolating or concatenating user input into that string (.where("this.age > #{params[:min]}"), .where("...'" + params[:name] + "'")) lets an attacker inject arbitrary JS to bypass the filter, run heavy loops (DoS), or exfiltrate data. String coercion does not neutralize it; only numeric coercion / Regexp.escape is treated as safe here. Full-line comments are suppressed.

rules.name: nosqli-mongoid-where-keyvalue-params
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Force each request value to a scalar before it reaches the selector: Model.where(username: params[:username].to_s, password: hashed(params[:password].to_s)), wrap ids in BSON::ObjectId, or validate through the schema; never compare a raw params value for auth.
rules.why: field: params[:field] in a Mongoid selector looks scalar but Rails may deliver params[:field] as a Hash when the client sends field[$ne]= or field[$gt]=, turning the equality into an operator query. The classic case Model.where(username: params[:username], password: params[:password]) becomes an auth bypass (password[$ne]=). Without .to_s/Integer coercion or a BSON::ObjectId cast the value is attacker-typed. Note: this shape is also common and safe under pure ActiveRecord/SQL (values are typed/quoted there), so on an AR-heavy codebase expect benign matches unless coercion is present; the notMatch coercion signals are the intended rescue. Full-line comments and String()/Integer()/BSON casts are suppressed.

rules.name: nosqli-mongoose-field-req-nocoerce
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Coerce each user-supplied field to the expected primitive (String(req.body.username), Number(...), or new ObjectId(...)), or validate the body with a schema so object/operator payloads are rejected before they reach the query.
rules.why: A filter field is set to a request value (e.g. { username: req.body.username }) without coercing it to a scalar, so a JSON body like { "username": { "$ne": null } } turns the field comparison into an operator query — the canonical login-bypass NoSQL injection.

rules.name: nosqli-mongoose-whole-req
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Never pass a raw request object as a filter. Build the filter from explicitly named, type-coerced scalar fields (String(req.body.x)), or validate req.body against a Joi/zod schema (or a class-validator DTO) and use the sanitized result.
rules.why: The entire req.body/req.query object is passed as the query filter, so an attacker who sends { "$gt": "" } or { "$where": "..." } controls the query operators directly — the classic auth-bypass / data-exfiltration NoSQL injection.

rules.name: nosqli-pymongo-field-value-request
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Coerce each field to the expected scalar type or validate against a schema before querying: db.users.find_one({'username': str(request.json['username'])}).
rules.why: A filter field is set to a raw request value without coercion, so an attacker can pass {"$ne": null} / {"$gt": ""} instead of a scalar and match unintended documents (e.g. password/auth bypass).

rules.name: nosqli-pymongo-wholebody-filter-request
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Never pass request.* straight to a query. Validate with a schema (pydantic/marshmallow) and build the filter from coerced scalar fields: db.users.find_one({'username': str(data['username'])}).
rules.why: The entire request body/query dict is passed as a Mongo filter, so an attacker can substitute query operators ({"$ne": null}, {"$gt": ""}) for scalar values — classic authentication/authorisation bypass.

rules.name: nosqli-query-annotation-spel
rules.message: Possible NoSQL injection — user input flows into a query object/operator without type coercion (CWE-943).
rules.remediation: Use positional parameter binding (?0, ?1) which is bound as a value, not spliced into the query string. Reserve SpEL only for trusted server context (e.g. ?#{principal.id}, ?#{@authService.currentUserId()}), never for raw user input.
rules.why: A Spring Data Mongo @Query that interpolates through SpEL (?#{[0]} / ?#{#arg}) rather than the safe positional binder (?0) inserts the raw evaluated value into the query document, letting attacker input land in operator position ($regex/$where). Trusted server-context SpEL is suppressed: principal/authentication ownership refs, bean references ?#{@svc...}, and type references ?#{T(...)}.

rules.name: otp-weak-random
rules.message: GraphQL/dev misconfiguration — introspection or a dev endpoint exposed, or a weak/predictable secret (CWE-200/489/307/770/330).
rules.remediation: Generate these values with a cryptographically secure source: crypto.randomInt/randomBytes, Python secrets, java.security.SecureRandom, crypto/rand, PHP random_int, or RandomNumberGenerator.
rules.why: OTPs, reset tokens, and verification/MFA codes generated with a non-cryptographic PRNG (Math.random, random.randint, java.util.Random, math/rand, mt_rand/rand) are predictable: an attacker who knows the algorithm and a few outputs can forecast the next code and bypass verification. Requires both an OTP/token keyword and a weak-RNG call; suppressed by any crypto-strong source (crypto.randomInt/randomBytes, secrets.*, SecureRandom, RandomNumberGenerator.GetInt32, crypto/rand, random_int).

rules.name: path-containment-hasprefix-no-sep-go
rules.message: Path-containment bypass — a startsWith/indexOf prefix check with no trailing separator lets a sibling directory escape (CWE-22).
rules.remediation: Append the separator after filepath.Clean: strings.HasPrefix(resolved, base+string(os.PathSeparator)); or rel, err := filepath.Rel(base, target) and reject on err != nil or strings.HasPrefix(rel, "..").
rules.why: strings.HasPrefix(resolved, base) confines a cleaned/absolute path to a base but omits the trailing separator, so /var/www/uploads_backup satisfies HasPrefix for /var/www/uploads (CWE-22). Tightened: the second (generic-first-arg) branch dropped its bare string-literal needle — it fired on `strings.HasPrefix(r.URL.Path, "/api")` HTTP-middleware routing, which is everywhere in Go and would have gotten the rule dropped; base literals are still caught when the FIRST arg is a resolved/clean-path name. Bare `dir` needle removed (too generic). notMatch clears base+string(os.PathSeparator) / base+"/", filepath.Rel, and // comments.

rules.name: path-containment-indexof-no-sep-js
rules.message: Path-containment bypass — a startsWith/indexOf prefix check with no trailing separator lets a sibling directory escape (CWE-22).
rules.remediation: Append the separator and accept exact equality: `p === base || p.indexOf(base + path.sep) === 0`; better, after path.resolve test `!path.relative(base, p).startsWith('..')` and reject otherwise.
rules.why: A resolved/absolute path is confined to a base with `path.indexOf(base) === 0` / `!== 0` — a prefix test with no trailing separator — so a sibling whose name only starts with the base (/var/www/uploads_backup vs /var/www/uploads) is treated as inside it (CWE-22). Tightened from the original: the generic-receiver branch no longer accepts a bare path string literal (only a dir-VARIABLE/const argument), because an absolute literal like '/api' is indistinguishable from a route-prefix check and made the rule fire on ordinary `reqPath.indexOf('/api')===0` routing code; path literals are still caught when the RECEIVER is a resolved-path name. Bare base/root/cwd are now `\b`-bounded so `baseUrl`/`baseName` no longer match.

rules.name: path-containment-startswith-no-sep-js-java
rules.message: Path-containment bypass — a startsWith/indexOf prefix check with no trailing separator lets a sibling directory escape (CWE-22).
rules.remediation: Append the separator and allow equality: `resolved === base || resolved.startsWith(base + path.sep)` (Java: `canonical.equals(base) || canonical.startsWith(base + File.separator)`); or compare Path objects / test path.relative for a leading '..'.
rules.why: A canonicalized/resolved path is confined with `resolved.startsWith(base)` (or Java `file.getCanonicalPath().startsWith(base)`) without a trailing separator, so /var/www/uploads_backup satisfies a check for /var/www/uploads (CWE-22). Tightened: the third (generic-receiver) branch dropped its string-literal alternative so it no longer matches `req.path.startsWith('/api')` / `resolvedUrl.startsWith('/api')` routing code — literals remain caught via the resolved-path-receiver and getCanonicalPath()/getAbsolutePath() branches. notMatch clears base+path.sep / File.separator / '/', a trailing-slash literal, path.relative, a baseWithSep var, and comments.

rules.name: path-containment-startswith-no-sep-py
rules.message: Path-containment bypass — a startsWith/indexOf prefix check with no trailing separator lets a sibling directory escape (CWE-22).
rules.remediation: Use os.path.commonpath([base, resolved]) == base, or compare with the separator (resolved == base or resolved.startswith(base + os.sep)); never a bare startswith.
rules.why: A realpath/abspath result is confined with `.startswith(base)` and no trailing os.sep, so /var/www/uploads_backup passes a check for /var/www/uploads (CWE-22). Tightened: the generic-receiver branch dropped its string-literal alternative, so `request.path.startswith('/api')` and `p.startswith('/')` (absolute/route checks) no longer fire; literals stay caught via the resolved-path-receiver and os.path.realpath()/abspath() branches. notMatch clears base+os.sep, os.path.join(base,''), commonpath, relpath, a trailing-slash literal, and '#' comments.

rules.name: path-containment-strpos-startswith-no-sep-php
rules.message: Path-containment bypass — a startsWith/indexOf prefix check with no trailing separator lets a sibling directory escape (CWE-22).
rules.remediation: Append the separator: strpos($resolved, $base . DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR) === 0 (or str_starts_with with the separator) and confirm realpath($resolved) !== false; ideally validate against an allowlist of canonical base paths.
rules.why: strpos($resolved, $base) === 0 / str_starts_with($resolved, $base) confines a realpath to a base with no trailing DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR, so /var/www/uploads_backup passes a check for /var/www/uploads (CWE-22). Tightened: the generic-haystack branches dropped their bare string-literal needle — they fired on `strpos($uri, '/api') === 0` / `str_starts_with($route, '/admin')` router code; base literals stay caught via the resolved-path-haystack branches ($resolved/$normalized/$canonical, first arg). Needle bare-var restricted to $base/$root and *Dir/*Root/*Base/_dir/_root/_base so `$baseUrl` no longer matches. notMatch clears the . DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR / . '/' twin, a trailing-slash literal, and comments.

rules.name: path-containment-substr-prefix-compare-no-sep
rules.message: Path-containment bypass — a startsWith/indexOf prefix check with no trailing separator lets a sibling directory escape (CWE-22).
rules.remediation: Do not compare a bare prefix; assert the boundary — resolved === base || resolved.startsWith(base + path.sep) — or use the platform containment helper (path.relative + '..' check, os.path.commonpath, filepath.Rel).
rules.why: A leading slice of a resolved path is compared to the base — resolved.slice(0, base.length) === base (JS), substr($resolved, 0, strlen($base)) === $base (PHP), resolved[:len(base)] == base (Python), canonical.substring(0, base.length()).equals(base) (Java) — a prefix-equality check with no separator at the boundary, so /var/www/uploads_backup matches base /var/www/uploads (CWE-22). This rule was already fully receiver/haystack-gated (the first arg must be a resolved-path name and the length must come from a variable via .length/strlen/len), so it never took a bare path literal and does not fire on route/URL prefix code — no structural change was needed, corpora expanded only. notMatch suppresses variants that fold the separator into the compared length/value (base + path.sep, a baseWithSep var), path.relative/relpath/filepath.Rel, and comments.

rules.name: path-prefix-bypass
rules.message: A path is validated with startsWith on a base directory (prefix bypass).
rules.remediation: Compare against the base plus a separator, or check path.relative(base, resolved) does not start with '..'.
rules.why: startsWith('/app/views') also matches '/app/views_secret', so '../views_secret/x' passes the check and a sibling directory is read — the boundary is not enforced.

rules.name: path-traversal-strip
rules.message: Path traversal is being removed with a single-pass string replace.
rules.remediation: Resolve the path (path.resolve/realpath) and verify it stays inside a fixed canonical base, rather than stripping strings.
rules.why: Removing '../' once does not sanitise the path: an input such as '....//' becomes '../' after one replacement, so the traversal survives.

rules.name: pathwrite-go-oswrite-filepathjoin
rules.message: Path traversal on write — a file is written to a user-controlled path without a containment check (CWE-22).
rules.remediation: Clean+resolve and enforce containment (e.g. rel, err := filepath.Rel(base, target); reject if err or strings.HasPrefix(rel, "..")), or reduce the name via filepath.Base()/an allowlist before joining.
rules.why: os.Create/os.WriteFile/os.OpenFile/ioutil.WriteFile writes to filepath.Join(dir, r.FormValue(...)/multipart Header.Filename); filepath.Join cleans but still follows '../', so request input controls the write path. Read-only os.Open is excluded by the sink and O_RDONLY-only OpenFile is suppressed by notMatch.

rules.name: pathwrite-java-fileoutputstream-reqparam
rules.message: Path traversal on write — a file is written to a user-controlled path without a containment check (CWE-22).
rules.remediation: Reduce the name with FilenameUtils.getName()/an allowlist, then verify file.getCanonicalPath().startsWith(baseDir.getCanonicalPath()+File.separator) before opening the stream.
rules.why: A FileOutputStream/FileWriter/PrintWriter is opened over new File(dir, request.getParameter(...)) or the multipart getSubmittedFileName()/Spring getOriginalFilename(); the File(dir, child) constructor does not block '../', so request input controls the write location.

rules.name: pathwrite-java-files-write-pathsget
rules.message: Path traversal on write — a file is written to a user-controlled path without a containment check (CWE-22).
rules.remediation: Normalize+resolve the target Path and confirm target.toRealPath()/normalize().startsWith(baseDir) before writing, and strip the name to a safe basename or allowlisted value.
rules.why: java.nio Files.write/writeString/newOutputStream/copy targets Paths.get(dir, <request param|upload filename>); Paths.get resolves traversal segments, so untrusted input steers the write outside the base directory. The optional leading-arg group also catches Files.copy(in, Paths.get(...)) where the target is the second argument.

rules.name: pathwrite-node-fs-concat-reqinput
rules.message: Path traversal on write — a file is written to a user-controlled path without a containment check (CWE-22).
rules.remediation: Never concatenate untrusted names into a path; join, then canonicalize and assert containment (resolved.startsWith(base+sep)), or replace the user segment with path.basename()/an allowlisted id.
rules.why: A write target is assembled by string concatenation (dir + '/' + userName) or a template literal (`${dir}/${req...}`) directly from request input, so '../' in the user value escapes the base directory and enables arbitrary file overwrite.

rules.name: pathwrite-node-fs-join-reqinput
rules.message: Path traversal on write — a file is written to a user-controlled path without a containment check (CWE-22).
rules.remediation: Resolve the final path and verify it stays within the base dir (path.resolve(dir, name).startsWith(path.resolve(dir)+path.sep)), or reduce the user value to path.basename() / a validated allowlist before joining.
rules.why: A write/create/mkdir target is built with path.join(dir, req.body|params|query...) from request input; because path.join happily traverses embedded '../', an attacker can steer the write outside the intended directory (overwrite config/code -> RCE).

rules.name: pathwrite-node-multer-originalname
rules.message: Path traversal on write — a file is written to a user-controlled path without a containment check (CWE-22).
rules.remediation: Generate the stored name server-side (crypto.randomUUID + path.extname) or run the original through path.basename()/an allowlist; never persist originalname directly.
rules.why: multer diskStorage / formidable use the client-supplied upload filename (file.originalname / originalFilename) verbatim as the stored filename or destination path, so a crafted name like '../../app.js' writes outside the upload folder.

rules.name: pathwrite-php-fileputcontents-superglobal
rules.message: Path traversal on write — a file is written to a user-controlled path without a containment check (CWE-22).
rules.remediation: Strip the user segment with basename()/an allowlist and verify realpath(dirname(target)) is inside the intended base (strpos===0) before writing; never concatenate a superglobal into a write path.
rules.why: file_put_contents / fopen(...,'w'|'a'|'x') builds the target PATH (first argument) from $_GET/$_POST/$_REQUEST/$_FILES/$_COOKIE, so '../' or an absolute path in the request writes anywhere the PHP process can (e.g. drop a webshell in the docroot -> RCE). The [^,] guard keeps the match on the path argument, not a superglobal used only as write content.

rules.name: pathwrite-php-move-uploaded-userfilename
rules.message: Path traversal on write — a file is written to a user-controlled path without a containment check (CWE-22).
rules.remediation: Choose the destination name server-side (uniqid()/hash + validated extension) or run $_FILES name through basename()/an allowlist, and confirm the resolved destination stays under the upload dir before moving.
rules.why: move_uploaded_file()'s destination (second argument) is built from the client-supplied name ($_FILES[...]['name'] or another superglobal), so an attacker-chosen name with '../' or a target extension lands the upload in the webroot (webshell) or overwrites arbitrary files. The [^,] structure requires the superglobal in the destination arg, not merely in the tmp_name source arg.

rules.name: pathwrite-python-open-join-reqinput
rules.message: Path traversal on write — a file is written to a user-controlled path without a containment check (CWE-22).
rules.remediation: Sanitize with werkzeug secure_filename() or os.path.basename(), then verify os.path.realpath(target) is inside os.path.realpath(base) (commonpath/startswith) before opening for write.
rules.why: open(os.path.join(dir, request.args/form/...), 'w'|'a'|'x'|'r+') opens a write/update handle at a path whose final segment is request input; os.path.join treats an absolute/traversing segment as escaping the base, giving arbitrary file write. The mode gate keeps read-only opens ('r'/'rb') out of scope.

rules.name: pathwrite-python-pathlib-write
rules.message: Path traversal on write — a file is written to a user-controlled path without a containment check (CWE-22).
rules.remediation: Compute (Path(base)/name).resolve() and assert it .is_relative_to(base.resolve()) (or use relative_to in a try/except) before writing, and reduce the user value to a basename/allowlisted name.
rules.why: A pathlib target is built as Path(dir) / request... (or .joinpath(request...)) and then .write_text/.write_bytes is called; the '/' operator lets a traversing or absolute user segment escape the base, yielding arbitrary write.

rules.name: pathwrite-python-shutil-user-dest
rules.message: Path traversal on write — a file is written to a user-controlled path without a containment check (CWE-22).
rules.remediation: Sanitize the destination name (secure_filename/os.path.basename) and canonicalize+contain the resolved destination under the base directory before copying/moving.
rules.why: shutil.copy/copy2/copyfile/move writes to a destination os.path.join(dir, <request/upload filename>); a traversing user segment relocates the written file outside the intended directory. The method name is anchored with '(' so copytree/copyfileobj do not match, and the source requires a .filename attribute or request.* so unrelated names are ignored.

rules.name: pathwrite-python-werkzeug-save-no-secure
rules.message: Path traversal on write — a file is written to a user-controlled path without a containment check (CWE-22).
rules.remediation: Wrap the upload name in werkzeug.utils.secure_filename() (or os.path.basename + allowlist) before joining, and confirm the resolved path stays under the upload root.
rules.why: A werkzeug/Flask FileStorage is saved to os.path.join(dir, file.filename) where filename is the raw client upload name; without secure_filename() a name such as '../../wsgi.py' writes outside the upload directory. The sink now requires a .filename attribute or a request.* source so it does not fire on unrelated local variables merely named 'name'.

rules.name: pathwrite-ruby-filewrite-filejoin-params
rules.message: Path traversal on write — a file is written to a user-controlled path without a containment check (CWE-22).
rules.remediation: Sanitize with File.basename()/an allowlist, then verify File.expand_path(target).start_with?(File.expand_path(base)) before opening the file for write.
rules.why: File.write/binwrite/open targets File.join(dir, params[:name] / uploaded.original_filename); File.join does not restrain '../', so a Rails/Rack param controls where the file is written. File.write/binwrite always write, while File.open is only flagged when opened with a write/append/update mode ('w'/'a'/'r+'), so read-mode File.open is out of scope.

rules.name: pbkdf2-iterations-webcrypto
rules.message: A PBKDF2 iteration count under 100,000 is too low.
rules.remediation: Use at least 600,000 iterations for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, or switch to bcrypt/scrypt/argon2.
rules.why: Few iterations make each password guess cheap, so leaked hashes are brute-forced quickly.

rules.name: php-eval-of-file-contents
rules.message: Write-then-execute — code is loaded or run from a user-controlled or writable path (potential RCE, CWE-829/95/98/94).
rules.remediation: Do not eval file contents. Load data via a parser (json_decode) and drive behavior from an allow-listed set of fixed, trusted code paths instead of evaluating file bytes.
rules.why: eval() of file_get_contents()/fread()/stream_get_contents() runs the contents of a file (or php://input) as PHP; if the source is user-supplied or sits in a writable/uploaded location, writing that file yields arbitrary code execution. The eval/read must be adjacent, so a split read-then-eval on one line and evaluate(...) / my_eval(...) do not match.

rules.name: php-include-require-variable-or-superglobal
rules.message: Write-then-execute — code is loaded or run from a user-controlled or writable path (potential RCE, CWE-829/95/98/94).
rules.remediation: Never include a path derived from input. Use a fixed switch/allow-list map from a validated key to a hardcoded file, keep templates under a read-only path, and basename()+realpath()-contain any dynamic segment.
rules.why: include/require with a variable, a superglobal, or a directory-constant concatenated with a variable pulls in and executes PHP from a runtime path; an attacker who controls the value or writes into the included/uploaded directory achieves RCE (classic LFI-to-RCE). Anchoring the keyword to a statement position (line start, ';', '{', '}') prevents it firing on the word 'include' inside a string such as echo "include $file"; the constant.literal form (__DIR__ . '/lib.php') stays inert because it lacks a trailing $. Trade-off: the uncommon assignment form $x = include $y; is not matched.

rules.name: php-preg-replace-eval-modifier
rules.message: Replacement-token injection — user input used as a replace() replacement or preg_replace /e is interpreted, not literal (CWE-116/94).
rules.remediation: The /e modifier was deprecated in PHP 5.5 and removed in 7.0 -- eliminate it. Use preg_replace_callback with the pattern minus the e modifier and a callback that builds the replacement safely from the matches, instead of eval'ing a string. Never let user input reach a pattern string carrying /e.
rules.why: The PCRE /e (PREG_REPLACE_EVAL) modifier makes preg_replace EXECUTE its replacement argument as PHP code after backreference substitution, so any attacker-influenced group interpolated into that eval'd string yields RCE. The sink matches a literal pattern (opening quote captured as \1, a delimiter captured as \2 from /#~!@%|, a body, the matching close delimiter \2, a trailing modifier run that contains the letter e, and the closing quote \1). Two precision fixes over the original: (1) the body is now (?:(?!\1)[^\\]|\\.)*? so it can never span past the pattern's own closing quote -- this kills the cross-argument false positive where a plain replacement string that merely looks like /x/e (e.g. preg_replace('/foo/','/replace/e',$s)) was matched even though arg1 carried no e modifier; the (?!\1) still permits the OTHER quote char inside the pattern, so preg_replace('/say "hi"/e',...) stays a true positive. (2) the pipe delimiter was added. Patterns without an e modifier never match (the modifier run requires an e before the closing quote), and preg_replace_callback plus comment lines are suppressed by notMatch (# only anchored at line start, so it never suppresses a real # delimiter mid-line).

rules.name: php-reflected-html-echo-superglobal
rules.message: Reflected / context-mismatched XSS — user input reaches HTML or JS output without proper contextual encoding (CWE-79/116).
rules.remediation: Wrap the value in htmlspecialchars($v, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8') (or htmlentities/strip_tags) for the correct context, urlencode() only for URL positions, or cast numeric params with (int)/intval().
rules.why: echo/print emits an HTML fragment built from a request superglobal ($_GET/$_POST/$_REQUEST/$_COOKIE/$_SERVER) with no output encoding, reflecting attacker markup into the page -> reflected XSS.

rules.name: pickle-loads
rules.message: pickle can execute code while it deserialises.
rules.remediation: Use JSON for anything that crosses a trust boundary.
rules.why: Unpickling is not parsing: a crafted payload runs arbitrary code as it is read.

rules.name: postmessage-no-origin
rules.message: A 'message' handler must verify event.origin.
rules.remediation: At the top of the handler, return unless event.origin is one you expect.
rules.why: Without an event.origin check, any page that can post to this window — an iframe, an opener, a malicious site — can drive this handler with attacker-controlled data.

rules.name: proto-guard-incomplete
rules.message: This guards only '__proto__', which is an incomplete prototype-pollution check.
rules.remediation: Reject 'constructor' and 'prototype' as well, or set into a null-prototype object.
rules.why: Blocking '__proto__' alone is bypassed by the path ['constructor','prototype', …], which reaches Object.prototype just the same and pollutes every object.

rules.name: protopollution-bare-merge-extend-req
rules.message: Prototype pollution — attacker-controlled keys can reach Object.prototype via a recursive merge/set (CWE-1321).
rules.remediation: Confirm the imported merge is recursive; if so, merge into an Object.create(null) target, drop __proto__/constructor/prototype keys before merging, or replace the raw merge with a schema-validated field copy so only known keys are written.
rules.why: A bare (non-method) merge(target, src) / extend(target, src) / defaultsDeep(target, src) imported from a merge library, where the source on the same line is client-controlled, is a likely recursive merge of untrusted keys into target and a prototype-pollution sink. The negative-position guard (?:[^\w.$]|^) requires the call to be a bare identifier so method calls (_.merge, obj.extend, Model.merge), deepmerge(...) and other prefixed identifiers (xmerge, emergeCallback) are left to the more specific rules and are not double-flagged. This is a medium-confidence heuristic: it cannot see across the line, so an unrelated merge() plus an unrelated user-input reference on the same physical line can still match.

rules.name: protopollution-direct-prototype-write
rules.message: Prototype pollution — attacker-controlled keys can reach Object.prototype via a recursive merge/set (CWE-1321).
rules.remediation: Never write a property onto __proto__, constructor.prototype, or Object.prototype from runtime data. If you must reassign an object's prototype use Object.setPrototypeOf with a fixed, trusted value; freeze Object.prototype (Object.freeze) at startup to make accidental pollution throw; and gate any dynamic key so it can never equal __proto__/constructor/prototype.
rules.why: A statement that assigns THROUGH a prototype-chain reference writes shared state: obj['__proto__'].x=, x.__proto__[k]=, foo['constructor']['prototype'].y=, o.constructor.prototype.z=, or Object.prototype.p= all land on Object.prototype, as do Object.defineProperty/defineProperties and Reflect.set/defineProperty targeting Object.prototype.
