The single-'=' with a (?!=|>) lookahead means only real assignments match, not comparisons (=== '__proto__' / obj.__proto__ === Object.prototype) or arrow bodies, and reads (return o.__proto__) have no trailing '='. Benign NamedClass.prototype.method= augmentation is NOT matched (only Object.prototype / constructor.prototype / __proto__ bases are), a denylist array literal like ['__proto__','constructor','prototype'] and Map.set('__proto__', v) don't match (no bracket-base + '='), and notMatch also drops comparisons, getPrototypeOf/isPrototypeOf, the Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call idiom, and legacy inheritance (this.__proto__ = Parent.prototype / x.__proto__ = Object.getPrototypeOf(y)). Verified robust — no change needed to the regex.

rules.name: protopollution-dotprop-generic-setpath-tainted
rules.message: Prototype pollution — attacker-controlled keys can reach Object.prototype via a recursive merge/set (CWE-1321).
rules.remediation: Use dot-prop v6+ which throws on __proto__/constructor/prototype, or in the hand-rolled helper reject those key segments and use Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call before descending; prefer a null-prototype object or a Map for user-keyed data.
rules.why: dot-prop (dotProp.set / setProperty), dset, pathval (setPathValue) and hand-rolled deepSet/setValue/setPath/setIn helpers all take (object, path, value) and walk/create the path from a caller string; a tainted '__proto__.x' path pollutes the prototype. AUDIT CHANGE: to stop the heavy name-collision false positives, the generic-name shape now requires (a) a non-string-literal FIRST argument (?!['"`]) — so Formik/React-Hook-Form setValue('email', req.body.value), where the field is a literal and only the VALUE is tainted, no longer fires; (b) a THIRD argument (trailing comma after the path) — so the 2-arg setValue(fieldName, req.body.value) / state.setIn(keyPath, value) forms don't fire; and (c) the taint keyword anchored at the ROOT of the path (2nd arg), so deepSet(obj, config.query, value) is ignored. A method-call negative lookbehind still rejects router.setPath(...) / obj.setIn(...), and the guard notMatch drops magic-key / hasOwnProperty / allowlist checks and Object.create(null) targets.

rules.name: protopollution-forin-recursive-merge
rules.message: Prototype pollution — attacker-controlled keys can reach Object.prototype via a recursive merge/set (CWE-1321).
rules.remediation: Skip dangerous keys before recursing: if (key === '__proto__' || key === 'constructor' || key === 'prototype') continue; and/or gate with Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(source, key). Prefer a null-prototype target (Object.create(null)) or a vetted merge library (lodash.mergeWith with a customizer) instead of a hand-rolled recursive copy.
rules.why: A single-line recursive merge body: a for-in (or Object.keys/entries forEach) over an untrusted source whose iteration variable indexes the target and is passed back into a recursive merge (target[key] = merge(target[key], source[key])). When key is '__proto__', target[key] resolves to Object.prototype and the recursion writes onto it. The regex requires BOTH the loop header AND a self-indexing merge-call assignment on the same line, so a bare for-in or a plain index write does not fire; no __proto__/constructor/prototype/hasOwnProperty/guard token is present on the line.

rules.name: protopollution-forin-usercopy-req
rules.message: Prototype pollution — attacker-controlled keys can reach Object.prototype via a recursive merge/set (CWE-1321).
rules.remediation: Guard the loop: skip keys that are __proto__/constructor/prototype, gate the write behind Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(src, key) or Object.hasOwn(src, key), copy into an Object.create(null) target, or replace the loop with an explicit allow-list of expected fields.
rules.why: A hand-rolled deep merge: for..in iterating a client-controlled object and writing target[key] = ... keyed by the same loop variable on the same line. for..in enumerates inherited enumerable keys and an attacker-supplied __proto__ key makes target[key] assign onto the prototype, poisoning Object.prototype. The loop variable is captured and backreferenced (\1) in the write so an unrelated bracket-assignment on the same physical line (config[env]=1) no longer matches; the =(?![=>]) guard excludes ===/==/=> comparisons that previously false-fired (map[k] === val); and notMatch now suppresses hasOwn (covering both hasOwnProperty and Object.hasOwn), same-line __proto__/constructor/prototype skips, and Object.create(null) targets.

positive: for (const k in req.body) target[k] = req.body[k];
negative: for (const k in req.body) if (Object.hasOwn(req.body, k)) target[k] = req.body[k];

rules.name: protopollution-hoek-applytodefaults-req
rules.message: Prototype pollution — attacker-controlled keys can reach Object.prototype via a recursive merge/set (CWE-1321).
rules.remediation: Upgrade hoek to a patched version (>=4.2.1/5.0.3) that ignores __proto__, merge into an Object.create(null) target, strip __proto__/constructor/prototype keys first, or validate the payload against a joi/schema allow-list before merging.
rules.why: Hoek.merge / Hoek.applyToDefaults (the hapi utility, also exposed as a bare applyToDefaults) recursively fold a source object into defaults. Passing client input as the source lets a __proto__ key walk into Object.prototype (hoek CVE-2018-3728). Each name requires an immediately-following `(` so Hoek.clone/reach, applyDefaults, and applyToDefaultsSync are not flagged, and the notMatch drops Object.create(null) targets and same-line proto-key filters.

rules.name: protopollution-jquery-extend-deep-req
rules.message: Prototype pollution — attacker-controlled keys can reach Object.prototype via a recursive merge/set (CWE-1321).
rules.remediation: Avoid deep-extending untrusted input. Use a shallow $.extend (no leading true) after schema validation, extend into an Object.create(null) target, strip __proto__/constructor/prototype keys first, or upgrade to jQuery >= 3.4.0 which guards __proto__.
rules.why: jQuery.extend/$.extend becomes a RECURSIVE deep copy only when the first argument is true. A deep $.extend(true, target, req.body) walks nested attacker keys into target and, via a __proto__ key, pollutes Object.prototype (jQuery <3.4.0 CVE-2019-11358). The `(\s*true\b` anchor requires the boolean-true first arg so shallow $.extend({}, ...) and $.extend(false, ...) are not flagged, and $ or jQuery must directly precede .extend so _.extend / element.extend are left alone.

rules.name: protopollution-jsonparse-request-into-merge
rules.message: Prototype pollution — attacker-controlled keys can reach Object.prototype via a recursive merge/set (CWE-1321).
rules.remediation: Strip prototype keys before merging: pass a reviver to JSON.parse ((k,v)=>k==='__proto__'?undefined:v), sanitize the parsed object, target Object.create(null), or use a merge that ignores __proto__/constructor/prototype. Validate the body against a schema (allowlist of expected fields) before merging.
rules.why: A raw request body is JSON.parse'd and passed directly into a deep merge/extend. JSON.parse faithfully materializes an own '__proto__' property from attacker JSON ({"__proto__":{"polluted":1}}), and a recursive merge then walks that key onto Object.prototype. This is the classic request->merge pollution bridge. The regex requires a merge-family callee, the literal JSON.parse, AND a request-derived argument (req/body/payload/ctx/msg/...), so parses of files, env, localStorage or Buffer do not fire, and reviver/sanitize/strip wrappers are suppressed.

rules.name: protopollution-lodash-merge-req
rules.message: Prototype pollution — attacker-controlled keys can reach Object.prototype via a recursive merge/set (CWE-1321).
rules.remediation: Never deep-merge attacker input directly. Merge into an Object.create(null) target, drop __proto__/constructor/prototype keys before merging, upgrade to a patched lodash and prefer _.mergeWith with a customizer that rejects those keys, or validate the body against an allow-listed schema (e.g. Ajv/Zod) so only known fields survive.
rules.why: lodash recursive merges (_.merge, _.mergeWith, _.defaultsDeep, _.defaults, _.assignInWith / lodash.merge) copy nested keys from the source into the target. When the source is a client-controlled object, a key named __proto__ (or constructor.prototype) walks the prototype chain and poisons Object.prototype process-wide (the classic lodash CVE-2018-3721 / CVE-2019-10744 pattern). Only deep/defaulting variants are flagged; the shallow _.assign / _.assignIn / _.cloneDeep are excluded by the token alternation, and the notMatch drops Object.create(null) targets, structuredClone copies, and lines that already reference __proto__/constructor/prototype (a guard or customizer).

rules.name: protopollution-lodash-set-user-path
rules.message: Prototype pollution — attacker-controlled keys can reach Object.prototype via a recursive merge/set (CWE-1321).
rules.remediation: Do not derive the deep-set path from user input. Validate the path against an allowlist of permitted keys, reject any segment equal to __proto__/constructor/prototype, or use a set implementation that refuses those segments. Prefer setting known fields explicitly over path-string writes.
rules.why: lodash.set / objectPath.set / dotProp.set / dset / deepSet create intermediate objects for each segment of the path string. When the path argument (2nd arg) is attacker-controlled (e.g. req.body.path = '__proto__.polluted'), the setter walks through Object.prototype and assigns onto it. The rule fires ONLY when the 2nd argument itself is request-derived, so a static path with a request value (_.set(config,'a.b',req.body.value)), array-literal paths, and Map/redis/formData .set (non-deep-set receivers) do not fire. FIX vs original: deepSet was moved from the receiver-'.set' group into the direct-call group alongside dset, so deepSet(config, req.body.path, val) now fires (it was a false negative before).

rules.name: protopollution-lodash-setpath-tainted
rules.message: Prototype pollution — attacker-controlled keys can reach Object.prototype via a recursive merge/set (CWE-1321).
rules.remediation: Do not feed request data straight into a path-set. Reject the segments '__proto__', 'constructor' and 'prototype' before setting (e.g. path.split('.').some(s => ['__proto__','constructor','prototype'].includes(s))), validate the path against an allowlist of expected keys, or store data in a Map / an Object.create(null) dictionary instead of a plain object.
rules.why: lodash _.set/_.setWith/_.update writes a value at a caller-supplied deep path; a request-derived path such as '__proto__.polluted' or 'constructor.prototype.x' lands on Object.prototype and poisons every object in the process. AUDIT CHANGE: the second (path) argument's taint keyword is now ANCHORED at the ROOT of the expression (immediately after the comma), so the rule fires on req.body.path / userInput.path / a destructured body.path, but NOT on an ordinary write where a benign local/config property merely happens to be named body/params/query (e.g. DEFAULTS.query, model.params.type) — that was the top over-broad risk. Quoted literal paths ('body.text', 'req.body.path') and array-literal paths (['req','body']) can't start with a keyword so they no longer match; the guard notMatch still drops magic-key / hasOwnProperty / allowlist checks and Object.create(null) targets.

rules.name: protopollution-mpath-setpath-tainted
rules.message: Prototype pollution — attacker-controlled keys can reach Object.prototype via a recursive merge/set (CWE-1321).
rules.remediation: Validate the path against an allowlist of schema fields before calling mpath.set, or reject any segment equal to __proto__/constructor/prototype; keep user-controlled dynamic keys out of the path argument entirely.
rules.why: mpath.set/setValue (used by mongoose internals) take the path as the FIRST argument: mpath.set(path, value, obj). A request-derived path such as '__proto__.polluted' walks and creates the prototype chain. AUDIT CHANGE: the taint keyword is anchored at the ROOT of that first argument, so it fires on mpath.set(req.body.path, ...) but NOT when only the VALUE is tainted (mpath.set(safePath, req.body.value, doc) / mpath.set(safePath, JSON.parse(req.body.data), doc)) and NOT on a benign leaf property (schema.query). Static string paths ('nested.path') and the .get/.has reads never match; the guard notMatch suppresses magic-key / hasOwnProperty / allowlist checks.

rules.name: protopollution-named-deepmerge-req
rules.message: Prototype pollution — attacker-controlled keys can reach Object.prototype via a recursive merge/set (CWE-1321).
rules.remediation: Merge into an Object.create(null) target, filter out __proto__/constructor/prototype keys before merging, pin a version of the merge library that blocks those keys (deepmerge does; deep-extend/merge-options historically did not), or validate against an allow-listed schema first.
rules.why: Standalone recursive-merge utilities (deepmerge, deep-extend, merge-options, assign-deep, ramda mergeDeepRight/Left, and hand-named deepMerge/mergeDeep helpers) copy nested keys from source to target. Merging a client-controlled object through them lets a __proto__/constructor.prototype key reach and poison Object.prototype. Each token requires an immediately-following `(` so lookalikes (deepEqual, shallowMerge, mergeArrays, deepMergeArrays, assignDeepEqual) do not match, and comparisons/array merges stay out of the alternation.

rules.name: protopollution-objectpath-setpath-tainted
rules.message: Prototype pollution — attacker-controlled keys can reach Object.prototype via a recursive merge/set (CWE-1321).
rules.remediation: Upgrade to an object-path version that blocks __proto__/constructor/prototype (or enable its withInheritedProps=false behaviour), reject those segments yourself before calling, or restrict writes to an allowlist of known keys / a null-prototype object.
rules.why: object-path's set/push/insert/ensureExists/del write to a deep path built from a caller string, and older versions had no __proto__ guard. Both call shapes are covered: objectPath.set(obj, path, val) (path is the 2nd argument) and objectPath(obj).set(path, val) (path is the 1st). AUDIT CHANGE: the path argument's taint keyword is now anchored at the ROOT of the expression in both alternatives, so leaf-keyword writes like objectPath.set(obj, meta.query, value) no longer fire, while req.body.path / ctx.request.body.path still do. Quoted-literal and array-literal paths don't match; the .get read and a non-library myObjectPathHelper.set stay out; the guard notMatch suppresses magic-key / hasOwnProperty / allowlist checks and Object.create(null) targets.

rules.name: protopollution-qs-allowprototypes-true
rules.message: Prototype pollution — attacker-controlled keys can reach Object.prototype via a recursive merge/set (CWE-1321).
rules.remediation: Remove allowPrototypes (default false) or set it to false; never enable it on user-controlled query/body strings. If nested proto keys must round-trip, use plainObjects:true so results have a null prototype, and guard any downstream merge.
rules.why: qs / query-string parse defaults to stripping __proto__ from decoded keys. Passing allowPrototypes:true re-enables prototype key names in the parsed output, so a request like ?a[__proto__][polluted]=1 can seed keys that a later deep-merge into config walks onto Object.prototype. This is the request-side half of the pollution bridge. The regex keys on the literal option-name=true pair; ignoreCase stays false because the qs option is camelCase.

rules.name: protopollution-recursive-merge-assign
rules.message: Prototype pollution — attacker-controlled keys can reach Object.prototype via a recursive merge/set (CWE-1321).
rules.remediation: In the merge loop skip dangerous keys — if (key === '__proto__' || key === 'constructor' || key === 'prototype') continue; — and only descend on Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(source, key). Prefer a vetted library (lodash.merge is hardened) or structuredClone, and merge into an Object.create(null) accumulator.
rules.why: The classic hand-rolled deep-merge / clone: a compact single-line for..in whose body immediately does target[key] = ... (the loop key becomes the write key), or an indexed assignment whose RHS is a merge/extend/deepAssign/deepClone/deepCopy call — target[key] = deepMerge(target[key], source[key]). If the source is untrusted and the loop lacks a key guard, a '__proto__' key recurses into and writes Object.prototype. The shape stays tight: a bare target[key]=value with no for..in and no merge call (dst[k]=src[k], cache[id]=computeValue(id)) does NOT match; for..of over an allowlist, plain for(;;) array copies, and spread merges ({ ...a, ...b }) are excluded by shape; Object.assign is out of scope (other angle) and doesn't match the merge-name list. A guarded merge whose body starts with an if(key==='__proto__')continue; guard breaks the direct for-in→assignment adjacency AND trips the quoted-magic-key notMatch. AUDIT CHANGE: notMatch now also excludes the hardened library merge _.merge/lodash.merge (out of scope for this angle), so out[key] = _.merge(...) no longer fires. notMatch further suppresses lines carrying hasOwnProperty, an allow/whitelist, or an Object.create(null) target.

rules.name: protopollution-recursive-self-merge-assign
rules.message: Prototype pollution — attacker-controlled keys can reach Object.prototype via a recursive merge/set (CWE-1321).
rules.remediation: Guard the key before the recursive call (skip __proto__/constructor/prototype), gate with hasOwnProperty, or descend into a null-prototype accumulator. Where feasible replace the hand-rolled recursion with a vetted, pollution-safe merge utility.
rules.why: The self-referential recursive descent that is the actual pollution sink inside a merge function: target[key] = merge(target[key], source[key]). It matches even when the for-in header is on a separate line (multi-line merge helpers). Precision comes from requiring the merge call's FIRST argument to also be an index access (\w+[\w+]) so plain shallow copies, math/array ops, non-merge callees (reducer, concat, Object.assign) and merge-as-value references do not fire; no magic-key guard is present on the line.

rules.name: protopollution-request-body-deep-merge
rules.message: Prototype pollution — attacker-controlled keys can reach Object.prototype via a recursive merge/set (CWE-1321).
rules.remediation: Never deep-merge raw request objects. Validate against a schema and merge only an allowlisted, typed subset (pick/omit the known fields). If a deep merge is required, use one that drops __proto__/constructor/prototype, merge into Object.create(null), or freeze Object.prototype at startup.
rules.why: An already-parsed request container (req.body / req.query / req.params, or ctx.request.body) is deep-merged/extended into config or defaults. Body parsers preserve '__proto__' / 'constructor' keys, and a recursive deep merge walks them onto Object.prototype. The regex requires a merge-family callee whose argument list contains a req/request/ctx receiver reaching a .body/.query/.params property; the request token must appear AFTER the merge '(', so a request-named receiver calling .merge (requestId.merge(a,b)) does not fire. Object.assign, spreads, pick/omit/allowlist and sanitize wrappers are excluded.

rules.name: prototype-pollution-merge
rules.message: This copies keys into an object without guarding __proto__.
rules.remediation: Skip the keys __proto__, constructor and prototype, or merge into an Object.create(null) target.
rules.why: A recursive merge that assigns target[key] = source[key] will, if the input carries a "__proto__" key, write onto Object.prototype — polluting every object in the program.

rules.name: proxy-raw-body-forward
rules.message: A proxy forwards the client's raw body downstream after validating a parsed copy.
rules.remediation: Re-serialise the validated data and forward that, not the original bytes; reject duplicate/unknown fields.
rules.why: This parser and the downstream one can disagree on a body with duplicate keys — the check passes on one reading, the dangerous action runs on the other (HTTP parameter pollution).

rules.name: public-env-inlined-secret
rules.message: Client-side token signing or embedded signing key — a secret/decision shipped to the browser is attacker-forgeable.
rules.remediation: Drop the public prefix and read the secret only in server-side code (a route handler, server component, or API), or move the operation that needs it behind a server endpoint. Public prefixes are for values that are safe to publish (URLs, publishable keys, analytics IDs, public verification keys).
rules.why: A secret-named value is read from a client-inlined env prefix (NEXT_PUBLIC_/REACT_APP_/VITE_/VUE_APP_/GATSBY_/EXPO_PUBLIC_). Bundlers statically replace these with their literal value at build time, so the secret is compiled into the JS delivered to browsers and is fully exposed — using it to sign or authorize is worthless.

rules.name: py-re-sub-user-replacement-backref
rules.message: Replacement-token injection — user input used as a replace() replacement or preg_replace /e is interpreted, not literal (CWE-116/94).
rules.remediation: Escape backslashes in the untrusted replacement before use, or pass a function replacement -- re.sub(pattern, lambda m: user_value, string) -- so no backreference expansion happens on the user data. Do not bind raw user input as the replacement argument.
rules.why: In re.sub(pattern, repl, string) / re.subn the replacement is not literal text: numbered and named backref tokens expand to captured groups and \g<0> to the whole match, so a user-controlled replacement can splice matched/adjacent content into the output (or raise 'invalid group reference'). The sink fires only when arg2 is a bare identifier/member (optionally subscripted) immediately followed by the comma that begins the required 3rd (string) argument -- so inline lambda replacements (an identifier is not followed by a comma; belt-and-suspenders in notMatch), literal-string replacements, and sanitizer/escaping CALL replacements such as str(x) / repl.upper() (a ( follows the callee, not a comma) are excluded. Two precision/recall fixes over the original: (1) the leading (?<![\w.]) lookbehind replaces \b so it excludes not only foo_re.sub / pre.sub / feature.sub (already handled by \b) but also a leading-dot member like obj.re.sub, which is an unrelated .re attribute and was a false positive; (2) arg1 now accepts raw/bytes/unicode string prefixes ([rbuRBU]{0,2}, e.g. rb'\d+') and an optional subscript (patterns[0]), closing two recall gaps. The engine supports backreferences (see the PHP rule), so this lookbehind is safe for it.

rules.name: py-reflected-html-request-concat-fstring
rules.message: Reflected / context-mismatched XSS — user input reaches HTML or JS output without proper contextual encoding (CWE-79/116).
rules.remediation: Escape with markupsafe.escape()/Markup or sanitize with bleach/nh3; rely on Jinja auto-escaping ({{ }}) via render_template rather than building HTML by concatenation, and return jsonify() for data.
rules.why: Flask/Django reflection: request.* is concatenated, f-string/{}-format, or %-format interpolated into an HTML string returned or wrapped in make_response/HttpResponse/render_template_string with no escaping -> reflected XSS (and SSTI when fed to render_template_string).

rules.name: rand-time-md5-as-token-rb
rules.message: Predictable session/token identifier — a security id from a non-CSPRNG or observable source (CWE-330/340).
rules.remediation: Use SecureRandom (SecureRandom.hex, SecureRandom.urlsafe_base64, SecureRandom.uuid) for session ids, reset tokens, and API keys.
rules.why: Ruby's Kernel#rand / Random.rand is a non-cryptographic PRNG, Time.now is observable, and Digest::MD5/SHA1 of such data adds no entropy; tokens built this way are predictable and forgeable.

rules.name: random-module-as-session-token-py
rules.message: Predictable session/token identifier — a security id from a non-CSPRNG or observable source (CWE-330/340).
rules.remediation: Use the secrets module (secrets.choice, secrets.token_hex, secrets.token_urlsafe) or random.SystemRandom for anything security-sensitive.
rules.why: Python's random module is a Mersenne Twister PRNG whose state is recoverable from observed outputs, so session ids and tokens built with random.randint/choice/getrandbits are predictable.

rules.name: rb-reflected-html-params-interp
rules.message: Reflected / context-mismatched XSS — user input reaches HTML or JS output without proper contextual encoding (CWE-79/116).
rules.remediation: Escape with CGI.escapeHTML / ERB::Util.html_escape (or the h() view helper, or Rails' default ERB auto-escaping via <%= %>); cast numeric params with .to_i; avoid html_safe/raw on user-controlled data.
rules.why: params[...] is interpolated into an HTML string literal (Sinatra route / inline render) with no escaping, reflecting attacker markup into the response -> reflected XSS.

rules.name: redirect-cookie-crlf-injection
rules.message: HTTP response splitting / header injection — user input placed into a response header without stripping CRLF (CWE-113).
rules.remediation: Validate redirect targets against an allowlist of known paths/hosts and strip CR/LF before building Location or Set-Cookie values; for cookies, use a cookie API that encodes values rather than concatenating raw request input.
rules.why: A redirect or cookie setter (res.redirect/sendRedirect/location, Flask redirect(), Django HttpResponseRedirect, res.cookie/clearCookie) is fed raw request input as the Location or Set-Cookie value. The header is emitted verbatim, so unstripped CR/LF allows response splitting and header injection (CWE-113); the same untrusted value also enables open redirect. The \bredirect( alternative requires '(' immediately after 'redirect' so redirectTo(/redirectMiddleware( do not match, and the input markers avoid client-router redirect(searchParams.get()).

rules.name: redos-nested-quantifier
rules.message: This regular expression has nested quantifiers (catastrophic backtracking / ReDoS).
rules.remediation: Rewrite without a quantifier applied to an already-quantified group; prefer a linear, possessive, or anchored pattern.
rules.why: A pattern like ([a-z0-9]+)+ can take exponential time on a long non-matching string, freezing the thread — a denial of service an attacker triggers with one crafted input.

rules.name: referrer-policy-unsafe-url-downgrade
rules.message: Data leakage — a downgraded Referrer-Policy or a secret carried in the URL (CWE-693/598).
rules.remediation: Use a protective referrer policy such as no-referrer, same-origin, strict-origin, or strict-origin-when-cross-origin instead of unsafe-url.
rules.why: Setting Referrer-Policy to unsafe-url (via an HTTP header, a <meta name=referrer>, a fetch referrerPolicy option, or a referrerpolicy attribute) downgrades referrer protection, causing the full URL (path plus query string, which may hold session ids or tokens) to leak in the Referer header to cross-origin and plain-HTTP destinations. The keyword is anchored within a 25-char window of the literal unsafe-url so safe policy values (no-referrer, strict-origin, same-origin) never match. The meta alternative now carries a word boundary (\bname) so the 'name' substring inside filename/pathname/hostname/basename/username assignments no longer matches a nearby 'unsafe-url' literal.

rules.name: regex-html-sanitizer
rules.message: HTML is being sanitised with a regular-expression blacklist.
rules.remediation: Sanitise with a real HTML parser such as DOMPurify, not string replacement.
rules.why: Stripping <script>, on… handlers or javascript: with a regex is bypassable: obfuscated encodings, alternate tags (<svg onload>, <iframe srcdoc>), and payloads that reassemble after one replacement pass all get through, giving a false sense of safety.

rules.name: regex-origin-anchor
rules.message: This origin/host regex uses a wildcard after the scheme and is bypassable.
rules.remediation: Compare new URL(origin).hostname to an allowlist, or anchor the pattern fully (…\.example\.com$).
rules.why: /^https?:\/\/.*app\.example\.com/ has no end anchor, so https://app.example.com.attacker.com and https://attacker-app.example.com both pass .test(origin) and defeat the cross-origin check.

rules.name: request-data-to-log
rules.message: A whole request object (body/headers/cookies) is written to the logs.
rules.remediation: Log only the specific non-sensitive fields you need; redact credentials, tokens, cookies and PII before logging.
rules.why: Logging entire request bodies, headers, or cookies routinely captures passwords, tokens, session cookies, API keys and personal data into log files that are broadly readable, shipped to third parties, and retained far longer than the data should be, turning the log store into a soft breach target.

rules.name: require-node-dynamic-var-specifier
rules.message: Write-then-execute — code is loaded or run from a user-controlled or writable path (potential RCE, CWE-829/95/98/94).
rules.remediation: Never require() a computed name. Map an allow-listed key to a fixed literal module ({plugins}[name]) and reject anything else; keep plugin code in a read-only directory resolved with a literal under __dirname.
rules.why: require() called with a bare variable, member/index expression, or concatenation resolves the module path at runtime; if that value is influenced by untrusted input or points at a writable/uploads directory, an attacker who can write a file turns it into arbitrary code execution when it is required. String-literal specifiers never match (they do not start with an identifier char), so require('fs') is inert.

rules.name: require-node-literal-concat-userpath
rules.message: Write-then-execute — code is loaded or run from a user-controlled or writable path (potential RCE, CWE-829/95/98/94).
rules.remediation: Resolve to an allow-listed literal instead of concatenating user input into the specifier; if a directory of plugins is loaded, enumerate a fixed read-only directory and validate each basename against a whitelist.
rules.why: require() built from a string prefix concatenated with a variable, or a template literal with an interpolation, forms a dynamic module path (base + userName, `plugins/${name}`); a writable target directory makes this file-write-to-code-execution. A ternary-of-literals never matches because the concat branch requires a quote-then-plus.

rules.name: role-session-file-keyed-by-user-js
rules.message: Broken session management — identity/role from an unverified client value or a writable store (CWE-807/302).
rules.remediation: Key session/role files by a random server-issued session id (CSPRNG), not by a username, and derive the id from verified state (req.session, a verified token).
rules.why: Authorization/session state is read from or written to a file whose path is built (concat/template) from a client-controlled username. A writable, user-keyed role/session file lets an attacker read or overwrite another user's privilege state. Fixed a real gap: the original tail matched userId but not camelCase userName/user_name; rewrote the tail to user(?:_?[Nn]ame|_?[Ii]d)? so all of user, userName, user_name, userId, user_id, uid fire. path.join(...) and CSPRNG/session-id keys are excluded.

rules.name: role-session-file-keyed-by-user-php
rules.message: Broken session management — identity/role from an unverified client value or a writable store (CWE-807/302).
rules.remediation: Use PHP's server-side session (keyed by a random session_id) and store roles there or in a trusted DB. Do not build session/role file paths from a raw username.
rules.why: Role/session state is read from or written to a file whose path is concatenated/interpolated from a client-controlled username. A writable, user-keyed authorization file lets an attacker reach or overwrite another user's privilege data. Sealed a real leak: added a leading \b before the identity group so $superuser / compound names no longer match the internal 'user' substring; session_id / session_id() / random_bytes keys and $_SESSION are excluded.

rules.name: role-session-file-keyed-by-user-py
rules.message: Broken session management — identity/role from an unverified client value or a writable store (CWE-807/302).
rules.remediation: Key session/role files by a random session id (secrets.token_hex/urlsafe), not by username, and derive that id from a verified session (request.session) or token.
rules.why: A session/role/auth file is opened with a path built (f-string/concat) from a client-controlled username. The user-keyed, writable store means an attacker can address or tamper with another account's authorization state. secrets.token_hex / uuid4 / session_id keys and request.session are excluded.

rules.name: role-session-file-keyed-by-user-rb
rules.message: Broken session management — identity/role from an unverified client value or a writable store (CWE-807/302).
rules.remediation: Store session/role state in the Rails session (signed/encrypted, keyed by a random id) or a trusted store, and key any file by a CSPRNG session id derived from verified state (session[:user_id]).
rules.why: A session/role/auth file is read or written at a path built (concat or #{} interpolation) from a client-controlled username. The user-keyed, writable file means an attacker can address or tamper with another account's authorization state. SecureRandom.uuid/hex, session_id, and session[...] keys are excluded.

rules.name: ruby-require-load-dynamic-path
rules.message: Write-then-execute — code is loaded or run from a user-controlled or writable path (potential RCE, CWE-829/95/98/94).
rules.remediation: Load only fixed literal paths of trusted code; if a plugin name is selected at runtime, validate it against an allow-list and resolve it under a read-only directory (reject '..' and absolute paths).
rules.why: require/require_relative/load with a local/instance variable, a string interpolation (#{...}), or a concatenation loads and executes a Ruby file chosen at runtime; a user-controlled name or a writable/uploaded path becomes code execution. The bareword branch is lowercase-anchored so uppercase constant helpers (File.join(...), ALLOWED[name], File.expand_path(...)) do not match, and word-boundaries keep payload()/download()/autoload from firing.

rules.name: runpy-run-path-user-path
rules.message: Write-then-execute — code is loaded or run from a user-controlled or writable path (potential RCE, CWE-829/95/98/94).
rules.remediation: Only run_path() a fixed literal path to trusted code; if a path must be chosen at runtime, canonicalize it and verify it is contained within a read-only, non-writable code directory before running.
rules.why: runpy.run_path() executes the Python file (or zip/dir with __main__) at the given path in a fresh namespace; a non-literal path lets an attacker point it at an uploaded or writable script and gain code execution. A single string-literal first argument (with or without run_name=) is suppressed; a bare reference `x = runpy.run_path` has no call paren and never fires.

rules.name: secret-assignment
rules.message: This looks like a hard-coded credential.
rules.remediation: Move it to an environment variable or a secrets manager.
rules.why: A password or key literal in source ends up in version control and in every build.

rules.name: secret-in-response
rules.message: A secret/signing key is sent in the HTTP response.
rules.remediation: Never send secrets to the client; return only the specific, non-sensitive values the caller needs.
rules.why: Returning the app's signing key or a server secret to the client hands an attacker the power to forge tokens or decrypt data — the whole trust model collapses.

rules.name: secret-in-url-query-string
rules.message: Data leakage — a downgraded Referrer-Policy or a secret carried in the URL (CWE-693/598).
rules.remediation: Never put secrets in a URL. Send them in a POST body or an Authorization header; if a link must carry a credential use a short-lived, single-use opaque value delivered out of band.
rules.why: A secret (token, api key, password, session id, jwt, otp, reset/access token) placed in a URL query string leaks through browser history, bookmarks, server and proxy access logs, and the Referer header when the page loads sub-resources or is linked out. The sink is gated on a literal '?' so only true URL query strings match (form-encoded POST bodies and object/dict bodies have no leading '?'); the optional [^"'\s]*& group anchors a param name either directly after the '?' or immediately after an '&', while forbidding quotes and whitespace so the match cannot cross string-concatenation boundaries; and the required immediate '=' after an exact param name means non-secret params (page, q, tab, sort, lang, limit, offset, id), longer names that merely contain a keyword (pageToken, tokenType, token_type, csrf_token, sort_token, tokenizer, access_token_expires, sessionType), and keywords that appear only as a value rather than a param (section=passwords) never fire.

rules.name: secret-logging
rules.message: A credential/secret is written to a log.
rules.remediation: Never log secrets; redact the field or log only a non-sensitive identifier.
rules.why: Logs are stored, shipped to aggregators, and read by many people; a password or token in stdout leaks it far beyond the process (OWASP A09, PCI-DSS/GDPR).

rules.name: secret-token-in-response
rules.message: GraphQL/dev misconfiguration — introspection or a dev endpoint exposed, or a weak/predictable secret (CWE-200/489/307/770/330).
rules.remediation: Never echo these values back; deliver them only through the intended side channel (email/SMS) and return just a status. Compare submitted codes server-side against a stored hash.
rules.why: Returning an OTP, password-reset token, verification/MFA code, API key, or private key in an HTTP response body hands the out-of-band secret straight to the caller, defeating email/SMS verification and letting an attacker complete resets or impersonate the service. Requires both a responder (.json/.send/jsonify/gin.H/c.JSON/JsonResult) and a bounded secret keyword; suppressed when the value is hashed, masked, redacted, starred, or null.

rules.name: server-jwt-signature-verification-disabled
rules.message: Broken access control — a security decision made from a client value, unverified identifier, or unauthenticated service.
rules.remediation: Never disable signature verification. Verify with the signing key and an explicit allow-list of strong algorithms (e.g. RS256/ES256/HS256); reject 'none' and any token that fails verification.
rules.why: Signature verification is explicitly turned off (verify=False / verify_signature:false / alg 'none'). The server accepts any token payload as authentic, letting an attacker forge arbitrary identity and role claims - a complete authentication bypass. The verify=False branch is anchored to a call context ([,(]) so a bare 'const verify = false' variable toggle does not match, and compression algorithm:'none' is suppressed by the notMatch.

rules.name: server-presence-only-auth-header-csharp
rules.message: Broken access control — a security decision made from a client value, unverified identifier, or unauthenticated service.
rules.remediation: Validate the token with JwtSecurityTokenHandler.ValidateToken and TokenValidationParameters (ValidateIssuerSigningKey = true) or the [Authorize] pipeline, and branch on the ClaimsPrincipal result. Reject present-but-invalid tokens.
rules.why: The middleware/action authorizes whenever Request.Headers["Authorization"] != null / ContainsKey / !IsNullOrEmpty - presence only. The bearer token's signature and claims are never validated, so any non-empty header authenticates the caller. The object is restricted to Request/HttpContext.Request so checking response.Headers or an unrelated dictionary does not match.

rules.name: server-presence-only-auth-header-go
rules.message: Broken access control — a security decision made from a client value, unverified identifier, or unauthenticated service.
rules.remediation: Parse and verify inside the guard: jwt.Parse/ParseWithClaims with a key func that checks the signing method and key, then act on token.Valid. A present but invalid/expired token must return 401.
rules.why: The handler/middleware proceeds whenever r.Header.Get("Authorization") != "", i.e. any non-empty header value. The token is never parsed or signature-verified, so an attacker authenticates with an arbitrary string. The sink requires the != "" to be immediately followed by the block brace, so a compound '!= "" && validateToken(...)' does not match, and w.Header() (response writer) is excluded.

rules.name: server-presence-only-auth-header-java
rules.message: Broken access control — a security decision made from a client value, unverified identifier, or unauthenticated service.
rules.remediation: Parse and verify the token inside the guard: Jwts.parserBuilder()...parseClaimsJws(token) (or validateToken/an introspection call) and only continue the chain when verification succeeds. A present-but-invalid token must be rejected.
rules.why: A servlet filter/interceptor treats the request as authenticated whenever getHeader("Authorization") != null, i.e. the header merely exists. The token is not parsed or signature-checked, so any value bypasses the filter. The sink requires the != null to close the if directly, so a compound '!= null && validateToken(...)' does not match.

rules.name: server-presence-only-auth-header-php
rules.message: Broken access control — a security decision made from a client value, unverified identifier, or unauthenticated service.
rules.remediation: After confirming presence, verify the credential: firebase/php-jwt JWT::decode with the key (throws on bad signature), a token validator, or Laravel's auth guard. Return 401 on both absence and verification failure.
rules.why: Access is granted because an auth header/cookie is set or non-empty (isset($_SERVER['HTTP_AUTHORIZATION']) / !empty(...) / truthy / $request->bearerToken() / $request->header('Authorization')). The credential itself is never verified, so any attacker-supplied value authenticates. The Laravel branch is name-restricted to auth headers/cookies so a $request->header('Content-Type') presence check does not match.

rules.name: server-presence-only-auth-header-python
rules.message: Broken access control — a security decision made from a client value, unverified identifier, or unauthenticated service.
rules.remediation: Compare or verify the credential: decode-and-verify the JWT (with verify_signature True), validate the API key against a store, or use the framework's authentication class. Branch on the verified outcome, not on presence.
rules.why: The view grants access on the truthiness of a header/cookie lookup (request.headers.get('Authorization') as a bare if-condition). Any non-empty value passes; the token/API key is never validated against a signature or store.

rules.name: server-presence-only-auth-header-ruby
rules.message: Broken access control — a security decision made from a client value, unverified identifier, or unauthenticated service.
rules.remediation: Decode and verify the token before allowing the action: JWT.decode(token, key, true, { algorithm: ... }) or a verify_token helper, and reject on a decode error. Do not gate on presence with .present?.
rules.why: The controller/before_action grants access whenever request.headers['Authorization'] is truthy or .present? - presence only. The token is never decoded-and-verified, so any non-empty header authenticates the request. The sink requires end-of-line or a then/do block start after the header (optionally .present?), so a value comparison, a .split parse, or a compound '.present? && valid_token?' does not match.

rules.name: service-auth-explicitly-disabled
rules.message: Broken access control — a security decision made from a client value, unverified identifier, or unauthenticated service.
rules.remediation: Remove the auth-off flag and require authentication (auth: true / authentication configured / drop --noauth). Enforce identity at the service on every request rather than assuming a trusted network.
rules.why: An explicit configuration flag disables authentication for a service or client (auth: false, authentication: 'none', AUTH_DISABLED=true, --noauth, skipAuth: true, requireAuth: false). Turning auth off by config is an insecure-by-design decision that leaves the service open. The \bauth\b anchoring means result/state vars such as authorized:false, isAuthenticated:false, requiresAuth:false and the strict-equality check auth===false are not flagged, and the visual/nav notMatch list suppresses purely-visual client toggles.

rules.name: service-broker-cache-noauth-uri
rules.message: Broken access control — a security decision made from a client value, unverified identifier, or unauthenticated service.
rules.remediation: Create a dedicated broker/cache user with a password (RabbitMQ user, memcached SASL) and connect with credentials from a secret: amqp://<user>:<pass>@host. Treat every internal service as internet-facing.
rules.why: An amqp(s):// or memcached:// URI with no userinfo reaches the message broker / cache with no authentication, letting any reachable client publish, consume, or read/poison cached data. Memcached and open brokers have no auth by default.

rules.name: service-default-credentials-uri
rules.message: Broken access control — a security decision made from a client value, unverified identifier, or unauthenticated service.
rules.remediation: Replace the default account with a unique per-service credential drawn from a secret manager and injected via env, and rotate/disable the shipped default account on the server.
rules.why: The connection URI embeds a well-known default credential pair (root:root, postgres:postgres, guest:guest, elastic:changeme, etc.). Default credentials are the first thing an attacker tries and are equivalent to no authentication. Note the pair must be immediately followed by @, so a real password merely prefixed with a default word (postgres:postgres_prod_x9@) is not matched.

rules.name: service-mongo-noauth-uri
rules.message: Broken access control — a security decision made from a client value, unverified identifier, or unauthenticated service.
rules.remediation: Enable MongoDB authorization (--auth) and connect with a per-service credential injected from a secret store: mongodb://<user>:<pass>@host. Never rely on network placement as the only access control.
rules.why: A mongodb:// or mongodb+srv:// URI with no user:pass@ userinfo connects to MongoDB with authentication effectively unused, leaving the datastore reachable by anyone who can reach the port. Network isolation is not authentication.

rules.name: service-redis-client-no-password
rules.message: Broken access control — a security decision made from a client value, unverified identifier, or unauthenticated service.
rules.remediation: Pass an explicit connection object/URL that includes a password/ACL user and host from configuration, e.g. createClient({ url, password }) or Redis(password=...). Ensure the target Redis has requirepass/ACLs set.
rules.why: A Redis client is constructed with empty arguments (redis.createClient(), new Redis(), redis.Redis()/StrictRedis()), which defaults to localhost:6379 with no password, so the app talks to an unauthenticated Redis instance by default. Requiring both a redis token AND an empty-paren constructor on the same line prevents the generic createClient() of Supabase/urql/graphql from matching.

rules.name: service-redis-noauth-uri
rules.message: Broken access control — a security decision made from a client value, unverified identifier, or unauthenticated service.
rules.remediation: Set requirepass / an ACL user on Redis and connect with redis://<user>:<pass>@host (or the password client option) sourced from a secret. Do not depend on the private network alone.
rules.why: A redis:// or rediss:// URI with no userinfo/password connects to Redis with no AUTH, so any client that can reach the port has full command access (KEYS, FLUSHALL, CONFIG). Redis has no auth by default and must be given a password.

rules.name: service-search-security-disabled
rules.message: Broken access control — a security decision made from a client value, unverified identifier, or unauthenticated service.
rules.remediation: Enable the security plugin (xpack.security.enabled: true / keep the OpenSearch security plugin) and configure users, roles, and TLS. Do not disable cluster security even on internal networks.
rules.why: Elasticsearch/OpenSearch security is turned off (xpack.security.enabled=false, plugins.security.disabled=true, DISABLE_SECURITY_PLUGIN=true), so the cluster accepts unauthenticated read/write on every index. This is an insecure-by-design default that exposes all indexed data. The pattern requires the literal security.enabled key with the false value directly after the separator, so ssl/transport/audit/enrollment sub-keys and true values are not matched.

rules.name: session-id-from-client-input
rules.message: A session identifier is taken from client-controlled input — session fixation.
rules.remediation: Never accept a session id from the client. Let the session store generate it, mark the cookie HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite, and regenerate the session on login.
rules.why: If the session id is set from a request parameter, a cookie the client already controls, or a URL value, an attacker can fix a victim's session to a known id (session fixation) and hijack the authenticated session after the victim logs in.

rules.name: session-resolver-call-with-raw-client-id-js
rules.message: Broken session management — identity/role from an unverified client value or a writable store (CWE-807/302).
rules.remediation: Pass a verified identity into the resolver: the subject of a validated JWT (jwt.verify), a value from req.signedCookies, or the user id stored in the server-side session (req.session.userId).
rules.why: An identity/session resolver (getSession, loadUser, findAccount, getRole, ...) is called with a raw client-supplied identifier straight from req.cookies/headers/query, so any caller can impersonate any user by setting that value. The resolver argument must sit directly after the call paren, so getUser(sanitize(...)) and getUser(jwt.verify(...)) are excluded.

rules.name: session-store-indexed-by-raw-client-id-js
rules.message: Broken session management — identity/role from an unverified client value or a writable store (CWE-807/302).
rules.remediation: Resolve the session from a verified credential: a random session id issued server-side and looked up in a server session store, or a signed/verified token (req.signedCookies, jwt.verify, express-session req.session.userId).
rules.why: A session/user/role object is looked up by directly indexing a collection with a raw client-controlled identifier (req.cookies/headers/query/params/body username/uid). The client can set that value to any account, so this is a full authentication/authorization bypass with no verified token gating the lookup.

rules.name: shared-web-lock-mutation
rules.message: A Web Lock is acquired in 'shared' mode.
rules.remediation: Use { mode: 'exclusive' } (the default) whenever the locked section changes state.
rules.why: A shared lock lets several tabs/threads hold it at once, so if the critical section mutates shared state they race and can corrupt it.

rules.name: shell-php
rules.message: This runs an operating-system command.
rules.remediation: Avoid the shell; if unavoidable, pass fixed arguments and escapeshellarg() every value.
rules.why: If any part of the command comes from a request, the request can run commands on the server.

rules.name: shell-python
rules.message: This runs a shell command.
rules.remediation: Pass an argument list and leave shell=False (the default).
rules.why: shell=True (and os.system) send the string through /bin/sh, so interpolated input can inject commands.

rules.name: spoofable-client-ip-header-as-security-key
rules.message: Spoofable client-IP header (X-Forwarded-For) used as a security key — rate-limit / identity bypass (CWE-348).
rules.remediation: Key rate limiting and lockout on a trusted source, not a raw client header. Configure the framework's trusted-proxy option and use its derived address: Express app.set('trust proxy', <hopCount|CIDRs>) then req.ip; Flask ProxyFix(x_for=<n>) then request.remote_addr; Go/Java a vetted RealIP middleware bound to known proxy CIDRs. If you must parse X-Forwarded-For, take the entry your own proxy appended (right-most trusted-to-untrusted), validate it as an IP, and combine it with an authenticated account id. Never trust the left-most/raw header value as the limiter key. If a trusted edge proxy sets the header, have it strip any inbound copy on ingress.
rules.why: A spoofable client-IP header (X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP, X-Client-IP, CF-Connecting-IP, True-Client-IP, RFC 7239 Forwarded, or PHP's HTTP_X_* mapping) is read straight into a clientIp/identity variable or used as the key of a rate limiter, failed-attempt counter, or account-lockout map. These headers are fully client-controlled and pass untouched through any proxy that does not strip them, so an attacker rotates the value per request to land in a fresh bucket and bypass the rate limit or brute-force lockout (or forge another user's identity/key). Complement of the netauthz forwardable-header rules, whose notMatch deliberately excludes this rate-limit / IP-extraction shape; here notMatch still prunes logging/audit/analytics/metrics, trusted-proxy allowlist validation, header-setting, ingress-stripping (delete), test assertions, and comments. req.ip / remoteAddress are intentionally NOT in notMatch so the header-first fallback (req.headers['x-forwarded-for'] || req.socket.remoteAddress) stays flagged.

rules.name: sql-concatenation
rules.message: A SQL statement is built by concatenation.
rules.remediation: Use a parameterised query (placeholders + bound values) so input can never be parsed as SQL.
rules.why: Joining a query string with a variable is the classic SQL-injection shape: the value can change the query's meaning, not just its data.

rules.name: ssrf-aiohttp-user-url
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Validate the host/scheme against an allowlist before the session call; do not forward request.* directly. Consider a custom connector that refuses private/link-local addresses.
rules.why: An aiohttp ClientSession request (session/sess/client .get/.post/.ws_connect, or .request with a method literal first) uses a request attribute in the URL position, so the async outbound fetch targets an attacker-controlled host (CWE-918). The URL-position anchor keeps request.* forwarded as json=/data=/params= from firing, and the \b before the receiver keeps db_session/other suffixed names out.

rules.name: ssrf-blocklist-only-validation
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Replace the blocklist with a positive allowlist of permitted destination hosts. If you must block internal ranges, do it after DNS resolution against the resolved IP and cover all private/link-local/loopback CIDRs, not string patterns.
rules.why: A blocklist/denylist that only enumerates internal addresses (127.0.0.1, localhost, 169.254.x, ::1, cloud metadata) is trivially bypassed via alternate encodings, DNS names that resolve to those IPs, IPv6, or redirects - it is not a valid SSRF defense (CWE-918). Requiring the internal address to be quote-delimited ('127.0.0.1', not a bare word in prose) keeps free-text log/error messages that merely mention 'blocked ... localhost' from firing.

rules.name: ssrf-c-curl-followlocation-enabled
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Keep redirects disabled for user-influenced requests, or set CURLOPT_REDIR_PROTOCOLS and re-validate every redirect target host against the allowlist (e.g. via CURLOPT_PREREQFUNCTION / opensocket callback).
rules.why: Enabling CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION makes libcurl transparently follow HTTP 3xx redirects; even a validated front-door URL can be redirected to an internal host or cloud metadata endpoint (SSRF-via-redirect). The regex fires when FOLLOWLOCATION is set to any non-empty value and the notMatch guard suppresses the explicit-disable forms 0, 0L, and false. Residual edge: an explicit hex disable (0x0) is not recognised by the guard and would still fire.

rules.name: ssrf-c-curl-setopt-url-nonliteral
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Resolve and validate the host against an allowlist before the request, or pin a constant base URL and only append a validated path. Do not pass raw user input to CURLOPT_URL.
rules.why: libcurl fetches the URL passed to CURLOPT_URL. When the third argument is a variable (request-derived) rather than a hardcoded literal, the request target is attacker-influenced, enabling SSRF to internal services or cloud metadata. The regex fires only when arg3 is a plain variable expression, structurally excluding a literal URL ("https://...") and a ternary/function-call form like validate_host(url)?url:def (which ends in '(' not ',)/)'); the notMatch guard additionally suppresses lines performing an inline allowlist/whitelist/validate_host check or a variable already named as allowlisted.

rules.name: ssrf-c-weak-blocklist-loopback
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Replace the denylist with an allowlist of permitted hosts, and enforce it AFTER DNS resolution on the resolved IP (block all private/link-local/loopback ranges), not on the pre-resolution string.
rules.why: Comparing a host/URL against loopback or link-local literals (127.0.0.1, localhost, 169.254.x, 0.0.0.0, ::1, cloud metadata) is a denylist trivially bypassed by decimal/octal/hex IP encodings, alternate DNS names resolving to loopback, IPv6-mapped forms, or a redirect. The regex flags str*cmp/strstr/memcmp comparisons whose quoted literal is one of these sensitive constants, optionally behind a scheme:// prefix so "http://127.0.0.1/" is also caught; an allowlist compares real allowed hostnames and does not match. The \b anchor avoids matching wrapper names like mystrcmp; the literal must sit directly after the quote (optionally after scheme://), so version strings ("1.2.7.0"), "local", and "10.0.0.1" do not fire.

rules.name: ssrf-dompdf-loadhtml-user
rules.message: Renderer resource embedding — a document/PDF/image converter resolves a user-controlled resource, enabling LFI or SSRF (CWE-918/73/611).
rules.remediation: Set isRemoteEnabled to false, configure chroot to a safe directory, and only load fixed/trusted HTML; never feed raw request input to loadHtml/loadHtmlFile.
rules.why: Dompdf $dompdf->loadHtml($userHtml)/loadHtmlFile($url) renders attacker markup; with isRemoteEnabled the engine fetches remote/internal URLs referenced by /CSS (SSRF), and it has a history of local file disclosure (LFI) through resource references.

rules.name: ssrf-flyingsaucer-setdocumentfromstring
rules.message: Renderer resource embedding — a document/PDF/image converter resolves a user-controlled resource, enabling LFI or SSRF (CWE-918/73/611).
rules.remediation: Render only trusted HTML, install a UserAgentCallback/URI resolver that rejects file:// and non-allowlisted hosts, and set a restricted base URL.
rules.why: Flying Saucer (org.xhtmlrenderer) ITextRenderer.setDocumentFromString(userHtml) resolves images/stylesheets and external references from attacker markup via its user-agent/URI resolver, enabling internal URL fetches (SSRF) and local file reads (LFI).

rules.name: ssrf-follow-redirect-location-header
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Re-run the same host allowlist validation on the redirect target before requesting it, or disable automatic redirects (HttpClientHandler.AllowAutoRedirect = false) and reject/allowlist any Location before following it.
rules.why: A second outbound request is made to a redirect Location header taken from a prior response (response.Headers.Location / Headers["Location"] / GetResponseHeader("Location")) without re-validating the new target. Manually following a redirect this way lets an attacker-controlled first hop redirect the fetch to an internal host, bypassing any check done only on the original URL.

rules.name: ssrf-follow-redirects-enabled
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Disable automatic redirect following (setInstanceFollowRedirects(false) / Redirect.NEVER) and manually validate the host of every redirect Location before following it.
rules.why: Following redirects without re-validating each hop lets an allowlisted URL 302-redirect to an internal target, defeating the front-door SSRF check.

rules.name: ssrf-go-blocklist-only-hosts
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Replace the denylist with a positive allowlist of permitted destination hosts, and resolve+re-check the IP after DNS resolution to defeat rebinding.
rules.why: SSRF protection implemented as a denylist that only blocks 127.0.0.1/localhost/169.254/0.0.0.0 is trivially bypassed (decimal/hex IPs, alternate DNS, other RFC1918 ranges, IPv6), so it does not actually stop internal access. Note: this is a heuristic 'weak-defense' rule (not a direct sink) and is the noisiest in the set, since a bare comparison against localhost/127.0.0.1 can also be an unrelated dev-mode or logging check.

rules.name: ssrf-go-checkredirect-follow-all
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Re-validate req.URL against the allowlist inside CheckRedirect, cap the redirect count, or return http.ErrUseLastResponse to stop following redirects.
rules.why: A CheckRedirect callback that unconditionally returns nil follows every redirect without re-validating the new target, so an allowlisted URL can 30x-redirect the client to an internal host (SSRF via redirect).

rules.name: ssrf-go-http-request-input-arg
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Parse the URL, resolve the host, and compare it against an allowlist of permitted hosts before issuing the request; reject internal/link-local addresses.
rules.why: An outbound http/client request is built directly from a request-input accessor (r.URL.Query().Get, r.FormValue, c.Query, mux.Vars, header/cookie) on the same line, so the attacker controls the target host without any allowlist.

rules.name: ssrf-go-http-user-url-var
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Validate the URL host against an allowlist before the call; do not fetch arbitrary user-provided URLs.
rules.why: An outbound request is made to a variable whose name denotes a user-supplied URL (userURL, targetURL, proxyURL, forwardURL, ...) with no allowlist check on the line, a common SSRF shape the multi-line taint engine may miss on a direct sink. The trailing \b keeps derived names like userURLValidated from matching.

rules.name: ssrf-host-string-method-allowlist
rules.message: Weak SSRF host allowlist — endsWith/startsWith/includes is a substring test, not a boundary check, so an attacker host passes (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Parse the URL and compare the host exactly: host === base for a single host, or host === base || host.endsWith('.' + base) for a domain plus its subdomains, or test membership in an allowlist array with ===. For a URL prefix, require the full origin plus separator: url.startsWith(base + '/').
rules.why: endsWith/startsWith/includes/indexOf on a hostname/host/url/origin/referer var is a substring test, not a boundary test. host.endsWith('domain.com') also accepts attacker-owned evildomain.com; url.startsWith('https://api.internal') accepts https://api.internal.evil.com; host.includes('mycorp.com') accepts mycorp.com.attacker.net. Attacker-chosen host reaches an internal target (SSRF). The sink now requires the compared literal to look like a host (a dotted label, an IPv4, or scheme://authority) so ubiquitous path/character/extension checks on a var literally named url (url.startsWith('/'), url.endsWith('.js'), url.includes('?'), host.includes(':')) do not fire and get the whole rule dropped by the harness.

rules.name: ssrf-host-suffix-allowlist-multilang
rules.message: Weak SSRF host allowlist — endsWith/startsWith/includes is a substring test, not a boundary check, so an attacker host passes (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Compare the parsed host exactly (host == base), or check base plus a dot-boundary subdomain (host == base or host.endswith('.' + base) / strings.HasSuffix(host, '.'+base) with an equality companion), or test membership in an allowlist. For a prefix, include the authority terminator.
rules.why: Suffix/contains/prefix host checks in Python (endswith), Go (strings.HasSuffix/Contains/HasPrefix), Java (endsWith/contains), PHP (str_ends_with/strpos), and Ruby (end_with?/include?) are substring tests without a boundary. HasSuffix(host, '.internal') / host.endswith('mycorp.com') / strpos($host,'example.com')!==false also accept an attacker-owned host that merely contains or ends with the string, enabling SSRF. Both alternations now require the second (literal) argument to look like a host (dotted label, IPv4, or scheme://authority), so the extremely common path/scheme/extension checks on a url var across all five languages (strings.HasPrefix(url,'/api/'), url.endswith('.png'), str_contains($url,'?'), strings.Contains(url,'://')) do not fire and get the rule dropped.

negative: if host == 'corp.internal' or host.endswith('.' + base): fetch(url)

rules.name: ssrf-htmlpdf-cli-wkhtmltopdf
rules.message: Renderer resource embedding — a document/PDF/image converter resolves a user-controlled resource, enabling LFI or SSRF (CWE-918/73/611).
rules.remediation: Pass --disable-local-file-access (or enableLocalFileAccess:false in the node binding), render from a fixed template, and put a strict allowlist/network-egress guard in front of any remote fetch; never concatenate raw request input into the command line.
rules.why: wkhtmltopdf/wkhtmltoimage/prince/weasyprint invoked via shell or the node binding with a user-controlled URL/HTML argument. By default these engines resolve file:// and local paths and fetch remote/internal URLs, so an attacker embeds <iframe src=file:///etc/passwd> (LFI) or points the input at http://169.254.169.254/ (SSRF). Taint gate now also recognizes Ruby #{} interpolation and PHP '. $var' concatenation; a log/print/echo suppressor kills the 'prince' English-word false positives on logging lines.

rules.name: ssrf-httpclient-request-user-url
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Resolve the user value against a fixed allowlist of permitted hosts/base URIs before the call, or fetch from a constant base URL and only let the user pick a path/id. Do not rely on blocklisting localhost/127.0.0.1.
rules.why: An HttpClient async method (GetAsync/GetStringAsync/PostAsync/SendAsync, etc.) is invoked with an argument taken directly from ASP.NET request input (Request.Query/QueryString/Form/Params/Headers/Cookies or Request[...]). The outbound host is attacker-controlled, so the fetch can be aimed at internal services or cloud metadata (169.254.169.254). The [^;]* is bounded to the same statement so a fixed-URL call followed by an unrelated Request read on the same line does not match.

rules.name: ssrf-httpx-user-url
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Check the destination host/scheme against an allowlist before issuing the httpx request; construct the URL from validated components rather than request.* values.
rules.why: An httpx call (module helper, request/stream with a method literal first, or a Client/AsyncClient(...) instance) takes a request attribute in the URL position, producing a server-side request to an attacker-controlled host (CWE-918). Requiring the request attribute at the URL slot (not inside params=/headers=/json=) is what suppresses the safe-URL-with-user-body twin.

rules.name: ssrf-imgkit-python-from-user
rules.message: Renderer resource embedding — a document/PDF/image converter resolves a user-controlled resource, enabling LFI or SSRF (CWE-918/73/611).
rules.remediation: Pass options={'disable-local-file-access': None}, never set enable-local-file-access, and allowlist remote URLs; only render fixed/trusted sources.
rules.why: python imgkit (wkhtmltoimage wrapper) rendering user-controlled HTML/URL to an image; default local-file access allows file:// disclosure and internal URL fetches (SSRF) inside the converted document.

rules.name: ssrf-incomplete-loopback-blocklist
rules.message: Incomplete SSRF loopback blocklist — misses cloud-metadata IP, IPv6, and alternate IP encodings (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Do not enumerate a denylist of loopback strings. After DNS resolution, resolve the hostname to its IP(s) and reject any address in a private/reserved range (RFC1918, 127.0.0.0/8, ::1, 169.254.0.0/16 link-local incl. 169.254.169.254, fc00::/7, 0.0.0.0/8) with a numeric IP-range check, normalizing alternate encodings first. Prefer a vetted SSRF-guard library and validate the final resolved address, pinning the resolved IP for the actual connection to defeat DNS-rebind.
rules.why: A positive-match-to-deny host check that blocks only a handful of loopback literals (127.0.0.1 / localhost / 0.0.0.0 / ::1) via array membership (.includes/.indexOf/.some/.has/.contains, in_array, Python `in [..]`) or an equality chain (hostname===literal, host.equals(literal)) is an SSRF blocklist with a hole: it never denies the cloud-metadata endpoint 169.254.169.254, and typically misses alternate loopback encodings (decimal 2130706433, hex 0x7f000001, octal 0177.0.0.1, IPv6 [::1]). An attacker supplies any of those forms and the request sails past the guard to internal/metadata services.

rules.name: ssrf-java-uri-construct-var
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Construct the URI from a constant base and validated components, and validate the host against an allowlist before issuing the request.
rules.why: URI.create(var) / new URI(var) constructs the target URI for HttpClient/WebClient/RestTemplate from user input, the core of an SSRF chain. (new URIBuilder(...) is excluded, since new\s+URI must be immediately followed by '(').)

rules.name: ssrf-java-url-openconnection-var
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Resolve the host and validate it against an allowlist of permitted destinations before opening the connection; reject internal/link-local ranges.
rules.why: new URL(userInput).openConnection()/openStream() opens an outbound connection to a host derived from user input, enabling SSRF against internal services and cloud metadata.

rules.name: ssrf-libreoffice-unoconv-convert
rules.message: Renderer resource embedding — a document/PDF/image converter resolves a user-controlled resource, enabling LFI or SSRF (CWE-918/73/611).
rules.remediation: Convert in a sandboxed, network-isolated profile, strip/deny external references before conversion, and validate the input path; do not build the command line from raw request data pointing at attacker documents.
rules.why: soffice/libreoffice/unoconv --convert-to on a user-supplied office document renders embedded external references (linked images, INCLUDETEXT/WEBSERVICE-style fields, OLE) which trigger outbound fetches to internal hosts (SSRF) and can pull local files (LFI) during conversion. Taint gate now covers Ruby #{} and PHP '. $var'; log/print/echo lines are suppressed to avoid noise from status logging that concatenates a job id.

rules.name: ssrf-localhost-only
rules.message: An SSRF guard blocks only localhost/127.0.0.1.
rules.remediation: Resolve the host to an IP and block all private/loopback/link-local ranges, and disable redirect following.
rules.why: The same address reaches the loopback through ::1, 0.0.0.0, the decimal form 2130706433, DNS rebinding, or a 302 redirect the fetch follows — so a string blocklist is bypassable.

rules.name: ssrf-okhttp-request-url-var
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Build the URL from a fixed base and validate the resolved host against an allowlist before calling .url()/HttpUrl.parse().
rules.why: OkHttp Request.Builder().url(var) / HttpUrl.parse(var) builds an outbound request to a user-derived URL, enabling SSRF.

rules.name: ssrf-pdfkit-python-from-user
rules.message: Renderer resource embedding — a document/PDF/image converter resolves a user-controlled resource, enabling LFI or SSRF (CWE-918/73/611).
rules.remediation: Set options={'disable-local-file-access': None} and validate/allowlist any URL; only pass fixed literal sources or content built from trusted templates.
rules.why: python pdfkit wraps wkhtmltopdf; from_string/from_url/from_file with user-controlled HTML or URL lets an attacker read local files via file:// or reach internal hosts (SSRF) because local-file access is enabled by default.

rules.name: ssrf-php-blocklist-weak-validation
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Replace the denylist with a positive host allowlist; resolve the target hostname and verify every resolved IP is publicly routable before connecting, and re-verify after each redirect.
rules.why: SSRF protection is implemented as a denylist of loopback/link-local/metadata literals. Denylists are trivially bypassed via octal/decimal/hex IPs, [::], DNS rebinding, wildcard DNS, or alternate metadata hostnames. Tightened from the original: the 'localhost' alternative now requires a preceding string/regex delimiter (quote, slash, hash, or pipe) so an identifier such as $localhostname no longer matches, while all quoted and regex denylist forms still do. The dotted/colon IP literals cannot occur inside identifiers, so they stay bare.

rules.name: ssrf-php-curlopt-url-userinput
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Validate the URL host against an allowlist of permitted hosts before curl_setopt; reject non-http(s) schemes and resolve/deny internal and cloud-metadata IP ranges.
rules.why: A request superglobal is set as CURLOPT_URL on the same line, so the outbound curl target is attacker-controlled with no allowlist - classic SSRF. Tightened from the original: the $_SERVER branch now requires an HTTP_ request-header key (e.g. HTTP_X_FORWARDED_HOST) instead of any $_SERVER key, so server-controlled keys like DOCUMENT_ROOT/SERVER_NAME no longer produce false positives. notMatch suppresses lines that gate the value behind an allowlist/in_array check.

rules.name: ssrf-php-fetch-fn-userinput
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Restrict the argument to an allowlisted set of hosts, or use a dedicated HTTP client with host validation; disable allow_url_fopen for genuine local file reads and canonicalize the path.
rules.why: A request superglobal flows directly into a URL-capable stream function (file_get_contents/fopen/get_headers/readfile). With allow_url_fopen enabled these fetch arbitrary remote URLs, giving SSRF (and local file disclosure when a path is supplied). The [^;]* guard is same-statement bounded so a superglobal after a ';' on the same physical line is not falsely joined; notMatch suppresses allowlist-gated reads.

rules.name: ssrf-php-follow-redirects-unvalidated
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Disable redirect following for user-supplied URLs, or cap CURLOPT_MAXREDIRS and re-validate every redirect Location target against the host allowlist before following.
rules.why: CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION is enabled (true/1), so curl silently follows 30x redirects. If the initial URL is user-influenced, a redirect can send the request to an internal target the initial validation never inspected - a common SSRF filter bypass. The trailing \b keeps '1' from matching inside '10' and the (true|1) value guard excludes the false/0 disable forms.

rules.name: ssrf-puppeteer-playwright-setcontent
rules.message: Renderer resource embedding — a document/PDF/image converter resolves a user-controlled resource, enabling LFI or SSRF (CWE-918/73/611).
rules.remediation: Render only trusted/templated HTML, run the browser with request interception that blocks internal hosts and file://, and never launch with --allow-file-access-from-files.
rules.why: Puppeteer/Playwright page.setContent(userHtml) followed by page.pdf()/screenshot() renders attacker markup with full network (and, with file-access flags, local) capability, so /

rules.name: ssrf-redirect-follow-tainted-url
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Set allow_redirects=False (follow_redirects=False for httpx) and, if redirects are needed, re-run the allowlist/IP checks on every hop's Location before following it.
rules.why: A user-controlled URL sits in the URL position of an HTTP call that is made with allow_redirects/follow_redirects=True, so even an allowlisted origin can 30x-redirect the client into internal services; the redirect target is never re-validated (CWE-918). Anchoring request.* to the URL slot of a concrete requests/httpx/session call (rather than 'request.* appears anywhere on a line with redirects=True') removes the false hit where request.* is only a header/param and the URL is a constant.

rules.name: ssrf-redirect-following
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Set maxRedirects: 0 (or redirect: 'manual' for fetch) and handle redirects yourself, re-running the full host allowlist + private-IP check on each Location before re-issuing the request; or supply a beforeRedirect/validateRedirect hook that re-validates every hop.
rules.why: The HTTP client is configured to follow redirects (maxRedirects > 0 / followRedirect:true / followAllRedirects:true / .redirects(n)) with no redirect-time re-validation hook.
