Even if the initial URL passed an allowlist check, a permitted server can 30x-redirect the client to an internal host, defeating front-door validation. maxRedirects requires `[1-9]` so `maxRedirects: 0` and `.redirects(0)` are excluded, and notMatch suppresses a beforeRedirect/validateRedirect hook or `redirect:'manual'`.

rules.name: ssrf-req-input-http-client
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Never build the request target from raw user input. Resolve the requested resource through a fixed server-side allowlist of scheme+host (exact match after parsing with `new URL()`), reject non-http(s) schemes, resolve DNS and re-check the resolved IP against private/link-local ranges, and pin the base URL as a constant to which only a validated path/id is appended.
rules.why: A request-input value (req.query/params/body/headers/cookies/url/originalUrl/hostname) sits in the FIRST (URL) argument of an outbound HTTP client call (fetch/axios/got/needle/superagent/request/http(s).get|request), so the attacker controls the destination host and can coerce the server into hitting cloud-metadata (169.254.169.254), localhost admin ports, or intranet hosts. The `[^,)]*` guard keeps the user token inside arg one, so an options object like `{headers: req.headers}` after a comma is not flagged. notMatch suppresses a hardcoded literal-URL first arg (single/double/backtick quoted) and common allowlist markers; note it still fires on `fetch("https://" + req.query.host)` because only the scheme is literal (no `[\w.-]` host after `https://`).

rules.name: ssrf-requests-user-url
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Resolve the target against a strict allowlist of permitted hosts and schemes before the call; never pass request.args/form/json/GET etc. straight into the URL. Disable redirects and block internal/link-local ranges at DNS-resolution time.
rules.why: requests.<method>() takes a Flask/Django/FastAPI request attribute in the URL position (first positional arg, or url=, or the arg after the method literal for requests.request), so the outbound destination is attacker-controlled with no allowlist (CWE-918). The URL-position anchor is what separates this from the safe case where request.* flows into data=/params=/headers=/cookies=/json= instead of the URL.

rules.name: ssrf-ruby-blocklist-only
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Replace the denylist with a positive allowlist of permitted hosts and resolve+validate the final IP; do not rely on blocking known-bad literals.
rules.why: SSRF protection that only denies 127.0.0.1/localhost/169.254/0.0.0.0/metadata is trivially bypassed (DNS rebinding, alternate IP encodings, IPv6, redirects). Tightened the third lookahead: it now requires an actual comparison (==), include?, or a deny verb, so config assignments like host = "127.0.0.1" if test_mode no longer false-fire on a bare if/unless.

rules.name: ssrf-ruby-faraday
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Pin Faraday to an allowlisted base and validate any user path/host; block private ranges.
rules.why: A Faraday connection/request URL (Faraday.get or Faraday.new url:) is derived from user input with no allowlist, enabling SSRF. Added \b and ENV suppression; note Faraday.new(url: "literal") is already safe because the string-literal arg does not match the taint alternation.

rules.name: ssrf-ruby-follow-redirects
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Disable automatic redirects (follow_redirects: false) or re-validate every redirect target host against the allowlist.
rules.why: A request to a user-controlled URL follows redirects, so even an allowlisted first hop can be redirected to an internal target without re-validation. Added \b so MyHTTParty and a plain options hash without a lib call do not match.

rules.name: ssrf-ruby-httparty
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Validate the parsed host against an allowlist and block RFC1918/link-local addresses before calling HTTParty.
rules.why: HTTParty issues a request to a user-controlled URL with no allowlist, enabling SSRF. Added \b so MyHTTParty.get does not match, and ENV suppression for URI(ENV[...]).

rules.name: ssrf-ruby-interpolated-host
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Do not interpolate untrusted data into the host portion; build the URL from a fixed base and an allowlist-validated host.
rules.why: The request URL string BEGINS with an interpolation, so the scheme/host itself is attacker-controlled (full SSRF), not just a path under a constant base. Added \b so MyHTTParty and File.open/logger.open do not match.

rules.name: ssrf-ruby-net-http
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Resolve and validate the host against a strict allowlist before the request; reject private/link-local IPs and non-http(s) schemes.
rules.why: Net::HTTP request target (URI/host) is built from request input with no allowlist, letting an attacker pivot to internal services or cloud metadata. Added a left \b so MyNet::HTTP does not match, and extended the URI-literal notMatch branch to also suppress URI(ENV[...]) config.

rules.name: ssrf-ruby-open-uri
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Never pass user input to open()/URI.open; use an HTTP client with an allowlisted host and disable file/pipe schemes.
rules.why: open-uri Kernel#open / URI.open fetches a user-supplied URL (also local file read and, with a leading pipe, command execution). This rule previously LACKED the URI-literal guard, so open(URI("https://literal")) false-fired; added it (plus ENV).

rules.name: ssrf-ruby-restclient
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Constrain the destination host to an allowlist and reject internal/metadata addresses before the RestClient call.
rules.why: RestClient sends a request to a user-controlled URL (including the RestClient::Request.execute url: form) without an allowlist, allowing SSRF. Added \b and ENV suppression.

rules.name: ssrf-spring-resttemplate-var-url
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Pass only a constant base URL and append validated path segments, or validate the full URL host against an allowlist before the call.
rules.why: Spring RestTemplate methods take the target URL as their first argument; a non-literal (user-derived) URL there allows SSRF to arbitrary hosts.

rules.name: ssrf-urllib-urlopen-user-url
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Validate the URL against an allowlist and restrict the scheme to http/https before opening it; never hand request.* directly to urlopen. Prefer a hardened HTTP client that blocks internal IP ranges.
rules.why: urllib.request.urlopen / Request / urlretrieve is invoked with a request attribute in the URL position (first argument or url=), fetching an attacker-chosen destination (CWE-918). urlopen also honours file:// and other schemes, widening the impact. Anchoring request.* to the first arg avoids flagging the safe case where request.* is passed as the POST data= or headers= of urlopen/Request.

rules.name: ssrf-user-url-variable
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Validate the URL against a fixed allowlist of permitted hosts before the request (parse with `new URL()`, compare host exactly), reject non-http(s) schemes, and re-validate after DNS resolution against private/link-local/loopback ranges. If the value is genuinely a constant base, rename it (e.g. apiBaseUrl) and keep it out of user control.
rules.why: An outbound HTTP client call is made with a variable whose name strongly signals externally-controlled intent (userUrl, targetUrl, redirectUrl, webhookUrl, callbackUrl, proxyUrl, remoteUrl, external_url, ...). These names almost always denote a URL sourced from request input, so the destination host is attacker-influenced. The keyword must sit immediately after `(` and be immediately followed by `_?url`, so `userProfile.url` (user not adjacent to url) and unrelated names (`baseUrl`, `apiEndpointUrl`) are not flagged. Complements the taint engine for the common case where the value was assigned to a suggestively-named local a line or two earlier.

rules.name: ssrf-weak-blocklist-host-check
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Replace the blocklist with a positive allowlist of permitted hosts, and resolve+validate the final IP after DNS rather than string-matching the input.
rules.why: A blocklist that only rejects 127.0.0.1/localhost/169.254 is trivially bypassed (DNS rebinding, decimal/hex IPs, alternate representations), so the SSRF guard is ineffective.

rules.name: ssrf-weak-blocklist-loopback-metadata
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Replace the denylist with a positive allowlist of permitted destination hosts, and resolve+re-check the address after DNS resolution (and after any redirect) rather than string-matching known-bad literals.
rules.why: An SSRF guard compares a host/url/ip variable against a hardcoded loopback or link-local/metadata literal (127.0.0.1, localhost, 169.254, 0.0.0.0, ::1). Denylist validation is trivially bypassed via alternate encodings, DNS rebinding, 0x7f.0.0.1, [::ffff:127.0.0.1], or a redirect, so it does not actually stop SSRF. notMatch suppresses allowlist/whitelist guards (e.g. ipWhitelist.Contains("127.0.0.1")).

rules.name: ssrf-weasyprint-html-writepdf
rules.message: Renderer resource embedding — a document/PDF/image converter resolves a user-controlled resource, enabling LFI or SSRF (CWE-918/73/611).
rules.remediation: Render only trusted/literal sources, or pass a sandboxed url_fetcher= that rejects file:// and non-allowlisted hosts.
rules.why: WeasyPrint HTML(string=/url=/filename=user).write_pdf() resolves external and local resources referenced by the document; user-controlled input enables file:// disclosure (LFI) and fetches of internal URLs (SSRF) unless a restricting url_fetcher is supplied. sinkRegex now tolerates whitespace before the '(' (HTML (string=...)).

rules.name: ssrf-webclient-httpclient-uri-var
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Use a fixed base URL with .uri(pathTemplate, values) or validate the host against an allowlist; do not pass a raw user string to .uri().
rules.why: WebClient/HttpRequest .uri(var) with a user-derived String target issues an outbound request to an attacker-chosen host (SSRF). A single-parameter uriBuilder lambda is excluded in the sink lookahead so that a real .uri(userUrl) call with a downstream lambda elsewhere on the line is no longer suppressed.

rules.name: ssrf-webrequest-webclient-request-user-url
rules.message: Server-side request forgery — an outbound request targets a user-controlled address (CWE-918).
rules.remediation: Validate the parsed Uri host against an allowlist before creating the request, or build the request from a constant base URI and a constrained path. Prefer HttpClient with a handler that disables auto-redirect when the target is user-influenced.
rules.why: WebRequest.Create / HttpWebRequest.Create or a legacy WebClient download/upload method (DownloadString/DownloadData/DownloadFile/OpenRead/UploadString, etc.) receives a URL taken straight from request input. The WebRequest/WebClient stack follows redirects and reaches arbitrary internal hosts, so a user-controlled URL is a direct SSRF sink. The [^;]* is statement-bounded to avoid matching an unrelated Request read after a fixed-URL call on the same line.

rules.name: ssrf-xslt-external-stylesheet-permissive
rules.message: Renderer resource embedding — a document/PDF/image converter resolves a user-controlled resource, enabling LFI or SSRF (CWE-918/73/611).
rules.remediation: Set ACCESS_EXTERNAL_STYLESHEET and ACCESS_EXTERNAL_SCHEMA to "" (empty) to forbid external resolution, or restrict to an explicit allowlisted protocol/host.
rules.why: A TransformerFactory / XSLT-FO processor set to allow external stylesheets/schemas (accessExternalStylesheet=all|http|file) fetches xsl:import/xsl:include and schema URLs from user-controlled documents, causing SSRF to internal hosts and file:// reads during rendering. Empty-string (disabled), symbolic constants (EMPTY), and bare references without a permissive value do not match.

rules.name: ssti-angularjs-compile-interpolate
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Only $compile/$interpolate fixed template strings and bind user input through scope properties with ng-bind/text interpolation; never compile HTML built from user input.
rules.why: AngularJS $compile/$interpolate parse their string argument as an Angular template and evaluate its {{ }} expressions, so a user-controlled string is client-side template injection that historically bypasses the expression sandbox to run arbitrary JS.

rules.name: ssti-art-template-render-compile
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Use template() with a fixed template id/file path and pass user input as the data object; never call render/compile on a template string derived from user input.
rules.why: art-template's render/compile turn the passed string into a JavaScript render function whose expression syntax executes JS, so a dynamic template source enables remote code execution.

rules.name: ssti-blade-compile-string
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Only compile fixed, developer-authored template strings; keep user input out of the compiled source and bind it as data at render time.
rules.why: compileString() on the Blade compiler (and Phalcon Volt) turns a template string into executable PHP, so a dynamic argument compiles attacker-controlled directives that run as code.

rules.name: ssti-bladeone-runstring
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Pass a fixed Blade string as the template and supply user values only through runString()'s data array, never as the template argument.
rules.why: BladeOne's runString() compiles and evaluates its first argument as a Blade template, so a dynamic template string permits directive injection and PHP execution.

rules.name: ssti-bottle-simple-template
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Create SimpleTemplate from a constant template string or a trusted template file (name=/lookup) and supply request data only as render keyword variables.
rules.why: Bottle's SimpleTemplate compiles its source argument into Python-backed template code, so constructing it from a dynamic string executes attacker-controlled template/Python expressions.

rules.name: ssti-bottle-template-function
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Call template('name', **data) with a constant template name and pass all user input as keyword data, never as an inline or concatenated template body.
rules.why: Bottle's template() helper treats a first argument that is not a bare template-name literal as inline SimpleTemplate source, so a dynamic first argument compiles attacker input as template code; a (?<![\w.]) guard limits matches to the bare template( / bottle.template( forms and rejects unrelated .template() method calls.

rules.name: ssti-chameleon-page-template
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Use PageTemplate with a constant template string or PageTemplateFile pointing at a trusted file, and pass user input only as template variables.
rules.why: Chameleon's PageTemplate compiles its string argument as a ZPT/TAL template that evaluates embedded Python, so a dynamic template body lets attacker input run as expressions (PageTemplateFile, which loads a fixed file, is intentionally excluded by requiring '(' immediately after PageTemplate).

rules.name: ssti-commons-jexl-create-expression
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Compile only fixed literal JEXL and pass user input as variables in the JexlContext; never build the expression string from user input.
rules.why: JexlEngine.createExpression/createScript compiles its argument as a JEXL expression/script; a dynamic argument is attacker-controlled JEXL that can call arbitrary Java and reach RCE.

rules.name: ssti-commons-text-stringsubstitutor-interpolator
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Interpolate only trusted templates, or build a StringSubstitutor with a restricted StringLookup that excludes script/url/dns lookups; keep user input as data, not as the interpolated template.
rules.why: StringSubstitutor.createInterpolator() enables active ${script:...}/${url:...}/${dns:...} lookups, so replacing a dynamic string interpolates attacker-controlled directives (the Text4Shell class of injection).

rules.name: ssti-cottle-document-createdefault
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Create the document from a fixed literal template and pass user input as values in the runtime store passed to Render, not as the template source.
rules.why: Cottle's Document.CreateDefault parses its argument as a Cottle template; a user-controlled source lets an attacker evaluate expressions and invoke exposed functions against the value store (SSTI).

rules.name: ssti-dot-template-compile
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Compile only a constant template literal and supply user input through the render function's data argument, never from request input.
rules.why: doT.template/compile builds a JavaScript function from its string argument and its {{= }} / {{ }} blocks run raw JS, so a dynamic template source lets an attacker execute code on the server.

rules.name: ssti-dotliquid-template-parse
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Parse only fixed literal Liquid templates and expose user input as registered drop/hash DATA passed to Render, never as the parsed source.
rules.why: DotLiquid's Template.Parse compiles its argument as a Liquid template; a user-controlled source lets an attacker traverse the object graph and disclose or manipulate server data (SSTI).

rules.name: ssti-dustjs-compile-rendersource
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Compile fixed template literals (or load named precompiled templates) and pass user input only through the context object; never build the source string from user input.
rules.why: dust.compile/renderSource parse their first argument as a Dust template, so a user-controlled source lets an attacker inject sections, helpers and context references that leak data and can reach registered helper code.

rules.name: ssti-dwoo-string-template
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Instantiate the file-based Dwoo template with a fixed path and pass user input through the Dwoo data object, not into a string-template constructor.
rules.why: Constructing a Dwoo string-template object from a dynamic value compiles that string as a Dwoo template, whose expression/PHP callbacks lead to code execution.

rules.name: ssti-ejs-render-compile
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Use ejs.renderFile with a fixed template path (or a constant string literal) and supply user input only as the data object, never build the template string from request input.
rules.why: ejs.render/compile evaluate their string argument as an EJS template whose <% %> scriptlets are executed as JavaScript, so a dynamic source is direct server-side code injection.

rules.name: ssti-eta-render-compile
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Render from a fixed template file or constant literal and pass user input as the data object; never build the Eta template string from user input.
rules.why: Eta compiles its string argument into a JavaScript function and its <% %> tags execute JS, so passing a dynamic template source results in server-side code execution.

rules.name: ssti-fenom-compile-code
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Compile only fixed template strings (or use display()/fetch() with a template name) and pass user input as the template variables array, not as the compiled source.
rules.why: Fenom's compileCode() compiles its first argument as Fenom template source into PHP, so a dynamic string allows template-expression injection and code execution.

rules.name: ssti-flask-render-template-string
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Render a fixed template file with render_template('page.html', name=value) and pass all user input only as named context data, never as the template source.
rules.why: Flask's render_template_string compiles its first argument as a Jinja2 template, so a dynamic (variable, concatenated, f-string, %/format) source lets attacker input reach the template compiler and execute.

rules.name: ssti-fluid-parser-parse
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Parse fixed literal templates and register user input as model values in the TemplateContext, never build the parsed source from request data.
rules.why: Fluid's FluidParser.Parse/TryParse compiles its first argument as a Liquid template; a dynamic source string lets an attacker read exposed model members and inject template logic (SSTI).

rules.name: ssti-freemarker-getplaintexttemplate
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Do not construct the content argument from request data; use a fixed template resource and supply user input only through the data-model.
rules.why: Template.getPlainTextTemplate builds a template from its String content argument; a dynamic content String is compiled as template source and enables directive injection reaching RCE.

rules.name: ssti-freemarker-template-constructor
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Load templates by name from a TemplateLoader/Configuration and pass user input only as data in the data-model; never build the Template source String/Reader from user input.
rules.why: The FreeMarker Template constructor compiles its second argument (a String source or a Reader over one) into an executable template, so a dynamic source lets an attacker inject FreeMarker directives that reach RCE.

positive: Template t = new Template("tpl", req.getParameter("tpl"), cfg);
negative: Template t = new Template("tpl", new StringReader("Hello"), cfg);

rules.name: ssti-genshi-markup-template
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Instantiate MarkupTemplate from a fixed template string or a trusted template file and inject user data only through the generate()/context values.
rules.why: Genshi's MarkupTemplate parses its first argument as an XML/markup template with embedded Python expressions, so a dynamic source string allows attacker-controlled template directives to execute.

rules.name: ssti-genshi-text-template
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Build TextTemplate/NewTextTemplate from constant template text and provide user-controlled values only via the render context.
rules.why: Genshi's TextTemplate/NewTextTemplate compile their argument as a text template containing evaluable Python expressions, so a dynamic source string lets user input execute as template directives.

rules.name: ssti-go-amber-compilestring
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Compile a fixed literal (or use amber.Compile on a trusted file) and pass user input only via the data given to the compiled template's Execute.
rules.why: amber.CompileString compiles its first argument as Amber template SOURCE (which lowers to Go html/template with embedded expressions), so a dynamic value is server-side template injection.

rules.name: ssti-go-fasttemplate-new-execute
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Build the fasttemplate from a fixed literal source and pass user input only through the substitution map given to Execute/ExecuteString (the t.ExecuteString(map) method call, which has no fasttemplate. prefix, is safe).
rules.why: fasttemplate.New/NewTemplate/ExecuteString take the template SOURCE as their first argument; it does only tag substitution (no expression evaluation) so impact is limited, but a user-controlled source is still template-source injection that can splice attacker placeholders/output.

rules.name: ssti-go-jet-loadtemplate
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Register templates from a trusted loader with fixed content and pass user input only through the vars/VarMap given to Execute.
rules.why: jet Set.LoadTemplate(name, content) compiles its second argument as template SOURCE, so passing user input as the content lets an attacker inject Jet actions and reach ranged/exposed data.

rules.name: ssti-go-liquid-parse-render-string
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Parse a fixed literal (or a file from a trusted path via ParseTemplateFile) and pass user input only through the bindings map handed to Render/ParseAndRenderString.
rules.why: liquid Engine.ParseString/ParseTemplate/ParseAndRenderString/ParseTemplateAndCache compile their first argument as Liquid template SOURCE, so a dynamic value (including a []byte(...) of request input) lets an attacker inject tags/filters and reach the bindings.

rules.name: ssti-go-mustache-render
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Pass a fixed literal template (or use RenderFile with a trusted path) and supply user input only through the data argument.
rules.why: mustache.Render/RenderInLayout/RenderInLayoutPartials/ParseString take the template SOURCE as their first argument, so a dynamic value there is template injection (data/context disclosure and, via partials/lambdas, further abuse) even though Mustache is logic-less.

rules.name: ssti-go-plush-render
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Render a fixed literal template and pass user input only through the plush.Context set with ctx.Set, never as the template source.
rules.why: plush.Render/Parse/BuildTemplate compile their first argument as Plush template SOURCE, which supports rich Go-like expressions and method calls, so a dynamic value is high-impact server-side template injection.

rules.name: ssti-go-pongo2-fromstring
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Compile a fixed literal (or a file from a trusted path via pongo2.FromFile) once and supply user input only inside the pongo2.Context data map.
rules.why: pongo2.FromString/FromBytes/RenderTemplateString compile their first argument as Django-style template SOURCE, so a dynamic value there (including a []byte(...) conversion of request input) lets an attacker inject tags/filters and traverse the context.

rules.name: ssti-go-raymond-handlebars-render
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Compile a fixed literal (or a file from a trusted path via raymond.ParseFile) and pass user input only through the context/data argument to Render/Exec.
rules.why: raymond.Render/Parse/MustParse compile their first argument as Handlebars template SOURCE, so a dynamic value lets an attacker inject expressions and calls to registered helpers.

rules.name: ssti-go-soy-addtemplatestring
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Add templates from fixed literal strings or trusted files via AddTemplateFile, and pass user input only as the data map at render time.
rules.why: soy Bundle/Tofu.AddTemplateString(name, contents) compiles its second argument as Closure Template SOURCE, so passing user input as the contents lets an attacker inject Soy commands and reach the render data.

rules.name: ssti-go-template-parsefiles-parseglob
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Resolve template file paths from a fixed allowlist, never from request-derived variables or concatenated paths, and pass user input only as data to Execute.
rules.why: ParseFiles/ParseGlob load and compile the template SOURCE from a filesystem path, so a user-controlled first path argument (variable or concatenation) lets an attacker point the engine at attacker-influenced or unintended files that are then rendered.

rules.name: ssti-go-text-html-template-parse
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Keep the Parse() source a fixed string literal and pass user input only as the data/context argument to Execute, never build the template source from request input.
rules.why: template.New(name).Parse(x) (and the template.Must(...New(...).Parse(x)) wrapper) compiles x as the template SOURCE, so a variable, concatenation, string() conversion or fmt.Sprintf result there lets an attacker inject template actions that read passed data and call exposed methods.

rules.name: ssti-go-velvet-render
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Render a fixed literal template and pass user input only through the velvet.Context set with ctx.Set, never as the template source.
rules.why: velvet.Render/Parse/BuildTemplate compile their first argument as Velvet (Handlebars-like) template SOURCE with helper support, so a dynamic value is server-side template injection.

rules.name: ssti-groovy-createtemplate
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Pass a File/URL/resource for the template and bind user input only through the binding map given to make(); never compile a user-supplied string.
rules.why: Groovy's template engines compile the String/Reader passed to createTemplate into Groovy code, so a dynamic template source is arbitrary Groovy execution (RCE) via ${...} and <% %> blocks.

rules.name: ssti-handlebars-compile
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Keep the template source a fixed string literal and pass user input only through the data/context object of the compiled function, never into compile() itself.
rules.why: Handlebars.compile/precompile turns its string argument into an executable template function, so a dynamic template source lets an attacker inject template/helper expressions that can escalate to RCE via prototype access.

rules.name: ssti-handlebars-java-compileinline
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Use handlebars.compile(location) with a fixed template resource and pass user input only through the model/context.
rules.why: Handlebars.compileInline compiles its argument as an inline template, so a dynamic argument lets an attacker inject Handlebars/helper expressions that can leak context or, via helpers, reach code execution.

rules.name: ssti-handlebarsnet-compile
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Compile a fixed literal template and pass user input as the DATA object when invoking the compiled delegate, not as the compiled source.
rules.why: Handlebars.Compile turns its string argument into a template delegate; a request-controlled source lets an attacker inject helpers/expressions and disclose context data (SSTI).

rules.name: ssti-hogan-compile
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Compile only fixed template literals and pass user input through the render data object; never derive the template string from user input.
rules.why: Hogan.compile turns its string argument into a Mustache template function, so a user-controlled template string lets an attacker inject sections and partials that disclose context data and enable stored XSS.

rules.name: ssti-jade-compile-render
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Render from a fixed .jade file with jade.renderFile and pass user input as locals; never build the compiled string from request data.
rules.why: Jade (the predecessor of Pug) compiles its string argument into an executable render function, so a dynamic template source allows arbitrary JavaScript execution on the server.

rules.name: ssti-jinja2-django-from-string
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Load a predefined template with get_template()/from_string on a constant, and supply user input only through the render context, not the template string itself.
rules.why: Environment.from_string (Jinja2) and Engine.from_string (Django) compile their string argument into a template, so a dynamic source string turns attacker-controlled text into executable template code.

rules.name: ssti-jinjava-render
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Keep the template string a fixed literal or resource and pass user-controlled values only in the context/bindings map.
rules.why: Jinjava.render/renderForResult compiles its first argument as a Jinja-style template; a dynamic template string lets an attacker inject expressions/filters that reach RCE.

rules.name: ssti-jmustache-compiler-compile
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Compile a fixed template string/resource and provide user input only through the context object passed to execute().
rules.why: JMustache's Mustache.compiler().compile(...) parses its argument as a Mustache template; a dynamic argument makes user input the template source, exposing the data model and lambda handling.

rules.name: ssti-laravel-blade-render
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Render a fixed view with view('name', $data) or pass a constant Blade string, and supply user input only through the second data array.
rules.why: Blade::render() compiles its first argument as a Blade template, which can embed raw PHP, so a dynamic template string gives an attacker arbitrary code execution.

rules.name: ssti-latte-string-loader
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Populate the StringLoader map only with fixed template strings and pass user data via the render parameters, never as a loader value built from request input.
rules.why: Latte's StringLoader serves its array values as compilable Latte template source, so a dynamic value registers attacker-controlled Latte code that Latte compiles and runs as PHP.

rules.name: ssti-liquidjs-parseandrender
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Render fixed templates via engine.renderFile with a constant path and pass user input as the scope object; never pass a user-controlled string to parseAndRender.
rules.why: LiquidJS parseAndRender/parseAndRenderSync compile their first argument as a Liquid template, so a user-controlled source lets an attacker inject tags and filters that leak context data and can invoke registered filter code.

rules.name: ssti-lodash-underscore-template
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Compile only a fixed literal template and feed user input through the data object of the returned function; never build the template string from user input.
rules.why: _.template compiles its string argument into a JavaScript function, and its <% %> interpolate/evaluate delimiters execute arbitrary JS, so a dynamic template source is direct server-side code injection.

rules.name: ssti-mustache-java-compile-reader
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Compile templates from fixed resource names and pass user input only in the scope object given to execute().
rules.why: MustacheFactory.compile(Reader, name) parses the Reader as a Mustache template; wrapping a dynamic string in a StringReader makes user input the template source, enabling context disclosure and lambda/section abuse.

rules.name: ssti-mustache-load-template
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Load a named/fixed template and pass user input as the data context to render(); do not build the template source from request data.
rules.why: Mustache_Engine::loadTemplate() compiles its argument as Mustache template source, so a dynamic string lets an attacker inject template syntax (and, via lambdas/partials, escalate) instead of supplying data.

rules.name: ssti-mustache-render-parse
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Pass a fixed template literal as the first argument and put user input in the view object; never derive the template string from request input.
rules.why: Mustache.render/parse interpret their first argument as the template, so a user-controlled template string lets an attacker inject Mustache sections and partials, leaking context data and enabling stored XSS.

rules.name: ssti-mustachio-parser-parse
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Parse a fixed literal template and supply user input as the data dictionary passed to the returned template, not as the parsed source.
rules.why: Mustachio's Parser.Parse compiles its argument into a Mustache template delegate; a dynamic template source lets an attacker inject sections and disclose model data (SSTI).

rules.name: ssti-nunjucks-renderstring-compile
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Call renderString/compile with a constant template literal and pass user input via the context object; render user-selected pages with env.render on a fixed template name instead.
rules.why: nunjucks.renderString / env.renderString / nunjucks.compile parse their string argument as a Nunjucks template, and a dynamic source lets an attacker inject expressions that reach the global scope and achieve RCE.

rules.name: ssti-nustache-stringtostring
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Render a fixed literal template string and pass user input only as the data argument, never as the template parameter.
rules.why: Nustache's Render.StringToString treats its first argument as the Mustache template source; user-controlled source lets an attacker traverse the data object and inject sections (SSTI).

rules.name: ssti-nvelocity-evaluate
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Evaluate only fixed literal VTL and place user input into the VelocityContext as data, never as the instring template argument.
rules.why: Velocity.Evaluate(context, writer, tag, instring) merges its fourth argument as a VTL template; a dynamic template string permits method invocation on context objects and can reach RCE (SSTI).

rules.name: ssti-pebble-getliteraltemplate
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Use getTemplate(name) to load a fixed template and pass user input only in the evaluation context map.
rules.why: PebbleEngine.getLiteralTemplate compiles its String argument directly as template source, so a dynamic argument lets an attacker inject Pebble syntax that can escalate to RCE.

rules.name: ssti-pug-compile-render
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Render from a fixed .pug file via pug.renderFile/compileFile and pass user input as locals, never assemble the template source from user input.
rules.why: pug.render/compile/compileClient compile their string argument into a JavaScript render function that executes inline Pug/JS expressions, so a dynamic template source yields server-side code execution.

rules.name: ssti-python-template-constructor
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Construct Template objects only from constant, developer-authored strings (or load them from trusted files via filename=) and pass user input exclusively as render/context data.
rules.why: The Template class in Jinja2, Django, Mako, Tornado and Cheetah compiles its source/text argument on construction, so building a Template from a dynamic string compiles attacker input as template code.

rules.name: ssti-razorengine-razor-parse-compile
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Keep the template source a constant literal and pass user input only through the model argument, never spliced into the parsed/compiled string.
rules.why: The Razor.Parse / Engine.Razor.Compile facade compiles its first argument as a Razor template, so a request-derived source string yields arbitrary code execution.

rules.name: ssti-razorengine-runcompile
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Pass user input as template DATA (the model/ViewBag), and give RunCompile a fixed string-literal template source, never a value derived from the request.
rules.why: Engine.Razor.RunCompile compiles its first argument as Razor source, so a dynamic template string lets an attacker execute arbitrary C#/.NET code (full RCE).

rules.name: ssti-razorenginecore-compile
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Compile a constant literal template once and bind user input via the model at RunAsync time instead of building the compiled source from input.
rules.why: RazorEngineCore's razorEngine.Compile turns its string argument into a compiled Razor template that runs C#, so a dynamic source string is remote code execution.

rules.name: ssti-razorlight-compilerenderstring
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Give CompileRenderStringAsync a fixed literal content template and pass user input through the model parameter only.
rules.why: In CompileRenderStringAsync(key, content, model) the second argument IS the Razor template source; a dynamic content string compiles attacker input as executable Razor.

rules.name: ssti-ruby-erb-new
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Keep the ERB template source a fixed string literal (or a trusted file) and pass user input only as data through the binding/hash given to result/result_with_hash, never spliced into the template string.
rules.why: ERB.new compiles its first argument into executable Ruby; a dynamic template source (variable, concatenation, #{} interpolation, or % formatting) lets attacker input run arbitrary code via <%= %>/<% %> tags.

rules.name: ssti-ruby-erubi-engine-new
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Instantiate Erubi engines only from constant/literal template text or trusted files, and feed user data through the evaluated binding rather than into the engine's source argument.
rules.why: Erubi::Engine (and CaptureEnd/CaptureBlock variants) turns its first argument into Ruby source (.src) that is later evaluated; a dynamic template argument makes that generated code attacker-controlled.

rules.name: ssti-ruby-erubis-eruby-new
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Build Erubis templates only from literal/trusted sources and supply user values as evaluation context, never concatenated or interpolated into the template string.
rules.why: Erubis::Eruby and its FastEruby/EscapedEruby/PI::Eruby variants compile the given string into evaluated Ruby; a dynamic template source lets user input execute code through the embedded expression tags.

rules.name: ssti-ruby-haml-engine-new
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Compile only constant/literal or trusted-file Haml, and pass user values through the render scope object rather than into the template string.
rules.why: Haml::Engine.new compiles its first argument as a Haml template into Ruby; a dynamic source lets user input inject Ruby via Haml's = / #{...} evaluation, giving SSTI/RCE.

rules.name: ssti-ruby-haml-template-new
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Give Haml::Template.new a fixed filename or a constant literal block, and route user data through the render scope, not into the template source.
rules.why: Haml::Template.new (Tilt-style) compiles the string returned by its block into Ruby; a dynamic block value makes the compiled Haml attacker-controlled, enabling SSTI/RCE.

rules.name: ssti-ruby-liquid-template-parse
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Parse only fixed, literal Liquid templates and pass user input as the assigns hash to render; never call parse on request-derived strings.
rules.why: Liquid::Template.parse compiles its argument as a Liquid template; parsing an attacker-controlled string is SSTI (data disclosure, DoS, and RCE via exposed/unsafe drops or filters) rather than passing input as render data.

rules.name: ssti-ruby-mustache-render
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Pass a constant literal template as the first argument and put all user input in the data hash (second argument); never make the template string itself from request data.
rules.why: Mustache.render treats its first argument as the template body; when that source is dynamic/user-controlled it is SSTI (template-tag injection, context/method exposure) instead of the intended data-passing via the second argument.

rules.name: ssti-ruby-rails-render-inline
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Render a named template (render template:/partial:) with a fixed literal path and pass user input via locals:/assigns; never build the inline: string from request data.
rules.why: render inline: (and render_to_string/render_to_body inline:) compiles the given string as an ERB template on the fly, so a dynamic value (params/variable/concatenation/interpolation) reaches the template compiler as source and yields SSTI/RCE.

rules.name: ssti-ruby-slim-engine-call
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Only pass literal/trusted template text to Slim::Engine#call and evaluate it against a scope that carries user data, never compile request-derived template strings.
rules.why: Slim::Engine#call compiles a Slim template string into Ruby source; a dynamic argument means attacker-controlled Slim (with #{...} and code) is compiled and later evaluated.

rules.name: ssti-ruby-slim-template-new
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Pass a fixed template filename to Slim::Template.new, or return only a constant literal from the block; deliver user data through the render() scope/locals instead.
rules.why: Slim::Template.new compiles the string returned by its block into Ruby; when that block yields dynamic/user input, Slim's Ruby interpolation (#{...}) and embedded code make it SSTI/RCE.

rules.name: ssti-ruby-tilt-new-block
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Point Tilt at a fixed template file, or return only a constant literal from the block, and pass user data through the render scope/locals rather than the block source.
rules.why: Tilt['erb'/'slim'/...] .new (and Tilt::*Template.new) compiles the string returned by its block as a template of the chosen engine; a dynamic block value hands attacker-controlled template source (often ERB/Slim/Haml, i.e. RCE) to the compiler.

rules.name: ssti-rythm-render
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Render fixed template files by name and pass user input only as named render arguments, never as the inline template string.
rules.why: Rythm.render/renderString treats its first argument as an inline Rythm template compiled to Java, so a dynamic template string permits @-directive/Java injection and RCE.

rules.name: ssti-scriban-template-parse
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Parse a constant literal template and supply user input as model members in the TemplateContext/ScriptObject, not inside the parsed string.
rules.why: Scriban's Template.Parse/ParseLiquid compiles its argument as a Scriban/Liquid template; dynamic source enables object-graph traversal and, via exposed .NET members, data disclosure or code execution.

rules.name: ssti-smartformat-format
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Use a constant literal format template and pass user input only in the args, never as the format string itself.
rules.why: SmartFormat's Smart.Format evaluates its first argument as a mini-template with reflection-based placeholders; a dynamic format string lets an attacker walk the object graph and disclose arbitrary member data (SSTI).

rules.name: ssti-smarty-string-eval-resource
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Use the file (default) resource with a fixed template path and pass user input through $smarty->assign(); never concatenate or interpolate request data into a 'string:' or 'eval:' resource.
rules.why: Smarty's string: and eval: resource prefixes make the remainder of the argument be compiled as Smarty template source, so concatenating or interpolating user input after the prefix yields template injection and PHP execution.

rules.name: ssti-spring-spel-parseexpression
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Parse only fixed literal expressions and feed user input as variables/root object via EvaluationContext; never concatenate user input into the parsed expression.
rules.why: ExpressionParser.parseExpression compiles its argument as a SpEL expression (often used as a template via TemplateParserContext); a dynamic expression string is arbitrary SpEL, e.g. T(java.lang.Runtime), and yields RCE.

rules.name: ssti-squirrelly-render-compile
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Pass a fixed template literal to render/compile and provide user input only in the data object; never construct the template from request input.
rules.why: Squirrelly's render/compile parse their first argument as a template whose helper and filter syntax can invoke JavaScript, so a user-controlled template string is a well-documented RCE vector.

rules.name: ssti-stubble-render
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Render a fixed literal template and pass user input as the data/view argument only, never as the template string.
rules.why: Stubble's renderer.Render takes its first argument as the Mustache template string; a user-controlled source lets an attacker inject template logic and read the view model (SSTI).

rules.name: ssti-swig-render-compile
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Use swig.renderFile with a fixed template path and pass user input as locals; never call render/compile on a template string built from user input.
rules.why: swig.render/compile parse their first argument as a Swig (Django/Jinja-style) template, and a dynamic source lets an attacker inject tags/filters that reach JavaScript execution on the server.

rules.name: ssti-thymeleaf-process-string-template
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Pass a fixed template name (resolved from the classpath) as the first argument and supply user input only via the Context variables.
rules.why: With a StringTemplateResolver, TemplateEngine.process treats its first argument as the template itself, and Thymeleaf's expression preprocessing (__${...}__) over dynamic template text yields SpEL execution and RCE.

rules.name: ssti-twig-array-loader
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Register only fixed, developer-authored template strings in the loader map and pass user input via the render() context; never as an array-loader value.
rules.why: Twig's in-memory string loader treats each array value as compilable template source, so a dynamic value registers attacker-controlled Twig source that is later executed.

rules.name: ssti-twig-create-template
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Load a fixed template file (or a constant string) and pass user input only through the render() context array; never build the template source from user data.
rules.why: Twig's createTemplate() compiles its string argument as a full Twig template, so a dynamic source lets an attacker inject Twig expressions that reach PHP and lead to RCE.

rules.name: ssti-twigjs-data-option
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Load templates via the `href`/`path` option or a constant `data` literal and pass user input only to .render(context); never set `data` from user input.
rules.why: Twig.js compiles the string given in the `data` option of twig({...}) as a Twig template, and a dynamic value there lets an attacker inject Twig expressions/filters that can leak data or escape the sandbox.

rules.name: ssti-velocity-evaluate
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Use Velocity.mergeTemplate with a named template file and pass user input only through the VelocityContext; never as the evaluate() template string.
rules.why: Velocity.evaluate(context, writer, logTag, instring) merges its final template argument as live VTL; a dynamic instring lets an attacker run VTL references that reach RCE via reflection.

rules.name: ssti-velocity-runtimeservices-parse
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Do not parse a StringReader built from user input; resolve templates by resource name and bind user data through the context.
rules.why: Velocity RuntimeServices.parse compiles the Reader it is given into a template AST; wrapping a dynamic string in a StringReader makes that user input executable VTL.

rules.name: ssti-velocityjs-render
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Render only fixed template strings and pass user input through the context object; never build the Velocity template from user input.
rules.why: velocityjs Velocity.render evaluates its first argument as a Velocity template whose $references and #directives can reach method calls on context objects, so a dynamic template source is server-side template injection.

rules.name: ssti-vue-compile
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Compile only static template literals and bind user input through component data/props; never pass a user-controlled string to Vue.compile.
rules.why: Vue.compile turns its string argument into a render function that evaluates the template's binding expressions, so a user-controlled template compiles attacker JavaScript expressions (client-side template injection / XSS).

rules.name: ssti-westwind-rendertemplate
rules.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) — user input is compiled as a template.
rules.remediation: Render a fixed literal Razor template and pass user input via the model argument; use RenderTemplateFromFile with a fixed path rather than building the source from input.
rules.why: Westwind.RazorHosting's RenderTemplate/RenderTemplateFromString compiles its first argument as Razor source, so a dynamic template string runs arbitrary C#/.NET code (RCE).

rules.name: static-iv-nonce
rules.message: The IV/nonce is a fixed/zero value rather than fresh random bytes.
rules.remediation: Generate a fresh random IV per message with crypto.getRandomValues()/randomBytes() and store it alongside the ciphertext.
rules.why: Reusing an IV with the same key in AES-GCM/CTR is catastrophic: it breaks confidentiality (XOR of two ciphertexts leaks plaintext) and, for GCM, lets an attacker forge the authentication tag.

rules.name: subprocess-run-script-from-upload-dir-py
rules.message: Write-then-execute — code is loaded or run from a user-controlled or writable path (potential RCE, CWE-829/95/98/94).
rules.remediation: Execute only interpreters/scripts from a fixed, non-writable directory; never pass an uploads/tmp path as the program or first argument, and validate any dynamic component against an allow-list.
rules.why: Spawning an interpreter or script whose path is built from an uploads/tmp/writable *directory variable* executes whatever an attacker managed to write there; the file-write primitive becomes code execution via the child process. The keyword set was tightened from bare 'upload'/'writable' (which fired on benign literal filenames like 'upload_report.py' and on 'uploads/' data args to rsync/tar) to variable-shaped tokens (upload*_dir/_path/_DIR/_PATH/_script, tmpdir, tmp_*, /tmp/, writable_dir), so a data-path argument in a quoted literal no longer floods.

rules.name: sw-cache-poisoning
rules.message: A synthetic Response is written into Cache Storage.
rules.remediation: Only cache Responses fetched from trusted origins; never store an attacker-controlled body.
rules.why: A Response stored in caches is served offline for the life of the service worker; if its body is attacker-influenced, one XSS persistently poisons the app's offline cache.

rules.name: time-as-session-token-py
rules.message: Predictable session/token identifier — a security id from a non-CSPRNG or observable source (CWE-330/340).
rules.remediation: Use the secrets module (secrets.token_urlsafe / secrets.token_hex) or os.urandom for security identifiers; a timestamp may be stored as expiry metadata but not used as the token value.
rules.why: Deriving a token or session id from time.time() / datetime.now() (even hashed) yields a value bounded by a small, guessable range of timestamps, so it can be brute-forced to hijack a session or forge a reset key.

rules.name: timestamp-as-session-token-js
rules.message: Predictable session/token identifier — a security id from a non-CSPRNG or observable source (CWE-330/340).
rules.remediation: Use crypto.randomUUID() or crypto.randomBytes(...) for the identifier; a timestamp may accompany a token as metadata (expiry) but must never be the token's value.
rules.why: Using Date.now() / new Date().getTime() as the value of a token or session id makes it guessable: timestamps are low-entropy and observable, so an attacker can brute-force the small window of millisecond values to recover a valid identifier.

rules.name: timing-secret-nonconst-eq
rules.message: Non-constant-time secret comparison — compare secrets with crypto.timingSafeEqual, not == / === (CWE-208).
rules.remediation: Compare secrets with a constant-time function: Node crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(a), Buffer.from(b)) (guard equal length first), Python hmac.compare_digest(a,b), PHP hash_equals($known,$user), Java MessageDigest.isEqual(a,b), Go subtle.ConstantTimeCompare(a,b)==1, Rails ActiveSupport::SecurityUtils.secure_compare(a,b). Never use ==/===/.equals on secrets.
rules.why: A secret (token, apiKey, password, hmac, signature, sig, mac, digest, csrf, otp) is compared with ==/===/!=/!== or String.equals, which short-circuits on the first differing byte. The time-to-answer leaks how many leading bytes matched, letting an attacker recover the secret byte-by-byte. The fix is a length-independent constant-time comparator.

rules.name: timing-unsafe-compare
rules.message: A secret (signature/HMAC/digest) is compared with ===/!== (not constant-time).
rules.remediation: Compare with crypto.timingSafeEqual (Node) or a constant-time equality that always scans both fully.
rules.why: === and a char-by-char loop return as soon as they differ, so the time taken leaks how many leading bytes matched — an attacker recovers the value byte by byte (timing side channel).

rules.name: tls-verification-off
rules.message: Certificate verification is turned off.
rules.remediation: Leave verification on; if a self-signed cert is needed, add that specific CA instead of disabling checks.
rules.why: With verification disabled, any machine on the path can present its own certificate and read or alter the traffic — TLS gives no protection.

rules.name: token-in-url-read
rules.message: An authentication token or secret is read from the URL query string.
rules.remediation: Send tokens in an Authorization header or an HttpOnly cookie, never in the query string.
rules.why: Tokens in the URL leak through browser history, the Referer header, and server/proxy access logs, so the credential is exposed far beyond the intended request.

rules.name: uniqid-rand-time-as-token-php
rules.message: Predictable session/token identifier — a security id from a non-CSPRNG or observable source (CWE-330/340).
rules.remediation: Use random_bytes()/bin2hex(random_bytes(32)) or random_int() (CSPRNG) for security tokens; never uniqid, rand, mt_rand, or time().
rules.why: PHP uniqid() is derived from the current microtime, and rand()/mt_rand() are non-cryptographic PRNGs; tokens built from them (often wrapped in md5/sha1) are predictable and enumerable, enabling session or reset-token forgery.

rules.name: unserialize-php
rules.message: unserialize() on untrusted data can be exploited.
rules.remediation: Use json_decode() for data, or pass allowed_classes: false.
rules.why: Object-injection gadgets let a crafted string trigger code paths during deserialisation.

rules.name: uuid-v1-time-based-token-js
rules.message: Predictable session/token identifier — a security id from a non-CSPRNG or observable source (CWE-330/340).
rules.remediation: Use a random UUID (uuid v4 / crypto.randomUUID()) or crypto.randomBytes for security identifiers, not the time-based uuid v1.
rules.why: UUID v1 encodes a timestamp plus the host MAC address, so it is largely predictable and enumerable; using it as a session id, reset token, or API key lets an attacker guess adjacent values.

rules.name: vue-svelte-html
rules.message: This renders a value as raw HTML.
rules.remediation: Bind text instead, or sanitise the HTML before rendering it.
rules.why: Vue's v-html and Svelte's {@html} both skip escaping, so any markup in the value becomes live elements.

rules.name: vuln-cve-2025-24893
rules.message: Direct output or evaluation of user-controlled template variable via response.writer.print or Velocity.evaluate can lead to remote code execution.
rules.why: Outputting or evaluating unescaped dynamic variables in Velocity or server template macros allows attackers to inject arbitrary template or Groovy expressions executed on the server.
rules.remediation: Use safe output macros such as

rules.name: vuln-cve-2025-32432
rules.message: Unvalidated request body parameter from getRequiredBodyParam used as transform/class handle allows object injection and remote code execution.
rules.why: In Yii2 and Craft CMS controllers, getRequiredBodyParam can return an attacker-controlled array (such as a __class definition) when not checked with is_string(), leading to arbitrary object instantiation and RCE.
rules.remediation: Validate that the returned parameter is a string using is_string() before passing it to transform or object creation routines.

rules.name: vuln-cve-2025-3248
rules.message: Unauthenticated code validation endpoint accepts arbitrary Python AST/code payloads without an authentication dependency, enabling remote code execution.
rules.why: Exposing a code validation handler that compiles and executes function defaults or decorators without requiring CurrentActiveUser or Depends() authentication allows unauthenticated RCE (CVE-2025-3248).
rules.remediation: Require authentication via Depends() or CurrentActiveUser on all code validation endpoints and never execute untrusted AST definitions.

rules.name: vuln-cve-2026-39987
rules.message: Marimo terminal WebSocket endpoint lacks authentication, allowing pre-auth RCE.
rules.why: The `/terminal/ws` WebSocket endpoint in Marimo's `terminal.py` accepts connections and forks a PTY shell without validating user authentication, leading to unauthenticated remote code execution.
rules.remediation: Ensure all sensitive WebSocket endpoints, especially those providing shell access, enforce proper authentication using `validate_auth(websocket)` or similar mechanisms before accepting connections or performing privileged operations.

positive:

        return

    await websocket.accept()
